title: [MOR/C1.4] Implement zone-wide revocation SLA with quorum-signed frontier

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text: WHAT: Add revocation_freshness_sla_secs: u64 to ZoneCheckpoint. The zone checkpoint (which is quorum-signed) includes the revocation frontier (revocation_head_seq) and its timestamp. All nodes MUST verify: if current_time - checkpoint_time > revocation_freshness_sla_secs, the zone is in DEGRADED revocation state. Operations with RevocationFreshnessClass::Critical MUST abort in degraded state. WHY: F7 Systems found that the delay between revocation issuance and enforcement is not bounded by the system. Without an SLA, operators have no way to know if revocation is working or has silently stalled. The SLA makes revocation timing an auditable, measurable guarantee. The quorum signature prevents a single compromised node from claiming fresh revocation state. WHERE: (1) crates/fcp-core/src/checkpoint.rs or zone_keys.rs — add revocation_freshness_sla_secs to ZoneCheckpoint. (2) crates/fcp-core/src/revocation.rs — add RevocationSlaChecker that compares observed_head_seq against checkpoint. (3) crates/fcp-mesh — background monitor that checks SLA compliance and emits alerts. ACCEPTANCE: (1) ZoneCheckpoint carries revocation SLA. (2) RevocationSlaChecker trait with check_sla() method. (3) Alert emitted when SLA is breached. (4) Critical operations abort when SLA breached. (5) Tests: SLA within bounds passes, SLA breached triggers alert, Critical op aborts on breach, quorum signature on checkpoint verified. ESTIMATED EFFORT: 3-4 days. DEPENDS ON: C1.1 (seal pattern) and C1.3 (freshness class) — the SLA uses the freshness class to determine which operations must abort vs warn vs proceed.

title: [FCP3/P7.4] Retire fcp-core as a semantic junk drawer
description:
Background: fcp-core is currently too broad a bucket for long term V3 architecture. The final state should either leave it as a truly minimal shared primitives crate or eliminate the broad bucket role entirely.

Scope: retire fcp-core as a semantic junk drawer by removing or relocating the meanings that no longer belong there, but only after the earlier proof gates and transition deletions show that every moved meaning has a better owner and preserved behavior. Any residue that remains must be intentionally minimal and clearly justified as shared primitives rather than latent ownership blur. The work should leave behind a crate graph and import surface audit, targeted unit and integration coverage, and detailed migration artifacts that prove semantics moved to better owners without dropping user visible behavior or diagnostic fidelity.

Acceptance: the broad bucket pattern is removed, the repo crate graph reflects the owner map locked earlier in the migration, and the final state is backed by proof, tests, and audit artifacts rather than by wishful refactoring.

title: [fcp-e2e] Enable kill_on_drop for connector subprocess runner
description: crates/fcp-e2e/src/subprocess.rs claimed to avoid zombie leaks in Drop, but it only called Child::start_kill(). The underlying asupersync Child docs state start_kill/kill do not wait and still require wait() to reap. Switch the spawned command to kill_on_drop(true), remove the misleading manual Drop path, and add regression coverage that a dropped long-running runner no longer leaves its PID present.

title: [FCP3/P5.4] Run a two node pilot with failure drills and evidence capture
description:
Background: the architecture needs a narrow but real proof slice. A two node pilot for one request response family is the smallest credible demonstration that placement, leases, checkpoint handoff, and evidence backed explanation actually work together.

Scope: run a scripted pilot that exercises initial placement, failover, resume, duplicate executor prevention, and operator visible explanation for one connector family across two nodes. Require detailed event timelines, cross node logs, captured control plane evidence, and artifact bundles that make the failure drills reproducible rather than anecdotal.

title: FIX: SymbolResponseBuilder was_bounded false positive when symbols exactly equal limit

comments.author: Jeff Emanuel
comments.text:
Root cause: add_from_repair_engine() used `available_count >= max_response_symbols` to detect bounding, but `select_symbols()` already caps its return at `max_response_symbols`, making `available_count == max_response_symbols` trigger even when all available symbols were returned.

Fix: Moved was_bounded computation to `build()` where `total_available` (the true object store count) is known. Now `was_bounded = sent_count < remaining` using the actual counts rather than relying on the post-selection count from the engine.

All 508 mesh tests pass (425 unit + 81 integration + 2 doc). The previously-failing `meshnode_symbol_request_is_final_when_all_sent` now passes, and the existing `response_builder_marks_bounded_when_request_limit_hits` continues to pass.

title: fcp.linkedin: Professional Networking Platform Connector
description:
# fcp.linkedin - Professional Networking Platform Connector


## Goal
Provide an FCP2-compliant LinkedIn connector for controlled access to profile/company content and posting workflows under strict policy.

## External surface (NetworkConstraints)
Default deny.
- Network egress MUST be restricted per-operation via manifest `NetworkConstraints` (defined in the connector’s manifest/cap map bead if present).
- Allow only the configured service host(s); HTTPS-only where applicable; deny redirects by default.
- Bound timeouts + response sizes; treat all remote responses as untrusted input; never leak secrets/PII in logs or errors.

## Manifest archetypes (closed set)

- `operational`
- `streaming`

> Interaction patterns (non-archetype): Request/Response + (optional) Webhook/Streaming

## Overview
Comprehensive LinkedIn integration supporting professional profiles, connections, job search, company intelligence, and messaging for recruiting, networking, and business development workflows.

## Value Assessment
- **Value Score**: 72/100 (Tier 4)
- **Use Cases**: Job market intelligence, professional networking, recruiting automation, company research, lead generation
- **Strategic Value**: Access to the world's largest professional network with 900M+ members

## Archetype
**Request-Response**
- LinkedIn APIs are strictly request-response based
- No native streaming or webhook support
- Polling required for real-time-like updates

## API Access Tiers
LinkedIn has multiple API tiers with different access levels:

### Consumer API (Basic)
- Profile read (authenticated user only)
- Share content to user feed
- Limited company page access

### Marketing API (Requires Partnership)
- Ad campaign management
- Audience insights
- Conversion tracking
- Lead gen forms

### Sales Navigator API (Premium)
- Advanced people search
- Lead recommendations
- Account insights
- InMail automation

### Recruiter API (Enterprise)
- Candidate search
- Job posting management
- Applicant tracking integration
- Recruiter InMail

### LinkedIn Learning API
- Course catalog access
- Learning progress tracking
- Skill assessments

## Key Operations

### Profile Operations (Consumer API)
- `linkedin.profile.me` - Get authenticated user profile
- `linkedin.profile.get` - Get profile by URN (limited fields)
- `linkedin.profile.picture.get` - Get profile picture
- `linkedin.profile.email.get` - Get primary email (requires r_emailaddress)

### Connection Operations
- `linkedin.connections.list` - List first-degree connections
- `linkedin.connections.count` - Get connection count
- `linkedin.connections.mutual` - Get mutual connections with user

### Sharing Operations
- `linkedin.share.create` - Create share/post on feed
- `linkedin.share.delete` - Delete owned share
- `linkedin.ugc.create` - Create user-generated content
- `linkedin.ugc.get` - Get UGC post details
- `linkedin.media.upload` - Upload images/videos for posts
- `linkedin.reactions.get` - Get reactions on content
- `linkedin.comments.list` - List comments on post
- `linkedin.comments.create` - Comment on post

### Company Operations
- `linkedin.company.get` - Get company page by ID
- `linkedin.company.lookup` - Lookup by vanity name/domain
- `linkedin.company.posts.list` - Get company updates
- `linkedin.company.followers.count` - Follower statistics
- `linkedin.company.admin.posts.create` - Post as company (admin only)

### Job Operations (Jobs API)
- `linkedin.jobs.search` - Search job listings
- `linkedin.jobs.get` - Get job details by ID
- `linkedin.jobs.recommended` - Get recommended jobs for user
- `linkedin.jobs.saved.list` - List saved jobs
- `linkedin.jobs.saved.add/remove` - Manage saved jobs
- `linkedin.jobs.apply.start` - Initiate Easy Apply flow

### Job Posting Operations (Recruiter API)
- `linkedin.jobs.post.create` - Create job posting
- `linkedin.jobs.post.update` - Update job posting
- `linkedin.jobs.post.close` - Close job posting
- `linkedin.jobs.applicants.list` - List applicants

### Messaging Operations (Messaging API)
- `linkedin.messaging.conversations.list` - List conversations
- `linkedin.messaging.messages.list` - Get messages in conversation
- `linkedin.messaging.messages.send` - Send message
- `linkedin.messaging.inmail.send` - Send InMail (Premium)

### Search Operations (Sales Navigator/Recruiter)
- `linkedin.search.people` - Advanced people search
- `linkedin.search.companies` - Company search
- `linkedin.search.jobs` - Job search with filters
- `linkedin.search.content` - Content/post search

### Marketing Operations (Marketing API)
- `linkedin.ads.accounts.list` - List ad accounts
- `linkedin.ads.campaigns.list/create/update` - Campaign management
- `linkedin.ads.creatives.list/create` - Ad creative management
- `linkedin.ads.analytics.get` - Campaign analytics
- `linkedin.leads.forms.list` - List lead gen forms
- `linkedin.leads.submissions.list` - Get form submissions

## Authentication
- **OAuth 2.0 (3-legged)**: Primary authentication method
- **Scopes**:
  - `r_liteprofile` - Basic profile (deprecated)
  - `r_basicprofile` - Basic profile data
  - `r_emailaddress` - Primary email
  - `r_organization_admin` - Company page admin
  - `r_organization_social` - Company social features
  - `w_member_social` - Post on behalf of member
  - `w_organization_social` - Post as organization
  - `rw_ads` - Advertising APIs
  - `r_marketing_leadgen_automation` - Lead gen access
  - `rw_organization_admin` - Full company admin
- **Token Refresh**: 60-day refresh token validity

## Rate Limiting
LinkedIn has aggressive rate limiting:
- **Daily call limit**: 100,000 calls/day per app
- **Per-member limit**: Varies by endpoint
- **Rate limit headers**: `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining`
- **Throttling**: 429 responses with retry-after
- **Rolling window**: Most limits use 24-hour rolling window

### Rate Limit Strategy
- Implement call budget tracking per day
- Per-user rate limit isolation
- Exponential backoff on 429
- Request queuing with priority
- Cache aggressively (profiles change infrequently)

## Zone Architecture

<!-- fcp2-single-zone-note -->
**FCP2 single-zone binding note:** A connector instance binds to exactly one `ZoneId` for its entire lifetime.
The *"zones"* described in this section are a **recommended deployment pattern** (run separate connector instances in separate zones with different capability grants/policies) and/or conceptual risk tiers.
The connector MUST NOT multiplex multiple zones internally.

```
Zone 0 (Public):     Public company pages, job listings
Zone 1 (Authorized): Own profile, connections list
Zone 2 (Private):    Messages, InMail content, saved jobs
Zone 3 (Sensitive):  OAuth tokens, ad account credentials
```

## API Quirks and Limitations
1. **URN-based identifiers**: All entities use `urn:li:*` format
2. **Projection fields**: Must explicitly request fields via projection parameter
3. **API versioning**: Uses dated versioning (e.g., `202401`)
4. **Strict TOS**: Many use cases require partnership approval
5. **Scraping prohibited**: Strict enforcement against unauthorized access
6. **No bulk operations**: Single-entity requests only
7. **Limited historical data**: Most APIs return recent data only

## Error Handling
- `401 Unauthorized`: Token expired or invalid
- `403 Forbidden`: Missing scope or TOS violation
- `429 Too Many Requests`: Rate limit exceeded
- `451 Unavailable For Legal Reasons`: Regional restrictions

## Dependencies
- `fcp-core`: Base connector traits, zone management
- `fcp-oauth`: OAuth 2.0 flow handling
- `fcp-ratelimit`: Daily/per-user rate limiting
- `fcp-telemetry`: API call metrics and monitoring

## Integration Considerations
- LinkedIn API access requires app review for most scopes
- Marketing/Sales Navigator APIs need partnership agreements
- Consider implementing profile caching layer
- URN resolution/mapping utilities needed
- Support both v1 and v2 API formats

## Implementation Priority
1. OAuth flow with proper scope management
2. Profile operations (me, basic get)
3. Sharing/posting operations
4. Company information retrieval
5. Job search and listings
6. Messaging (requires additional approval)
7. Marketing APIs (partnership dependent)

## Compliance Notes
- GDPR data export support required
- User consent for data access must be clear
- Respect user privacy settings
- LinkedIn Professional Community Guidelines apply

## Acceptance Criteria
- The functionality described in this bead is implemented with typed schemas + validation (no unstructured “stringly” interfaces).
- Errors map to the FCP error taxonomy with correct retry semantics and no secret/PII leakage.
- Mock-only unit/integration tests cover success paths and common failures and emit structured JSON logs per `flywheel_connectors-1n78.35`.

Automate provisioning and configuration with minimal human steps.

This bead owns:
- auth setup (OAuth / API keys / webhook secrets) via `CredentialObject`/`CredentialId` (egress proxy injection preferred)
- endpoint configuration
- `fcp doctor` readiness checks
- deterministic, mockable provisioning flows

## FCP2 requirements
- Secrets never touch disk.
- Provisioning is deterministic and testable.
- Error messages are actionable and do not leak secrets/PII.

## Acceptance Criteria
- No real external calls in unit tests.
- Provisioning emits structured logs per `flywheel_connectors-1n78.35`.

title: fcp.postgresql: PostgreSQL Database Connector
description:
# fcp.postgresql - PostgreSQL Database Connector


## Goal
Provide an FCP2-compliant PostgreSQL connector for safe SQL query/transaction execution and optional LISTEN/NOTIFY streaming.

## External surface (NetworkConstraints)
Default deny.
- Network egress MUST be restricted per-operation via manifest `NetworkConstraints` (defined in the connector’s manifest/cap map bead if present).
- Allow only the configured service host(s); HTTPS-only where applicable; deny redirects by default.
- Bound timeouts + response sizes; treat all remote responses as untrusted input; never leak secrets/PII in logs or errors.
- For DB connectors, constrain raw TCP connects to explicit host:port (or unix socket path) only; deny private ranges unless explicitly allowed by policy.

## Overview
PostgreSQL database connector for SQL queries, transactions, and connection pooling.

## Manifest archetypes (closed set)
- `storage`
- `operational`
- `streaming`

> Interaction patterns (non-archetype): Database access (SQL) + (optional) LISTEN/NOTIFY streaming

## Key Operations

### Query Operations
- `pg.query` - Execute parameterized SQL query
- `pg.execute` - Execute non-returning statement
- `pg.batch` - Execute multiple statements
- `pg.prepared` - Execute prepared statement
- `pg.explain` - Explain query plan

### Transaction Operations
- `pg.transaction.begin` - Start transaction
- `pg.transaction.commit` - Commit transaction
- `pg.transaction.rollback` - Rollback transaction
- `pg.transaction.savepoint` - Create savepoint
- Isolation levels: READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE

### Schema Operations
- `pg.schema.tables` - List tables
- `pg.schema.columns` - Get column info
- `pg.schema.indexes` - List indexes
- `pg.schema.constraints` - Get constraints

### Advanced Features
- COPY protocol for bulk load/unload
- LISTEN/NOTIFY for event handling
- Row streaming for large results
- JSON/JSONB operations
- Full-text search support
- PostGIS spatial queries

### Connection Pool
- Configurable pool size
- Connection health checks
- Statement timeout
- Query logging

## Authentication
- Password authentication
- SSL/TLS connections
- Certificate authentication
- AWS IAM (RDS)
- Cloud SQL IAM (GCP)

## Providers Supported
- PostgreSQL (self-hosted)
- AWS RDS/Aurora
- Google Cloud SQL
- Azure Database
- Supabase
- Neon
- CockroachDB (compatible)

## Zone Architecture

<!-- fcp2-single-zone-note -->
**FCP2 single-zone binding note:** A connector instance binds to exactly one `ZoneId` for its entire lifetime.
The *"zones"* described in this section are a **recommended deployment pattern** (run separate connector instances in separate zones with different capability grants/policies) and/or conceptual risk tiers.
The connector MUST NOT multiplex multiple zones internally.

\`\`\`
Zone 0 (Public):     Schema metadata
Zone 1 (Authorized): Read queries
Zone 2 (Private):    Write operations
Zone 3 (Sensitive):  DDL, admin operations
\`\`\`

## Security
- Parameterized queries (no SQL injection)
- Query whitelisting option
- Statement timeout enforcement
- Connection limit enforcement

## Dependencies
- fcp-core, fcp-config, fcp-testkit, fcp-telemetry

## Acceptance Criteria
- The functionality described in this bead is implemented with typed schemas + validation (no unstructured “stringly” interfaces).
- Errors map to the FCP error taxonomy with correct retry semantics and no secret/PII leakage.
- Mock-only unit/integration tests cover success paths and common failures and emit structured JSON logs per `flywheel_connectors-1n78.35`.

- Optional CLI warning in `fcp new --check` and `fcp manifest fix`.

- Unit tests with bad capability IDs (contains `.com`, `:443`, etc.).

title: [FWC] Standalone flywheel connectors CLI (agent-first, toon-default, all connectors)
description:
# [FWC] Standalone flywheel connectors CLI (agent-first, toon-default, all connectors)

## Goal
Design and deliver a standalone binary CLI named `fwc` (`flywheel connectors`) that becomes the dedicated operator and agent surface for connector work in this repository.

`fwc` must:
- expose the operations of every connector in this workspace
- expose connector management flows (discover, install/verify where appropriate, enable/disable, configure, start/stop/restart, status)
- default to token-efficient TOON output using `/dp/toon_rust`
- fully support JSON and machine-readable flows without ambiguity
- present a command system and help surface that is extremely intuitive for agents, not just humans reading a terminal manually

## Why this deserves its own binary
The existing `fcp` CLI is broad platform tooling. `fwc` should be the focused connector console: one place where agents can discover what connectors exist, what each connector can do, how to configure them safely, and how to invoke them without memorizing inconsistent per-connector details.

A dedicated binary matters because it lets us optimize for:
- connector-centric information architecture
- aggressive token-efficiency defaults
- progressive disclosure instead of wall-of-schema output
- connector-specific examples and next-step suggestions
- a stable mental model for agents operating across dozens of providers

## Core design principles
1. **Host/introspection as source of truth**. `fwc` must not become a parallel metadata silo with hand-maintained fake command tables.
2. **TOON by default, JSON always available**. Human/agent efficiency is the default; structured interoperability is never sacrificed.
3. **Progressive disclosure**. Default output is concise; deeper detail appears only when requested by subcommands or flags.
4. **Schema-driven extensibility**. Adding a new connector should mainly mean improving its manifest/introspection/config schema, not hardcoding bespoke CLI logic.
5. **Safety clarity**. Dangerous operations, approvals, lifecycle changes, and config writes must be explicit, auditable, and easy to simulate before execution.
6. **No connector left behind**. The CLI must work across the full connector inventory in this repo, not only the highest-profile services.

## Expected command families
- Discovery/search/help: list connectors, inspect one connector, inspect one operation, search by capability/category/risk.
- Lifecycle: install/verify/update/pin/unpin/enable/disable/start/stop/restart/status.
- Configuration: schema/get/set/unset/import/export/edit/doctor.
- Execution: invoke/simulate/batch/stream/logs/explain.
- UX support: completions, examples, short/long help, format control, output depth control.

## Non-goals
- Do not hand-maintain thousands of connector-specific subcommands in source when schemas can drive them.
- Do not duplicate existing `fcp` features just for branding; reuse or wrap host/platform surfaces where sensible.
- Do not privilege pretty output over determinism, machine readability, or token efficiency.

## Acceptance criteria
- There is a complete bead graph covering product definition, host/admin surfaces, connector readiness work, CLI implementation, tests, benchmarks, and docs.
- The graph is self-contained enough that future implementation sessions do not need to revisit this prose for intent.
notes: Sixth-pass plan-space review found one remaining ergonomic gap substantial enough to deserve its own bead: approval-backed work needed a first-class blocked or resumable queue surface instead of living only inside preflight and safety prose. This pass added an explicit history bead for pending approvals, blocked actions, expiry or supersession, and resume or abandon guidance, then wired that surface into snapshot coverage, host-backed invoke integration, operator and agent E2E playbooks, confusion-corpus cases, and debugging docs. It also tightened two workflow foundations that had still been slightly too implicit: the macro catalog now explicitly includes auth bootstrap or repair or profile-switch job families, and cross-connector pipeline capsules now depend directly on durable result handles plus projection surfaces rather than only the invoke parent umbrella. The bar remains unchanged: granular unit or snapshot tests, host-backed integration, and detailed E2E scripts with structured logs, receipts, and replayable evidence are mandatory.

title: [FWC] UX contract, command taxonomy, and progressive disclosure model
description:
# [FWC] UX contract, command taxonomy, and progressive disclosure model

## Goal
Define the canonical interaction model for `fwc` before implementation so every later bead has a stable target for naming, help text, examples, and default output depth.

## Why this exists
A CLI that exposes dozens of connectors and hundreds of operations can easily become unusable if we let naming drift, bury the dangerous operations, or print giant schema blobs for basic discovery. We need a deliberate contract first.

## Scope
- Define top-level nouns/verbs and their semantic boundaries.
- Decide what belongs at top level versus nested subcommands versus generated aliases.
- Define the progressive disclosure ladder for agent interactions.
- Define global flags that every command should honor consistently.
- Define the rules for examples, suggestions, and short-vs-long help.

## Design questions this bead must settle
- Should the top-level model be `fwc connector ...`, `fwc <connector> ...`, or a hybrid with generated aliases?
- How do we expose operation schemas without drowning the default help path?
- What is the minimum information every list/show/help command returns by default?
- How do we encode risky/destructive operations so agents cannot miss the danger level?

## Deliverables
- A written command taxonomy with canonical verbs and nouns.
- A progressive disclosure spec, e.g.:
  - `fwc list` -> minimal inventory summary
  - `fwc show <connector>` -> expanded connector summary
  - `fwc op show <connector> <operation>` -> operation details
  - `fwc ... --schema` / `--examples` / `--verbose` -> explicit deep detail
- Rules for short help, long help, examples, and next-step suggestions.
- Rules for sorting and grouping output so token cost stays low.

## Must-have UX properties
- Commands should be guessable from connector/operator intent.
- Help output should suggest the next 1-3 most likely commands, not generic prose.
- Dangerous operations should be visible through names, badges, and dry-run/explain affordances.
- Default output should be compact enough to paste into an agent conversation without wasting tokens.

## Acceptance criteria
- The taxonomy is concrete enough for implementation and testing.
- Global behavior is specified so all command families feel consistent.
- The progressive disclosure rules clearly separate default, expanded, and schema-level outputs.

title: [FWC] Invoke/simulate/batch/stream/logs/explain commands with approval-aware execution UX
description:
# [FWC] Invoke/simulate/batch/stream/logs/explain commands with approval-aware execution UX

## Goal
Expose actual connector operations through `fwc` in a way that is agent-intuitive, schema-guided, and safe by default.

## Scope
- `fwc invoke <connector> <operation>` with input from args/stdin/file
- `fwc simulate` / dry-run and explain-before-execute flows
- batch/multi-invoke support where host/runtime allows it
- streaming/event/log-tail surfaces for connectors that support them
- explain/decision-receipt integration for denials or risky actions

## Why this is separate from discovery
Discovery tells agents what exists. This bead defines how they actually execute operations consistently across every connector family.

## Required behaviors
- Accept structured input without forcing giant inline JSON blobs every time.
- Surface output in TOON by default but preserve full JSON fidelity.
- Highlight required capabilities, approvals, and risk before execution.
- Distinguish read-only, stateful, external, and destructive operations in both UX and exit semantics.
- Support simulation/explain as a first-class step, not an afterthought.

## Deliverables
- Invocation command implementations and input-decoding rules.
- Approval-aware explain/simulate flow design.
- Streaming/log-tail UX contract for event-capable connectors.
- Tests for representative safe, risky, denied, and streaming operations.

## Acceptance criteria
- Agents can reliably run the same mental workflow across all connectors: discover -> inspect -> simulate/explain -> invoke -> inspect result/logs.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Invoke/simulate/batch/stream/log surfaces are built on real host execution, real auth/approval enforcement, honest simulate semantics, and real inventory/tool routing.
2. The UX stays agent-intuitive while making denial, unsupported, unavailable, and partial-success states explicit.
3. Unit/snapshot, host integration, and transcript-style E2E verification with detailed logging are required across safe, risky, denied, unsupported, and streaming cases.
notes: This parent invoke branch now explicitly includes reusable payload ergonomics, not only one-shot execution. The advanced path should remain: discover or inspect -> author or derive -> template or scaffold if reusable -> explain or simulate -> invoke -> inspect, with the reusable-template bead treated as a first-class user productivity feature rather than an optional add-on.

title: [FWC] Invoke UX: universal input acquisition and payload authoring
description:
# [FWC] Invoke UX: universal input acquisition and payload authoring

## Goal
Let agents supply operation input in the most natural form for the job instead of forcing giant inline JSON blobs for every connector.

## Scope
- args, stdin, files, references, templates, and task-bound values as first-class input sources
- typed coercion and schema-guided payload construction for nested objects, arrays, enums, and unions
- compact previews that show what will actually be sent without dumping every field every time
- error handling for ambiguous input sources, partial payloads, and schema mismatches

## Deliverables
- input-source and payload-authoring contract for `invoke`, `simulate`, and related commands
- examples covering common agent patterns from tiny reads to complex write payloads

## Acceptance criteria
- agents can author request payloads quickly without sacrificing correctness
- the same input rules work consistently across discovery-driven workflows, direct invokes, and workflow capsules
acceptance_criteria:
1. Input acquisition and payload authoring support real schema-driven authoring, file and stdin sources, templates, and explicit conflict handling across input modes.

# [FWC] Invoke UX: explain, simulate, and approval-aware preflight

## Goal
Make the safe path the obvious path by turning explain and simulate into a polished preflight experience instead of a hidden side branch.

## Scope
- risk summaries, required capabilities, approval boundaries, and likely side effects before execution
- simulation output that is honest about what was checked versus what remains hypothetical
- approval token or confirmation handoff points with deterministic next steps
- denial and ambiguity paths that immediately surface the smallest useful follow-up command

## Deliverables
- preflight UX contract shared by invoke, workflow macros, and task execution
- examples for read-only, risky, denied, and partially specified operations

## Acceptance criteria
- a caller can understand whether an operation is safe, blocked, or ready before pressing execute
- explain and simulate become default muscle memory for risky work rather than afterthoughts
acceptance_criteria:
1. Explain and preflight or simulate surfaces are backed by real host semantics and remain explicit about approvals, unsupported simulate behavior, and bounded receipts.
2. Preview output never implies that execution has already happened, and denial reasons remain machine-readable.
3. Integration and transcript-style E2E verification with detailed logging are required for allow, deny, and unsupported cases.
notes: Make approval handling explicitly resumable, not just a yes-or-no preflight. Cover pending-approval artifacts, expiry, supersession, inspect/wait/resume/abandon flows, and deterministic receipts for approved, denied, expired, or changed-context executions. Fast tests should lock down the preflight envelope, and host integration plus E2E should prove an agent can recover from a stale or expired approval request without guessing.

# [FWC] Invoke UX: reusable input templates, schema-seeded drafts, and parameterized payload scaffolds

Make repeated complex operations cheap and reliable by letting agents save, inspect, and reapply validated payload drafts instead of rebuilding similar request bodies from scratch every time.

## Scope
- named reusable templates per connector and operation, with clear ownership and visibility
- draft generation from schema examples, partially authored payloads, and validated example inputs
- parameter placeholders for values that must vary per run, with preview and validation before execution
- diff and render flows that show exactly what a template or scaffold will materialize into before it is used

## Acceptance criteria
- agents can turn recurring operation shapes into explicit reusable assets instead of copying ad hoc JSON fragments between sessions
- templates remain inspectable, validation-aware, and safe enough that reuse reduces mistakes rather than hiding them
acceptance_criteria:
1. Reusable input templates and schema-seeded drafts accelerate authoring without hiding required values, approvals, or connector-specific constraints.
2. Parameterized scaffolds remain inspectable and safe to reuse across sessions without smuggling stale secrets or unsupported defaults.
3. Snapshot, integration, and transcript-style verification with detailed logging are required for create, fill, reuse, and repair flows.
notes: This should cover save/list/show/render/diff/apply/export/import flows for named templates, plus schema-example seeding and promotion of validated ad hoc payloads into reusable scaffolds. Templates should carry stable fingerprints and provenance, support safe handoff across agents or workspaces, remain redaction-safe, and never smuggle live secrets. title: [FWC] Generated connector aliases, shell completion, and did-you-mean suggestions

# [FWC] Generated connector aliases, shell completion, and did-you-mean suggestions

## Goal
Add the quality-of-life layer that makes `fwc` feel amazing in day-to-day use without turning the codebase into a hand-maintained maze of bespoke connector commands.

## Scope
- Generated alias surfaces where they materially improve ergonomics (for example, short connector-prefixed entrypoints derived from metadata).
- Shell completion for connectors, operations, flags, and generated aliases.
- “Did you mean …” suggestions for unknown connectors, operations, or similar config keys.
- Context-sensitive next-step suggestions after discovery and failure flows.

## Design constraint
Any alias/completion system must be driven by canonical host/connector metadata, not a second parallel registry of names.

## Deliverables
- Alias-generation rules and collision policy.
- Completion generation and test strategy.
- Suggestion engine for common operator/agent mistakes.
- UX examples demonstrating how this layer reduces token use and command retries.

## Acceptance criteria
- Ergonomic sugar improves usability without creating metadata drift.
- Unknown-command recovery is helpful enough that agents need fewer corrective turns.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Alias/completion/suggestion behavior is derived from canonical live metadata and explicit unknown-state handling, never from a second parallel registry.
2. The layer improves user efficiency without inventing unsupported operations or misleading connector/operation names.
3. Unit/snapshot tests and transcript-style recovery examples are required so suggestion quality and truthfulness regressions are caught early.
notes: Generated aliases/completions/suggestions should cover the full modern `fwc` surface, including `plan`, `do`, and `task` workflows, not just primitive connector commands. They should use the readiness matrix, workflow hints, and recovery metadata as sources of truth, and they should be validated with shell-transcript-style tests so we can see exactly what an agent or operator would have been offered at the terminal.

# [FWC] Connector metadata gap audit and readiness matrix across the full connector inventory

## Goal
Audit every connector crate in this repository against the `fwc` readiness contract and produce a deterministic matrix of what is ready, what is partially ready, and what is missing.

## Why this exists
The repo contains a very large and uneven connector surface. Before we promise that `fwc` exposes every connector cleanly, we need an explicit inventory of metadata gaps instead of relying on intuition.

## Scope
- Enumerate every connector crate currently in `connectors/`.
- Check discovery/introspection/config/doctor/lifecycle metadata quality against the readiness contract.
- Classify each connector by readiness state and gap category.
- Group remediation work into implementation cohorts so later beads are tractable.

## Output this bead must produce
A matrix or machine-readable inventory that, for each connector, records at minimum:
- connector id / crate path / cohort
- operation metadata completeness
- config schema completeness
- examples/agent hints presence
- health/doctor coverage
- event/stream support metadata
- known blockers that prevent `fwc` parity

## Acceptance criteria
- Every connector in the workspace appears in the matrix.
- Later cohort beads can reference the matrix directly without rediscovering scope.
- The gap categories are precise enough to drive implementation, not just documentation.
notes: The readiness matrix should explicitly include validation-oriented columns, not only metadata gaps. For each connector record: representative scenario IDs, identifier-discovery quality, redaction class, approval/risk class, expected structured-log tags, and which unit/integration/e2e fixtures are supposed to cover it. This keeps the later cohort beads, integration harness, and e2e suite aligned around the same inventory instead of drifting into separate spreadsheets in people’s heads.

- `semanticscholar`, `arxiv`, `annas-archive`, `spotify`, `metabase`, `retool`, `posthog`, `mixpanel`, `amplitude`, `segment`
- `stripe`, `salesforce`, `hubspot`, `plaid`, `1password`, `bitwarden`
- `google-calendar` is intentionally excluded because it lives in the workspace cohort above

## What parity means here
- schemas/examples that clarify resource naming and filtering patterns
- config surfaces that explain credentials, tenancy, and environment URLs precisely
- operation metadata that distinguishes safe queries from mutations, deletes, or billing-sensitive actions
- enough help context that agents can discover collections/tables/indexes/projects before invoking write paths

## Special considerations
This cohort is heterogeneous. The main risk is papering over connector-specific constraints with overly generic help. The readiness work should normalize metadata without erasing the important differences between databases, analytics APIs, archives, and business systems.

## Acceptance criteria
- The cohort is explicitly covered by the readiness matrix and has a concrete parity path for `fwc`.
- Long-tail connectors do not remain permanently “second class” because the CLI only optimized for chat/social services.
notes: This cohort bead is not complete until it has representative automated coverage, not just metadata cleanup. Require at minimum: (1) focused unit/snapshot tests for the cohort’s sharpest schema/help/recovery cases, (2) at least one host-backed integration scenario covering the cohort’s most representative high-value workflow, and (3) at least one end-to-end script with structured logs for the cohort’s hardest or most failure-prone user journey. The output should feed back into the readiness matrix rather than living as isolated one-off test code.

title: [FWC] Snapshot/unit tests for help, TOON/JSON rendering, examples, and error UX
description:
# [FWC] Snapshot/unit tests for help, TOON/JSON rendering, examples, and error UX

## Goal
Lock down the token-efficient and agent-ergonomic contract of `fwc` with fast tests that catch regressions before integration work even runs.

## Scope
- command parsing and global flag behavior
- short help vs long help vs schema/example expansion
- TOON default rendering and JSON fallback behavior
- stable exit-code/error payload mapping
- next-step suggestions and did-you-mean recovery text

## Why this matters
The biggest value of `fwc` is not only that it works, but that it stays concise, predictable, and readable for agents. Snapshot and unit tests are the cheapest way to keep that contract intact.

## Deliverables
- snapshot fixtures for representative help/output/error surfaces
- unit tests for format selection, progressive disclosure, and suggestion logic
- golden outputs for representative connectors/operations in both TOON and JSON modes

## Acceptance criteria
- The UX/output contract is protected by fast tests with deterministic fixtures.
- Regressions in token-heavy or noisy output are easy to spot in review.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Fast tests cover truthful live-vs-offline wording, explicit unknown/unsupported rendering, auth-related refusal messaging, and stable TOON/JSON envelopes in addition to general UX concerns.
2. Snapshot fixtures and unit logs are detailed enough to diagnose semantic regressions without running host/E2E suites.
3. This bead remains fast by depending on the unit/snapshot truthfulness contract, not on transcript-E2E logging work.
notes: This bead should become the fast-contract suite for the entire agent UX, not only primitive command rendering. Include golden cases for `plan/do/explain`, `task` projections, `task resolve/ask`, recovery envelopes, token-count assertions, redaction invariants, and command-suggestion stability. Failure output should be artifact-friendly and diff-friendly so reviewers can see exactly which field got noisier or less helpful.

- ambiguity handling stays consistent across command families instead of drifting ad hoc
acceptance_criteria:

notes: Include auth bootstrap and auth-repair ambiguity cases (missing credential, expired token, wrong scope/profile, revoked handle), history lookup misses, replay preflight denials, and reversal-unsupported responses. acceptance_criteria:

notes: Extend invariants to auth-state, approval, and history bundles: secret-versus-reference redaction, bounded verbosity for receipt or replay or pending-approval summaries, stable exit or status codes for auth-repair flows, approval wait or expiry or denial states, replay preflight denials, and irreversible-action guidance. title: [FWC] Output/rendering contract with toon_rust default, JSON fallback, and stable exit semantics
description:
# [FWC] Output/rendering contract with toon_rust default, JSON fallback, and stable exit semantics

## Goal
Define exactly how `fwc` renders output and errors so it is token-efficient by default, deterministic under test, and still robust for machine workflows.

## Background
`/dp/toon_rust` already provides a native Rust path for token-efficient serialization via TOON, including deterministic output and guidance for format selection. `fwc` should adopt that work instead of inventing another lightweight text format.

## Scope
- Use `/dp/toon_rust` as the default response renderer for human/agent-facing output.
- Provide first-class JSON output for scripts, automation, and schema-heavy inspection.
- Decide when TOON is always safe, when JSON is required, and when the CLI can auto-fallback.
- Define stable exit codes and structured error payloads.

## Required behaviors
- Global format control: `--format toon|json|jsonl` plus ergonomic aliases like `--json`.
- Environment/config override support so agents can set a preferred format once.
- Stable key ordering and deterministic serialization in both TOON and JSON outputs.
- Error payloads that preserve FCP reason codes, approval requirements, and actionable next steps.
- Optional token stats output so we can quantify savings and guard regressions.

## Specific TOON integration expectations
- Prefer `toon_rust::encode` on canonical `serde_json::Value` outputs.
- Reuse the `toon_rust` integration-guide pattern for format selection and token estimation.
- Define safe defaults for delimiter, indentation, and key folding that preserve readability.
- Ensure schemas/examples that become unreadable in TOON can still be force-rendered as JSON.

## Deliverables
- Output format spec with examples for discovery, show, config, invoke, and error cases.
- Exit code map for success, validation failure, auth/policy denial, connector error, transport error, and internal error.
- Testable rules for when `fwc` emits TOON vs JSON vs JSONL.
- A benchmarkable definition of “token-efficient by default.”

## Acceptance criteria
- Every command family has a deterministic default render path.
- JSON is never a second-class citizen; it remains complete and stable.
- Error semantics are explicit enough to drive both snapshot tests and agent decision-making.
close_reason: Completed deterministic FWC output contract, exit metadata, and token stats validation

comments.author: Jeff Emanuel

Implementation covers all acceptance criteria: (1) Global format control via --format toon|json|jsonl + --json shortcut, (2) FWC_FORMAT env var for persistent override, (3) deterministic output for all formats, (4) structured error payloads with FCP reason codes/did_you_mean/examples/next_actions, (5) stable exit codes (Success=0, Internal=1, Parse=2, Unknown=3, Ambiguous=4, Validation=5, PolicyDenied=6, Connector=7, Transport=8), (6) TOON integration via toon_rust::encode, (7) new --token-stats flag for byte-count comparison, (8) 33 render tests covering determinism, round-trips, edge cases, error payloads, and token stats. 222 total fwc tests pass, clippy clean. — SunnyMoose

title: [FWC] End-to-end scenario suite plus token-budget and performance regression harness
description:
# [FWC] End-to-end scenario suite plus token-budget and performance regression harness

## Goal
Prove that `fwc` works as an amazing day-to-day connector console under realistic workflows and remains token-efficient enough to justify its dedicated UX.

## Scope
- end-to-end scenarios covering discover -> inspect -> configure -> simulate -> invoke -> inspect/logs
- lifecycle-heavy scenarios (enable/disable/start/stop/update/pin where supported)
- approval/denial scenarios with explain output
- TOON-vs-JSON token-budget comparisons for representative command outputs
- basic latency/throughput benchmarks for high-frequency discovery and invoke surfaces

## Why this exists
The user asked for an agent-intuitive, token-efficient CLI. That promise needs an explicit regression harness, not vibes.

## Deliverables
- scenario matrix and runner for `fwc`
- token-budget measurement strategy using representative connector outputs
- performance baseline for discovery/help/rendering and selected invoke paths
- structured logs/artifacts suitable for later CI automation

## Acceptance criteria
- We can demonstrate both functional correctness and measurable token-efficiency wins.
- Regressions in verbosity, latency, or output determinism become visible early.
acceptance_criteria:
1. E2E scenarios cover real operator and agent flows with no fake runtime shortcuts, including artifact install/update, config mutation, preflight/simulate, invoke, history/replay, and denial/remediation paths.
2. Scenario scripts emit detailed redaction-safe logs, timestamps, receipts/correlation IDs, and replay artifacts suitable for regression triage.
3. Token-budget and performance checks are preserved without weakening the no-fakes runtime guarantee.
notes: The end-to-end suite must include real scripts with extremely legible logging and artifact bundles, not just assertions in code. Each scenario should emit a transcript, structured step logs, key receipts, TOON-vs-JSON token deltas, timing data, and a single-command replay path. Cover both primitive flows and the higher-level agent workflows (`plan/do/task/resolve/ask`) so we can prove the CLI is genuinely easier to operate, not merely feature-rich.

comments.author: RainyGate
comments.text: [Extreme-software-optimization uplift] Treat the benchmark gates as a profile-first optimization loop, not a handful of threshold snapshots. Require baseline artifact packs for representative scenarios with hyperfine-style latency runs, p50/p95/p99, peak RSS, and at least one CPU/allocation/syscall profile on the dominant paths. Any optimization that follows should name its baseline comparator, score the opportunity before implementation, preserve golden outputs plus ordering or tie-break invariants, and land one lever at a time with a rollback path so performance wins do not smuggle in behavior drift.

# [FWC] Documentation, migration guidance, and operator/agent playbooks

## Goal
Make `fwc` self-explanatory to future operators and agents without requiring them to reverse-engineer the implementation or read old planning artifacts.

## Scope
- binary-level README/usage docs for `fwc`
- migration guidance from existing `fcp connector` / related surfaces
- operator playbooks for discovery, lifecycle, config, and invoke workflows
- agent-oriented examples that demonstrate the progressive disclosure path and TOON-default usage

## Deliverables
- concise but complete docs for the new binary
- examples for common workflows and failure recovery
- explicit notes on when to prefer `fwc` vs more general platform CLIs
- references to the readiness contract and testing expectations

## Acceptance criteria
- A new agent can learn the intended `fwc` workflow from repo-local docs and examples.
- The documentation does not require the reader to consult the original planning conversation to understand the system intent.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Docs teach the live-vs-offline boundary, the no-fakes rule, the evidence/logging model, and the main remediation paths clearly enough for a future engineer or agent to operate without planning-history context.
2. Playbooks cover happy path, unsupported, denied, unavailable, and recovery cases, not only ideal flows.
3. Documentation references the unit, integration, and E2E evidence surfaces so readers can verify behavior, not just trust prose.
notes: Docs and playbooks should teach people how to use the validation evidence, not only how to use the CLI. Include a debugging section for reading scenario bundles, explain the log schema and replay workflow, show how to interpret recovery artifacts, and point future implementers at the readiness matrix, confusion corpus, and structured-log contract so they can extend the system without consulting the original planning conversation.

title: [FWC] Workflow macros and next-action guidance for common connector jobs
description:
# [FWC] Workflow macros and next-action guidance for common connector jobs

## Goal
Add explicit workflow-level command surfaces and response hints so agents can complete common multi-step connector tasks with fewer turns, fewer retries, and less guesswork.

## Why this exists
A great connector CLI should not only expose primitives. It should also guide the caller through the natural multi-step flows: discover -> inspect -> configure -> validate -> simulate -> invoke, or inspect -> disable -> verify -> restart -> confirm health. Smaller or tired agents do materially better when the interface offers high-confidence next steps instead of making them reconstruct every workflow from scratch.

## Scope
- define reusable next-action hints emitted by discovery, config, lifecycle, and invoke commands
- identify a minimal set of workflow macros or guided entrypoints that bundle common multi-step jobs without hiding important state
- support explain/preview-first UX for risky lifecycle and invoke paths
- ensure workflow surfaces remain token-efficient and do not devolve into giant narrative help blocks

## Candidate macro/guided flows
- discovery to runnable operation: `list` -> `show` -> `ops` -> `schema` -> `simulate`
- safe config change: `config schema` -> `config set` -> `config doctor` -> `status`
- lifecycle change: `status` -> `disable|enable|restart` -> `status`
- risky write: `show` -> `ops` -> `schema` -> `simulate` -> `invoke`

## Deliverables
- explicit workflow-hint contract (`next_actions`, `why_next`, maybe `suggested_command_lines`)
- design for task-oriented helper commands or macro flows where justified
- tests ensuring hints remain deterministic, concise, and useful under TOON and JSON output
- docs/playbooks showing how agents should compose the workflows

## Acceptance criteria
- a caller can move through common connector jobs with less trial-and-error
- next-step guidance is targeted and compact, not generic fluff
- macro/guided flows improve reliability without obscuring lifecycle/config/invoke state transitions
acceptance_criteria:
1. Workflow macros and guidance reduce retries while preserving truthful visibility into state, side effects, approval boundaries, and unsupported/offline-only cases.
2. Suggested next actions never imply that a live runtime action already occurred or is currently available when it is not.
3. Deterministic unit/transcript coverage and scenario logging are required so misleading guidance is caught early.
notes: This parent workflow branch now explicitly includes both transient working context and saved resumable context. Keep the distinction sharp: session context is the live scoped state for the current job; presets or bookmarks are the deliberate persisted handoff or resume mechanism; neither may become invisible ambient authority. Tests and docs should teach when to use each one.

comments.author: RainyGate
comments.text: PLAN-SPACE REFINEMENT: Workflow guidance is one of the highest-risk user surfaces because a wrong next step wastes turns and can hide state. This branch should not close without deterministic next-action transcript tests, confusion-corpus coverage for misleading or ambiguous guidance, and replayable scenario logs that prove macros, session mode, presets, and safety hints help the caller recover rather than drift. Preserve visibility of state transitions and approval boundaries while reducing guesswork.

## Scope

- approval propagation and boundary reporting when higher-level flows include risky steps
- explicit display of assumptions, pinned context, and unresolved ambiguity in workflow views
- refusal rules for cases where the workflow layer would otherwise hide too much risk or uncertainty

## Deliverables

- examples showing good and bad abstraction boundaries for agent-facing automation

## Acceptance criteria
- higher-level workflow power does not come at the cost of hidden state or surprise side effects
- future implementers have explicit guardrails for deciding when the workflow layer must stop and ask for clarity
acceptance_criteria:
1. Safety, visibility, and approval rules are enforced consistently across macro, session, and pipeline flows and remain explicit in both TOON and JSON outputs.
2. Guidance distinguishes previewable actions from executable actions and preserves receipt or audit visibility for state-changing steps.
3. Unit, integration, and transcript-style E2E verification with detailed logging are required for approval, denial, and blocked-workflow cases.
notes: Workflow safety must spell out how pending approvals propagate through macros, session context, and pipeline stages. Every guided flow should reveal the exact risky step, the active pinned context, the approval request or receipt identifiers, expiry conditions, and the command to resume or discard the flow. Include refusal rules when a workflow would otherwise mask a pending approval behind ambient state, plus confusion-corpus and E2E coverage for expired or superseded approvals.

# [FWC] Workflow UX: named context presets, bookmarks, and resumable workspace starters

## Goal

## Scope

- save, list, inspect, diff, activate, and clear flows for those presets
- resume-friendly handoff points that remain visible and explicit rather than becoming hidden ambient authority
- invalidation and freshness rules when a saved context references stale profiles, handles, or assumptions

## Acceptance criteria
- agents can resume a job in one deliberate step with the active context made obvious before any risky action happens
- bookmarks and presets improve handoff and long-running work without creating invisible state that surprises later callers
acceptance_criteria:
1. Presets, bookmarks, and workspace starters preserve useful context without smuggling stale credentials, secrets, or unsupported defaults into future sessions.
2. Named starters remain inspectable, editable, and explicit about what runtime state they assume.
3. Snapshot, integration, and transcript-style E2E verification with detailed logging are required for create, inspect, apply, and repair flows.
notes: Presets and bookmarks must be explicit, diffable, exportable, and safe to inspect before activation. Include import/export/share semantics, stable fingerprints, stale-context detection, profile or zone mismatch handling, and handoff-friendly summaries so one agent can leave a resumable workspace starter for another without hidden ambient authority. Cover with workflow snapshots, confusion-corpus cases, and E2E scenarios that log preset creation, activation, invalidation, portability, and resume paths.

title: [FWC] Intent recovery, forgiving aliases, and structured recovery hints for agent mistakes
description:
# [FWC] Intent recovery, forgiving aliases, and structured recovery hints for agent mistakes

## Goal
Make `fwc` behave like an agent-aware interface rather than a brittle human-only parser by detecting common mistaken command shapes, normalizing the safe ones automatically, and returning structured recovery payloads for the unsafe ones.

## Why this exists
The current plan covers aliases and suggestions, but that is not enough. Agents will still try obvious-but-wrong shapes such as `fwc connector list`, `fwc info github`, `fwc op show github issues.create`, or malformed config/invoke calls copied from older CLIs or inferred from English intent. The CLI should detect what the agent probably meant, make the right thing obvious, and only reject when auto-correction would be unsafe.

## Design principles imported from agent-friendly MCP design
- anticipate intent, not only literal syntax
- fail helpfully with typed, structured recovery data
- forgive by default for safe command-shape mistakes
- keep recovery output short, explicit, and immediately actionable

## Scope
- normalize safe legacy/common forms such as redundant `connector` prefixes and high-confidence verb aliases
- reject ambiguous or dangerous corrections with structured error payloads rather than plain clap text
- provide `did_you_mean`, `next_actions`, and short rationale fields on parse/validation errors
- assign stable exit codes for parse failure, unknown command, ambiguous correction, validation error, and runtime denial
- include explicit examples in error payloads so an agent can retry in one turn

## Examples this bead should cover
- `fwc connector list` -> normalize to `fwc list` and note the correction
- `fwc info github` -> normalize to `fwc show github`
- `fwc exmaples slack` -> reject with a suggestion like `examples`
- `fwc invoke github` -> reject with a structured explanation that an operation is missing and suggest `fwc ops github`
- `fwc config set github` with missing key/value -> reject with a repair path and example

## Deliverables
- intent-normalization layer before clap dispatch or equivalent recovery layer around clap parsing
- structured error envelope with machine-readable `type`, `message`, `recoverable`, `did_you_mean`, `examples`, and `next_actions`
- stable exit-code mapping for the full recovery/error surface
- tests covering safe auto-corrections, ambiguous inputs, typo recovery, and dangerous non-corrections

## Acceptance criteria
- obvious, low-risk mistakes are corrected automatically with a visible note
- ambiguous or risky corrections are never silently applied
- every failure teaches the caller what to do next in one compact response
- `fwc` parse/validation failures stop looking like generic CLI parser noise and start looking like an agent-ergonomic interface contract
notes: Treat the current normalization/recovery work as the first slice, not the full finish line. Remaining scope should explicitly cover recovery across `task` surfaces, lifecycle mutations, config revisions, mixed-format mistakes, stale workflow IDs, conflicting payload sources, unsafe auto-correction candidates, and ambiguous object references. The bead should also maintain the mistake taxonomy that powers the confusion corpus and specify what the smallest useful retry hint looks like for each failure class.

comments.author: Jeff Emanuel
comments.text: Implemented in e112729b. New recovery.rs module (1489 lines, 132 tests) with extended alias table (80+ aliases), typo correction table (80+ typos), safety classification (safe/ambiguous/dangerous), config+task subcommand aliases, dangerous shape detection, redundant prefix stripping, Levenshtein-based fuzzy matching. Enhanced normalize_args with 5-phase pipeline. 33 new integration tests in main.rs. Total fwc tests: 684 (up from 519). All clippy clean.

title: [FWC] Identifier discovery and disambiguation helpers across connector object models
description:
# [FWC] Identifier discovery and disambiguation helpers across connector object models

## Goal
Reduce one of the biggest practical failure modes in connector automation: agents knowing the action they want but not the exact project, workspace, channel, page, issue, document, table, or account identifier they need to supply.

## Why this exists
Many connectors are not hard because the final operation is conceptually difficult. They are hard because the agent lacks the exact IDs or scope handles needed to form a valid request. The CLI should explicitly help agents discover and narrow those handles instead of assuming the information is already known.

## Scope
- define command patterns for identifier/resource discovery before write operations
- standardize how connectors expose lookup/search/list-by-name metadata for IDs and object references
- design disambiguation output when multiple candidate resources match a human-ish name
- ensure identifier discovery output is compact enough for agent use and easy to feed into the next command

## Connectors most affected
This matters especially for productivity/workspace/business/data connectors such as Notion, Jira, Linear, Gmail, Google Calendar, Microsoft365, Airtable, Figma, Dropbox, Box, Salesforce, HubSpot, BigQuery, Snowflake, and similar APIs where name-to-id discovery is unavoidable.

## Deliverables
- identifier-discovery UX contract, likely as part of discovery/search/show flows or an explicit helper surface
- canonical disambiguation payload shape with candidate summaries and follow-up commands
- readiness requirements for connectors to expose name lookup / object listing metadata where appropriate
- tests for single match, multiple matches, no matches, and stale identifier scenarios

## Acceptance criteria
- agents are guided toward valid resource identifiers instead of failing deep inside invoke/config commands
- disambiguation output remains concise and points directly to the next command to run
- connector-specific object models remain visible enough that the CLI does not flatten away important distinctions
notes: Identifier discovery must do more than list candidate IDs. It should define evidence-backed ranking, freshness/staleness hints, concise disambiguation payloads, and direct handoff into `task bind`, `task resolve`, or the next primitive command. This bead should explicitly protect against the common agent failure mode where the name lookup seemed successful but the chosen identifier is stale, revoked, cross-workspace, or otherwise unsafe.

comments.author: Jeff Emanuel
comments.text: Implemented identifier discovery and disambiguation as crates/fwc/src/identifier.rs. Deliverables: (1) LookupRequest builder with connector/resource_type/operation_hint/query, (2) LookupResult with tagged LookupOutcome enum (Resolved/Ambiguous/NotFound/Unsupported), (3) ResourceCandidate with id/display_name/context/match_quality (Exact>Prefix>Partial>Fuzzy ordering), (4) DisambiguationPrompt with binding_key/question/options/next_commands, (5) ConnectorResourceModel and ResourceTypeDescriptor for connectors to declare lookup surfaces, (6) RESOURCE_FAMILIES constant with 8 well-known resource families mapping to connectors (project, issue, page, channel, document, record, contact, workspace), (7) resolve_candidates() function producing appropriate outcomes, (8) find_resource_family() and suggest_discovery_commands() helpers, (9) 25 unit tests covering builders, serde, resolution (single/multiple/none), disambiguation, resource families, edge cases. Total fwc tests: 327, clippy clean. — SunnyMoose

title: [FWC] Test observability, scenario artifact, redaction, and replay contract
description:
# [FWC] Test observability, scenario artifact, redaction, and replay contract

## Goal
Define the logging, artifact, redaction, and replay contract that all `fwc` validation layers will use so failures are easy to diagnose and successful runs produce durable evidence.

## Why this bead exists
The user explicitly asked for comprehensive unit tests and end-to-end scripts with great, detailed logging. That does not happen automatically. If artifact structure, replayability, redaction, and trace fields are designed late, the test suite becomes noisy when green and useless when red.

## Scope
- define a shared scenario identifier scheme across unit, integration, and e2e layers
- define a structured log envelope for CLI steps, host requests, host receipts, approvals, token counts, and replay metadata
- define artifact bundle layout for golden snapshots, integration traces, scenario transcripts, and perf/token-budget reports
- define redaction rules so secrets and sensitive payloads never leak while preserving enough detail to debug
- define deterministic replay instructions so a failing scenario can be rerun from one saved bundle

## Deliverables
- canonical structured-log schema for `fwc` validation
- artifact directory/file naming contract for local runs and CI artifacts
- redaction and payload-digest rules
- replay instructions / minimal environment capture contract
- guidance for what every later test bead must emit on failure

## Acceptance criteria
- A failing `fwc` test run yields a compact, structured bundle that tells future implementers what happened without requiring ad hoc reproduction work.
- Logs are rich enough for debugging but safe enough to store and review.
- Unit, integration, and e2e layers share enough artifact vocabulary that reviewers can correlate failures across layers quickly.
acceptance_criteria:
1. All FWC verification layers share one structured observability contract for scenario IDs, trace IDs, receipt linkage, artifact bundle layout, and replay metadata.

- examples showing before-and-after transformations for tricky sensitive cases

title: [FWC] Agent confusion corpus and recovery evaluation harness across plan/do/task and primitive commands
description:
# [FWC] Agent confusion corpus and recovery evaluation harness across plan/do/task and primitive commands

## Goal
Create a reusable evaluation corpus that captures how real agents are likely to misunderstand, misuse, or partially specify `fwc`, then use that corpus to harden recovery behavior across discovery, config, lifecycle, invoke, and workflow surfaces.

## Why this bead exists
An agent-first CLI is only as good as its behavior under confusion. Happy-path tests are not enough. We need a durable corpus of malformed commands, partial identifiers, ambiguous intents, stale task references, unsafe correction candidates, missing approvals, and mixed-format mistakes so we can prove that `fwc` educates callers instead of dumping generic parser noise.

## Scope
- define confusion-corpus categories for discovery, config, lifecycle, invoke, `plan`, `do`, `task`, `task resolve`, and `task ask`
- encode expected recovery outcomes: auto-correct, explicit ambiguity, blocking question, next-action hint, or hard denial
- cover identifier-heavy cases, typo cases, stale state cases, and conflicting input-source cases
- make the corpus reusable by snapshot tests, integration tests, e2e scripts, and documentation/playbooks
- ensure outputs remain TOON-efficient while preserving JSON fidelity and structured error typing

## Deliverables
- machine-readable confusion corpus with expected outcomes and rationale
- evaluation harness that can run the corpus against `fwc`
- coverage map showing which recovery classes are protected by unit, integration, and e2e layers
- guidance for adding new regression cases when agent failures are discovered later

## Acceptance criteria
- Recovery behavior is measured against a deliberate corpus instead of vague intuition.
- New recovery regressions are easy to add as permanent cases.
- The corpus meaningfully exercises the implemented `plan/do/task/resolve` features as well as the primitive command families.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The confusion corpus covers primitive commands plus workflow surfaces such as plan, do, task, resolve, and ask, including ambiguous, stale, unsafe, and partially specified agent inputs.
2. Expected recovery outcomes are explicit and measurable, including autocorrect, ambiguity, blocking question, denial, and next-action guidance, with no hand-wavy parser fallbacks.
3. The harness is reusable across unit, integration, docs, and transcript-style E2E runs, and every failure case emits detailed logs explaining why the response was or was not acceptable.

title: [FWC] Confusion corpus: schema, taxonomy, and expected-outcome vocabulary

# [FWC] Confusion corpus: schema, taxonomy, and expected-outcome vocabulary

## Goal
Create a shared language for the mistakes, ambiguities, and partial intents that an agent-first CLI must recover from gracefully.

## Scope
- corpus schema for command text, context, expected interpretation, expected recovery class, and rationale
- taxonomy covering primitive commands, workflow commands, session state, stale handles, and risky corrections
- outcome vocabulary such as auto-correct, ambiguity, ask, deny, suggest, and no-op-with-explanation
- conventions that let later tests and docs consume the same corpus without translation layers

## Deliverables
- machine-readable confusion corpus schema and taxonomy
- examples that illustrate why each recovery class exists and where it should be used

## Acceptance criteria
- future contributors can add new confusion cases without re-litigating the vocabulary every time
- the corpus is structured enough to drive tests, reports, and documentation from one source of truth
acceptance_criteria:
1. The confusion corpus schema defines stable categories, expected outcomes, rationale fields, and severity or risk tags for agent misunderstanding cases.
2. Vocabulary distinguishes ambiguity, unsafe suggestion, denial, missing prerequisite, and recoverable typo or state drift cases without overlap.
3. Documentation and validation checks keep the corpus internally consistent and easy to extend.

3. Corpus runs and documentation emit detailed logs showing what the CLI should have done and why.
notes: Workflow confusion cases must include saved-preset and bookmark failures: activating stale context, wrong pinned profile, wrong zone, hidden assumptions carried across handoff, and resume attempts whose referenced handles or artifacts are no longer valid.

title: [FWC] Auth and credential lifecycle UX for bootstrap, verification, rotation, and profiles
description:
# [FWC] Auth and credential lifecycle UX for bootstrap, verification, rotation, and profiles

## Goal
Make authentication and credential handling a first-class `fwc` experience so agents can actually bring connectors online, inspect auth health, switch accounts, and repair broken auth without dropping into bespoke per-connector setup rituals.

## Why this bead exists
The current `fwc` graph was strong on discovery, config, lifecycle, and invocation, but it still treated auth as an implicit side effect of configuration. That is not good enough if `fwc` is supposed to be the place where an agent can do absolutely anything useful with every connector. For many connectors, auth bootstrap and auth repair are the difference between “looks nice” and “actually usable.”

## Scope
- credential inventory and auth-status views per connector/profile/account/workspace
- guided bootstrap/connect flows for OAuth, device-code, API-key, webhook-secret, and similar connector auth patterns
- verify/test/refresh/rotate/revoke/repair flows for existing credentials and tokens
- multiple auth profiles or account contexts per connector, including explicit switching and zone/workspace scoping
- redaction-safe display and audit-friendly attribution for auth actions

## Testing mandate
Implementation under this branch is not complete unless it lands with:
- focused unit/snapshot coverage for auth status, redaction, and guidance surfaces
- host-backed integration coverage for bootstrap/verify/repair flows where test fixtures allow it
- end-to-end scripts with detailed structured logging and replay artifacts

## Acceptance criteria
- an agent can answer “is this connector authenticated, with what profile, and is it healthy?” from `fwc`
- an agent can bootstrap or repair auth using guided workflows rather than connector-specific tribal knowledge
- auth surfaces remain safe-by-default and explicit about what is secret, what is referenced, and what changed
acceptance_criteria:
1. Auth UX covers inventory, bootstrap, verification, repair, switching, and revocation in a way that matches the real runtime auth/enforcement model.
2. The bead includes focused unit/snapshot checks, host-backed integration scenarios, and detailed E2E logs for remediation flows.
3. Secret handling, provenance, and change visibility remain safe-by-default while still being operationally useful.

title: [FWC] Operation history, receipt inspection, replay, comparison, and safe reversal guidance

# [FWC] Operation history, receipt inspection, replay, comparison, and safe reversal guidance

## Goal
Make prior `fwc` actions explorable and reusable so agents can inspect receipts, compare runs, replay prior work safely, and understand whether any reversal path exists.

## Why this bead exists
The current graph added durable result handles and rich observability, but it still did not promise a first-class user-facing history and replay surface. That is a usability gap. Agents often need to answer “what happened last time?”, “can I replay that with one changed input?”, and “is there a safe way back?” without reconstructing a command from logs manually.

## Scope
- history and receipt queries for prior operations, tasks, and workflow runs
- replay or clone flows with input override, dry-run, and approval-aware preflight
- compare or diff views between prior runs, result handles, and projected outputs
- safe reversal or undo guidance where connectors explicitly advertise reversibility, with hard refusals where they do not
- redaction-safe, audit-friendly operation history displays

## Testing mandate
Implementation under this branch is not complete unless it lands with:
- focused unit/snapshot coverage for history, receipt, replay, compare, and reversal guidance surfaces
- host-backed integration coverage for replay and receipt resolution flows
- end-to-end scripts with detailed logging, receipts, and replay artifacts

## Acceptance criteria
- an agent can inspect prior work and reuse it without manually spelunking transcripts
- replay is safe-by-default, approval-aware, and explicit about what is being reused or changed
- compare and reversal guidance help callers reason about consequences before they act
acceptance_criteria:
1. History/replay surfaces are built on real receipts, logs, and replayable evidence rather than reconstructed guesses.
2. Replay, compare, and reversal guidance remain approval-aware and explicit about what is and is not reversible.
3. Unit/snapshot, host integration, and transcript-E2E verification with detailed logging are required.

# [FWC] History UX: reversal and undo guidance with connector-aware safety boundaries

## Goal
Tell the truth about reversal. Where a connector advertises a real reversible action, `fwc` should help the caller find and preflight it. Where no safe reversal exists, `fwc` should say so clearly instead of implying an undo fantasy.

## Scope
- capability-aware reversal guidance and explicit non-reversible classifications
- links from history or receipts to the appropriate reversal or repair path when it exists
- approval and safety boundaries for reversal actions that themselves are risky
- error and explanation surfaces for unsupported or unsafe undo attempts

## Acceptance criteria
- callers can quickly tell whether a safe way back exists after an action
- reversal guidance reduces operational fear without making false promises about undoability
acceptance_criteria:
1. Reversal and undo guidance is connector-aware, approval-aware, and explicit about what can only be compensated versus truly reversed.
2. Guidance never over-promises safety for destructive or externally visible actions.
3. Unit, integration, and transcript-style E2E verification with detailed logs are required for reversible, irreversible, and blocked cases.
