title: Cloud/data evidence bundles, cleanup discipline, and risky-mutation documentation
description:
Background:
- This family has the highest cleanup and accidental-mutation risk, so the evidence bundle has to say more than “tests passed.”

Deliverables:
- Consolidate cleanup discipline, seeded-data documentation, risky-mutation proofs, and rerun guidance for the cloud/data family.
- Make it obvious what each suite mutates, what it cleans up, and which environments are safe to reuse.

Acceptance criteria:
- Cloud/data acceptance artifacts are explicit enough to support safe reruns by future agents.

title: Commerce, CRM, analytics, and business-app connectors: non-mock acceptance wave
description:
Background:
- Commerce, CRM, communication, and analytics connectors often combine authentication, pagination, webhooks, uploads, and money/customer-impacting mutations.
- The acceptance bar here must be especially explicit because a wrong mutation can be expensive even in test/sandbox environments.

Scope:
- Stripe, PayPal, Square, Shopify, Salesforce, HubSpot, Mailchimp, Sendgrid, Twilio, Intercom, Docusign, Plaid, Airtable, Asana, Trello, Monday, ClickUp, Zendesk, Segment, Amplitude, Mixpanel, Datadog, Grafana, Metabase, Posthog, and adjacent business-app connectors.

Deliverables:
- Add non-mock acceptance coverage for auth, paging/search, write semantics, attachment or file flows, webhook ingress, receipts/ids, and rate-limit behavior.
- Separate read-only and mutation acceptance evidence so risky operations are not hidden behind generic smoke tests.
- Ensure all family tests emit structured evidence and close any missing compliance E2E coverage.

Acceptance criteria:
- Customer/business-impacting connectors have explicit acceptance evidence for both safe and risky surfaces.
- Mock-backed suites remain useful but no longer stand alone as sign-off.

title: Payments and commerce connector acceptance sweep
description:
Background:
- Payments and commerce connectors combine cost-bearing mutations, webhook ingress, reconciliation IDs, and provider sandbox requirements.
- They are some of the worst candidates for vague or fake-only acceptance proof.

Deliverables:
- Sweep Stripe, PayPal, Square, Shopify, Plaid, and related commerce/payment connectors for truthful unit, contract, local, host-backed, and sandbox coverage as appropriate.
- Split read-only validation from risky mutation evidence so operator sign-off is explicit.

Acceptance criteria:
- Commerce/payment connectors have acceptance evidence that is safe to trust for money- or customer-impacting flows.

title: CRM, support, and work-management connector acceptance sweep
description:
Background:
- CRM, support, and work-management connectors mix search/list flows with mutations, attachments, comments, and webhook/event ingress.

Deliverables:
- Sweep Salesforce, HubSpot, Intercom, Zendesk, Docusign, Airtable, Asana, Trello, Monday, ClickUp, and related business-workflow connectors for truthful acceptance and stronger pure-unit floors.
- Make attachment handling, idempotency, and webhook semantics part of the verification story.

Acceptance criteria:
- Business-workflow connectors no longer present fake-backed tests as final confidence.

title: Analytics, marketing, and observability connector acceptance sweep
description:
Background:
- Analytics, marketing, and observability connectors often look read-heavy, but they still involve auth, batching, eventual consistency, and sometimes cost-bearing or privacy-sensitive mutations.

Deliverables:
- Sweep Mailchimp, Sendgrid, Segment, Amplitude, Mixpanel, Datadog, Grafana, Metabase, Posthog, and related connectors for truthful acceptance coverage and high-signal logging.
- Verify batching, retries, throttling, and diagnostic surfacing.

Acceptance criteria:
- Analytics/marketing/observability connectors have a real acceptance path with debuggable artifacts.

title: Business-family risky-mutation evidence bundles and sandbox documentation
description:
Background:
- This family needs one operator-friendly place to see which suites are read-only, which mutate third-party state, and which require sandboxes.

Deliverables:
- Consolidate risky-mutation evidence, sandbox prerequisites, cleanup guidance, and rerun commands for the business-app family.
- Make promotion criteria explicit for connectors that can affect customer-facing or financial state.

Acceptance criteria:
- Business-family verification bundles are explicit enough to support safe sign-off and safe reruns.

title: AI, search, research, and media connectors: non-mock acceptance wave
description:
Background:
- AI/search/research/media connectors often look stateless, but they still need truthful handling for retries, streaming, large payloads, pagination, uploads, and policy/usage semantics.
- Several of these connectors already have compliance E2E, but much of the existing acceptance still depends on mock-backed services.

Scope:
- OpenAI, Anthropic, Google AI, OpenRouter, LLM Router, Whisper, Arxiv, Semantic Scholar, Annas Archive, Hacker News, YouTube, Reddit, Wolfram, Algolia, Logseq, and related search/research/content/media connectors.

Deliverables:
- Establish non-mock acceptance coverage for request/response fidelity, streaming or chunking behavior where applicable, retries, auth, throttling, large responses, and artifact logging.
- Convert mock-only E2E confidence into real fixture or live-sandbox acceptance as appropriate.
- Close the family’s missing compliance E2E coverage and align outputs with the shared evidence standard.

Acceptance criteria:
- The family has truthful acceptance coverage for both short-read and richer media/streaming cases.
- AI/search connector failures can be diagnosed from artifacts without rerunning against live vendors blindly.

title: LLM and provider API connector acceptance sweep
description:
Background:
- LLM/provider connectors are often introduced with happy-path HTTP tests, but the real acceptance story also needs rate limits, long responses, cost controls, and sometimes streaming or tool-call semantics.

Deliverables:
- Sweep OpenAI, Anthropic, Google AI, OpenRouter, Mistral, Hugging Face, and related provider connectors for truthful acceptance coverage and stronger pure-unit baselines.
- Capture rate-limit, auth, large-payload, and provider error semantics in reusable artifacts.

Acceptance criteria:
- Provider connectors have a clear non-fake acceptance story rather than only request stubs.

- Search and research connectors often appear simple because they are request-response APIs, but they still need truthful handling for auth, pagination, ranking parameters, throttling, and large result sets.

- Sweep Brave Search, Perplexity Search, Tavily, Exa, Firecrawl, Algolia, Annas Archive, Hacker News, and related retrieval connectors for stronger pure-unit floors and non-mock acceptance.

- Search/research connectors have acceptance evidence beyond fake HTTP responses.

title: Media, voice, transcription, and streaming connector acceptance sweep
description:
Background:
- Deepgram, ElevenLabs, Whisper, YouTube, Reddit, and related media or voice connectors have chunking, streaming, upload/download, or long-running job semantics that require better acceptance coverage than static fixtures.

Deliverables:
- Sweep media, voice, transcription, and other streaming-heavy connectors for truthful acceptance across uploads, streamed outputs, retries, chunking, and artifact logging.
- Reuse the shared HTTP and streaming harnesses where possible.

Acceptance criteria:
- Media/voice connectors have high-signal acceptance evidence that surfaces streaming and large-payload failures clearly.

title: AI, search, and media evidence bundles, cost ceilings, and rerun documentation
description:
Background:
- AI/search/media connectors often need extra operational context around tokens, cost ceilings, and partial-result interpretation.

Deliverables:
- Consolidate family-wide artifact expectations, rerun commands, cost-ceiling guidance, and redaction rules for AI/search/media connectors.
- Make it easy for a future agent to understand whether a failing run was local fixture, host-backed, or live-provider evidence.

Acceptance criteria:
- AI/search/media verification becomes self-contained and safe to rerun.

title: Provider-sandbox and nightly live-suite program for connectors that cannot stop at local fixtures
description:
Background:
- Some connectors cannot be fully proven by local fixtures alone; they need vendor sandboxes, bridge daemons, or nightly live runs with controlled credentials and cost caps.
- Without a formal live-suite policy, teams either skip live checks entirely or run fragile ad hoc scripts that produce poor diagnostics.

Deliverables:
- Define and implement the provider-sandbox/nightly-live layer for connectors that need it.
- Establish secret management, account provisioning, cost ceilings, cleanup policies, scheduling, flaky-test quarantine, and artifact retention.
- Record which connectors must have live suites, which can rely on local fixtures, and which require both.

Acceptance criteria:
- Live verification is part of the official testing story rather than tribal knowledge.
- Failures from nightly/provider suites produce the same structured artifacts and redaction guarantees as local E2E runs.

title: Classify the connectors that require live or nightly suites and document why
description:
Background:
- Some connectors cannot truthfully stop at local fixtures because the real boundary is a managed SaaS sandbox, a device lab, or a provider behavior that cannot be emulated safely.
- The repo needs an explicit classification of those exceptions instead of ad hoc tribal knowledge.

Deliverables:
- Classify which connectors require `live` or nightly suites, record why local_non_mock is insufficient, and map the minimum acceptable live boundary.
- Feed the result back into the connector-family sweeps and CI expectations.

Acceptance criteria:
- There is a stable list of connectors that genuinely require live/nightly verification and an explicit justification for each.

title: Shared secret, account, cost, cleanup, and environment-manifest layer for live suites
description:
Background:
- Once live-required connectors are identified, the biggest operational risk becomes unsafe secret handling, runaway cost, and inconsistent cleanup.

Deliverables:
- Define shared secret/account provisioning, cost ceilings, cleanup rules, synthetic tenant labeling, and environment manifests for live/nightly suites.
- Make these rules compatible with the artifact and redaction requirements from the acceptance contract.

Acceptance criteria:
- Live-suite prerequisites are documented and safe enough for repeated automated use.

- Nightly/live verification behaves like a maintained system, not an informal side script.

title: Live-suite operator playbooks and failure triage rules
description:
Background:
- Future agents and maintainers need clear rules for when to run live suites, how to interpret failures, and when to quarantine or promote a flaky scenario.

- Publish the operator playbooks, failure-taxonomy guidance, rerun commands, and escalation rules for the live/nightly lane.
- Make cleanup expectations and redaction requirements explicit.

Acceptance criteria:
- A future maintainer can run or triage the live lane without guessing at policy.

title: CI gates, coverage dashboards, and maintainer playbooks for the testing-completeness program
description:
Background:
- A testing program is not real until CI and maintainer workflows enforce it.
- The workspace needs both a quality gate and a practical operator story for running, triaging, and extending the new suites.

Deliverables:
- Add CI/reporting gates that fail when connectors lack required suite classification, when E2E artifacts do not validate, or when redaction/logging policies are violated.
- Generate machine-readable and human-readable dashboards for coverage status by connector family and archetype.
- Publish maintainer/operator playbooks describing how to run local acceptance suites, how nightly live suites behave, how to inspect artifacts, and how to classify or quarantine flakes.
- Ensure new connector work cannot silently ship with only fake-backed tests unless explicitly exempted under the policy.

Acceptance criteria:
- Coverage policy and artifact policy are enforceable by automation.
- A future agent can pick up any connector and know exactly which suites to run and how to debug failures.

title: Coverage scanner for suite classification, pure_unit floor, and minimum acceptance presence
description:
Background:
- The coverage inventory and taxonomy work need to become a machine-enforced gate rather than a document humans periodically read.

Deliverables:
- Build the scanner that verifies suite classification, minimum acceptance presence, and the pure-unit floor for connectors and core crates.
- Make the output diff-friendly so new regressions are obvious in CI.

Acceptance criteria:
- The repo has an automated answer to whether a connector is missing required unit/acceptance layers.

Background:
- Great logging is only useful if CI rejects malformed, under-redacted, or incomplete artifacts before they become the new normal.

Deliverables:
- Add CI validation for JSONL schema compliance, secret/PII redaction, replay bundle completeness, and artifact retention behavior.
- Ensure failures point directly at the missing or invalid artifact.

Acceptance criteria:
- Artifact quality and redaction policy are enforceable rather than aspirational.

- Once the repo has real enforcement, maintainers still need a fast human view of what is covered, what is missing, and what changed.

Background:
- The enforcement and dashboards only help if maintainers also know how to rerun suites, quarantine flakes, and promote evidence cleanly.

- Publish the maintainer playbooks for local reruns, flaky-suite quarantine, evidence promotion, and regression triage across the testing-completeness program.

- A future maintainer can operate the testing program without tribal knowledge.

title: Workspace-wide pure_unit coverage normalization and unit-test floor enforcement
description:
Background:
- The acceptance contract now distinguishes `pure_unit` from `deterministic_contract`, but the current workspace still mixes those labels in practice.
- The coverage inventory proves that many connectors either stop at fake-backed contract tests or have thin unit coverage that would not satisfy the explicit pure-unit floor.

Deliverables:
- Create a cross-cutting workstream that normalizes what counts as a unit test, finds fake-backed leakage, and raises the minimum pure-unit floor across the connector workspace.
- Feed the results into CI so future connector work cannot quietly reintroduce the same ambiguity.

Acceptance criteria:
- Future agents can answer the unit-coverage question from Beads alone without re-auditing the repo by hand.
notes: This workstream is about making unit-test claims truthful: raise the real `pure_unit` floor, and reclassify fake-backed tests into `deterministic_contract` instead of pretending they are non-mock unit proof. Real boundary coverage belongs in the acceptance and live-suite waves.

title: Reclassify the current test inventory by suite class and identify fake-backed unit leakage

- The repo needs a mechanical inventory of which tests are truly `pure_unit`, which are fake-backed `deterministic_contract`, and which are real acceptance suites.
- Without that classification pass, later family sweeps will argue about labels instead of closing gaps.

Deliverables:
- Re-scan connector and core-crate tests, reclassify suite names where needed, and record where fake-backed tests are still masquerading as unit coverage.
- Emit a list of connectors/crates that fail the current pure-unit floor or naming rules.

Acceptance criteria:
- There is a definitive backlog-ready inventory of unit-floor gaps and naming leaks that other beads can consume directly.

- Request-response connectors have a truthful pure-unit baseline independent of their mock-backed or live acceptance suites.

title: CI and documentation enforcement for pure_unit minimums and naming hygiene
description:
Background:
- A one-time cleanup will decay unless CI and docs enforce the pure-unit rules.
- Future connector work needs a simple automated answer to: does this connector meet the minimum pure-unit floor and are the suite names truthful?

Deliverables:
- Turn the classification rules into enforceable CI/docs checks: naming validation, minimum pure-unit presence, and explicit escalation when a connector relies only on fake-backed tests.
- Update maintainer docs so contributors know how to fix violations instead of papering over them.

Acceptance criteria:
- Pure-unit floor regressions fail fast and the remediation path is documented.

title: Define testing policy and acceptance taxonomy for unit, non-mock integration, host-backed E2E, and live suites
description:
Background:
- "Full unit coverage without mocks/fake stuff" needs a precise repo-specific translation or people will talk past each other.
- For many connectors, pure unit tests are still valuable, but a mock-backed suite cannot be the final acceptance boundary.

Deliverables:
- Define a testing taxonomy covering at minimum: pure unit, deterministic contract/integration (mock-backed), local non-mock fixture integration, host-backed subprocess E2E, and provider-sandbox/nightly live verification.
- State the minimum required suite for each connector archetype (request-response, webhook, streaming, queue, DB, file/blob, CLI/process, browser, bridge-backed/mobile, local-platform).
- Make the naming rule explicit: if a suite depends on `wiremock`, fake polling APIs, stub connectors, or mock servers, it is supplemental confidence and must not be mislabeled as the only acceptance evidence.
- Define acceptable exceptions and the evidence required when a fully local non-mock path is impossible.

Acceptance criteria:
- New and existing connectors can be evaluated against one unambiguous checklist.
- The policy closes the ambiguity between deterministic contract coverage and real acceptance coverage.
- The policy includes logging/redaction expectations for every E2E-capable suite.
close_reason: Defined explicit testing taxonomy, archetype acceptance minimums, and E2E logging/redaction policy in the V3 contract

title: Harden shared E2E logging/reporting across fcp-e2e, fcp-testkit, and fwc
description:
Background:
- The repo already has structured E2E logging in `crates/fcp-e2e/src/logging.rs`, a CLI runner in `crates/fcp-e2e/src/bin/fcp-e2e.rs`, log scanning in `crates/fcp-testkit/src/log_scan.rs`, and scenario machinery in `crates/fwc/src/e2e_scripts.rs`.
- Those pieces need to become the standard acceptance surface rather than a partial helper library.

Deliverables:
- Expand the shared JSONL schema so each run records per-step command metadata, stdout/stderr capture, artifact paths, retries, timing, correlation IDs, prerequisite state, and failure reason summaries.
- Ensure the runner can persist machine-readable reports and human-readable summaries without losing detail.
- Integrate redaction/secret scanning into the normal E2E flow, not as an optional afterthought.
- Make failure bundles self-sufficient for debugging: if a test fails in CI or nightly, the artifact set should explain what happened without rerunning interactively.

Acceptance criteria:
- `fcp-e2e`, `fcp-testkit`, and `fwc` expose one coherent reporting story.
- All required log artifacts validate against a shared schema and are scanned for secret leakage.
- The resulting output is detailed enough to support large-scale connector sweeps and flaky-test triage.

title: Build reusable non-mock HTTP fixture harnesses for request-response connectors
description:
Background:
- A large share of connectors currently validate HTTP behavior through `wiremock` or `MockApiServer`.
- That is useful for deterministic contract checks, but it is not sufficient for the requested no-mock acceptance bar.

Deliverables:
- Build reusable non-mock HTTP/SaaS fixture harnesses that run as real subprocess services and exercise auth, pagination, rate limits, webhooks, uploads/downloads, retries, redirects, error bodies, and timeout behavior through real networking stacks.
- Provide fixture startup/teardown helpers and seeded scenarios that Rust tests can invoke deterministically.
- Standardize request/response recording and structured diagnostics so family-wave tasks can reuse the same evidence format.

Acceptance criteria:
- HTTP connector waves can stop depending on `wiremock` as their only acceptance path.
- Fixtures are reusable across multiple connector families instead of one-off per connector.
- The fixture harnesses integrate cleanly with the logging/reporting stack from the E2E task.
close_reason: All 3 children closed. HTTP fixture harness complete.

title: Canonical subprocess HTTP fixture contract and scenario inventory
description:
Background:
- The coverage inventory shows request-response connectors still lean heavily on `wiremock`, `MockApiServer`, or connector-local fake servers for their final confidence story.
- Before more family sweeps start, the repo needs one canonical subprocess HTTP fixture contract that uses a real networking stack and standardized artifact output.

Deliverables:
- Define the fixture service contract, scenario manifest shape, required auth/pagination/retry/error/upload cases, and the artifact schema these runs must emit.
- Identify which existing `fcp-testkit` / `fcp-e2e` helpers can be promoted instead of replaced.

Acceptance criteria:
- Future connector beads can target one stable HTTP acceptance contract instead of inventing connector-specific fake worlds.
close_reason: Contract defined: 8 scenarios, 8 artifact types, 6 promoted helpers, real TCP HttpFixtureServer with 15 tests. Downstream 4.2 can implement scenario packs.

description:
Background:
- Once the contract exists, the repo still needs a real reusable fixture implementation that can exercise the behaviors mock servers currently flatten away.

Deliverables:
- Implement a reusable subprocess HTTP fixture harness with seeded auth flows, redirects, retries, pagination, throttling, upload/download, timeout, and structured request/response recording.
- Ensure the harness emits redacted, replayable evidence instead of opaque stdout.

Acceptance criteria:
- Multiple connectors can share the same non-mock HTTP fixture service and scenario packs without bespoke per-connector harness code.

- A reusable harness only matters if it is wired into the existing E2E stack and proven on real connector slices.

Deliverables:
- Thread the HTTP fixture harness into `fcp-e2e` / `fwc`, convert representative request-response connectors away from fake-only acceptance, and publish a connector-adoption guide.
- Capture the exact log/artifact expectations so later family sweeps can adopt the harness mechanically.

Acceptance criteria:
- There is at least one end-to-end path showing the HTTP fixture harness is real, reusable, and compatible with the shared evidence standard.

title: Build reusable non-mock streaming, webhook, and session-lifecycle fixture harnesses
description:
Background:
- Messaging, webhook, and streaming connectors need more than request/response mocks: they need reconnects, heartbeats, ordering gaps, dedupe, attachment ingress, and cancellation paths.

Deliverables:
- Build reusable local harnesses for websocket/SSE/long-poll/webhook/bidirectional flows.
- Support deterministic event scripts for reconnects, out-of-order delivery, partial failures, rate limits, attachment/media fetches, and shutdown/cancellation behavior.
- Capture inbound/outbound transcripts and structured timing so regressions in session lifecycle become obvious from the logs.

Acceptance criteria:
- Streaming and webhook connectors can be tested against real session behavior without inventing connector-specific fake worlds each time.
- Host-backed E2E runs can prove session lifecycle correctness, not just payload parsing.
- The harness supports both success-path and recovery-path scenarios.

title: Session-script DSL and transcript schema for websocket, SSE, long-poll, and webhook acceptance
description:
Background:
- Streaming, bidirectional, polling, and webhook connectors fail in ways that simple request/response harnesses cannot expose: reconnects, duplicate delivery, ordering gaps, shutdown races, and partial receipts.
- The shared harness needs a canonical session-script DSL and transcript schema before more connector-local solutions diverge.

Deliverables:
- Define the event-script model, timing controls, replay/ack semantics, and transcript format for websocket/SSE/long-poll/webhook acceptance.
- Align the schema with the structured E2E evidence model so session bugs are readable from artifacts alone.

Acceptance criteria:
- Future session-oriented harnesses all speak the same scripting and transcript vocabulary.

title: Implement webhook ingress, signature, redelivery, and attachment fixture harnesses
description:
Background:
- Webhook acceptance has its own failure modes: signature verification, duplicate delivery, delayed retries, attachment fetches, and listener recovery after restarts.

Deliverables:
- Implement reusable webhook ingress harnesses with signed payload builders, duplicate-delivery scenarios, retry semantics, listener restarts, and attachment/media ingress coverage.
- Make the resulting transcripts and environment artifacts line up with the shared E2E logging vocabulary.

Acceptance criteria:
- Webhook connectors can prove real ingress behavior without connector-specific fake listeners.

title: Build reusable DB, storage, queue, browser, and local-process fixture harnesses
description:
Background:
- Database, storage, queue, browser, bridge-backed, and local-process connectors cannot all be validated through one HTTP fixture story.
- Many of these surfaces require seeded local services, temp directories, subprocess orchestration, or platform-specific helper layers.

Deliverables:
- Build reusable harnesses for DB/storage/queue/local-process categories: seeded PostgreSQL/MySQL/SQLite/Redis-style fixtures, object/blob fixtures, local CLI/process wrappers, browser harness integration, and bridge-backed/mobile-desktop helper flows where the connector truthfully depends on a sidecar or daemon.
- Standardize startup contracts, health probes, cleanup, seeded data, and artifact capture.
- Document where truly platform-specific coverage must live (for example macOS-only connectors) versus what can run in generic CI.

Acceptance criteria:
- Connector families that depend on databases, local filesystems, subprocesses, or bridge daemons have a credible non-mock acceptance path.
- Platform-specific constraints are explicit rather than hidden inside flaky tests.
- The harnesses compose with host-backed E2E and shared logging/reporting.
close_reason: Closed after completing 6.1 seeded DB/storage fixture packs, 6.2 queue/browser/local-process/bridge harness artifacts, and 6.3 platform/host_e2e guidance.

title: Seeded DB and storage fixture packs plus deterministic cleanup contracts
description:

- Database, storage, and object connectors need truthful local engines with seeded data and deterministic cleanup, not SQL mocks or static fixture files.

Deliverables:
- Build seeded local fixture packs for relational, embedded, object/blob, and closely related stateful services, with startup probes, teardown discipline, and standard artifact capture.
- Record what state is seeded, what state is mutated, and how cleanup is verified.

Acceptance criteria:
- Stateful data connectors have a shared local_non_mock path that is reproducible and safe to rerun.

title: Queue, browser, local-process, and bridge harnesses with standardized artifact capture
description:
Background:
- The remaining hard boundaries in this family are queues, local daemons, browsers, CLI tools, and bridge-backed subprocesses.
- Those surfaces need real process supervision and artifact capture rather than fake stdout fixtures or mocked broker clients.

Deliverables:
- Build shared harnesses for queue/pub-sub brokers, browser sessions, CLI/local-process invocations, and bridge/daemon-backed connectors.
- Capture stdout/stderr, exit status, temp directories, receipts, and replay metadata in a standardized way.

Acceptance criteria:
- Browser/process/bridge connectors can reuse one truthful harness story instead of inventing ad hoc local runners.

title: Platform matrix, skip policy, and host_e2e adoption guide for stateful and local fixtures

- Some of these fixtures are platform-specific or only safe in certain environments, which means the run matrix has to be explicit before later sweeps begin.

Deliverables:
- Publish the platform matrix, skip rules, cleanup guarantees, and host_e2e adoption guidance for DB/storage/queue/browser/local fixtures.
- Make it obvious which suites can run in generic CI, which require dedicated hosts, and how failures should be triaged.

Acceptance criteria:
- Platform constraints are documented up front instead of buried inside flaky tests or tribal knowledge.

title: Core platform crates: expand non-mock coverage and host-backed verification
description:
Background:
- The connectors are only as trustworthy as the platform crates underneath them.
- Some crates already have `no_mock_integration.rs`, golden vectors, host integration suites, and log-schema checks, but the coverage is uneven.

Scope:
- `fcp-core`, `fcp-protocol`, `fcp-crypto`, `fcp-cbor`, `fcp-manifest`, `fcp-sdk`, `fcp-host`, `fcp-store`, `fcp-mesh`, `fcp-webhook`, `fcp-oauth`, `fcp-telemetry`, `fcp-ratelimit`, and adjacent runtime-support crates that materially affect connector behavior.

Deliverables:
- Expand no-mock integration and host-backed coverage for lifecycle, policy, receipts, cancellation, restart/recovery, rollout, telemetry, redaction, and schema/logging guarantees.
- Close gaps where current coverage stops at golden vectors or mock-backed helpers.
- Make core-crate failures easy to localize via structured artifacts rather than giant opaque test logs.

Acceptance criteria:
- The platform layer has an explicit acceptance story independent of any single connector.
- Core regressions are caught before connector-family sweeps start blaming downstream crates.

title: Protocol, manifest, crypto, and core semantic crate truth sweep
description:
Background:
- The protocol, manifest, and crypto crates define the invariants every connector inherits.
- Their verification cannot stop at golden vectors that are hard to map back to operator-facing failures.

Deliverables:
- Sweep `fcp-core`, `fcp-protocol`, `fcp-crypto`, `fcp-cbor`, and `fcp-manifest` for missing pure-unit floors, vector coverage, schema conformance, and non-mock validation where applicable.
- Make failure output specific enough that downstream connector sweeps can trust the core layer.

Acceptance criteria:
- Core semantic crates have a truthful and debuggable verification story independent of any one connector.

title: Messaging and community connectors: replace mock-only confidence with real acceptance paths
description:
Background:
- Messaging/community connectors are the place where mock-only confidence breaks down fastest because session behavior matters as much as payload schemas.
- The current family includes both connectors with existing compliance E2E and connectors still missing it, and many still rely heavily on mock-backed integration coverage.

Scope:
- Slack, Discord, Telegram, Signal, WhatsApp, Matrix, Mattermost, Nextcloud Talk, Synology Chat, IRC, QQ, Nostr, WeCom, DingTalk, Teams, Line, Feishu, BlueBubbles, iMessage, and other session-oriented community or bridge-backed messaging surfaces.

- For each connector, add a required non-mock acceptance path that exercises connection lifecycle, auth/bridge prerequisites, join/send/receive semantics, retries, reconnects, attachments/media, and logging/redaction behavior.
- Convert existing mock-backed suites into supplemental contract tests where they remain useful, but ensure they are no longer the only evidence.
- Fill known family gaps where connectors currently lack compliance E2E coverage entirely.

Acceptance criteria:
- Every connector in the family is mapped to a truthful local fixture and/or nightly live path.
- Messaging regressions are diagnosable from durable artifacts instead of ad hoc stdout.

title: Hosted webhook and bot messaging connectors acceptance sweep
description:

title: fcp-store: WAL/snapshot replay accepts attacker-chosen object_id without verifying canonical content hash
description:
**Files**:
- crates/fcp-store/src/durable.rs:224-230 (`insert_loaded`)
- crates/fcp-store/src/durable.rs:257-265 (`apply_loaded_mutation` — Put branch)
- crates/fcp-store/src/object_store.rs:399-433 (`MemoryObjectStore::put` — runtime API)

**Lens**: Axiom 7 ("the recovery path is a shadow codebase") + Axiom 9 ("server-authoritative state").

**Root cause**: `StoredObject` has the invariant
`object_id == canonical_hash(b"FCP2-OBJECT-V1" || canonical_cbor(header) || body)`
(see `StoredObject::canonical_bytes` at fcp-core/src/object.rs:221-238). This is the FCP3 content-addressing contract: an object_id must be derivable from its bytes.

But neither the runtime API nor the WAL/snapshot replay verifies this:

- `MemoryObjectStore::put` (object_store.rs:399) accepts any `StoredObject` and trusts the supplied `object.object_id` field. It indexes/dedupes by the claimed ID without recomputing.
- `DurableObjectState::insert_loaded` (durable.rs:224) — called from both snapshot recovery (`from_snapshot` at line 210) and WAL replay (`apply_loaded_mutation` Put branch at line 263) — directly trusts `object.object_id`.
- `apply_loaded_mutation` only checks `!self.objects.contains_key(&object.object_id)` for duplicates; it never verifies the ID matches the body.

**Concrete attack scenario** (local-attacker / post-compromise persistence vector):

Setup: a process gains write access to the persistent WAL file at `<root_dir>/objects.wal.jsonl` (compromised host, malicious snapshot import from another node, restored backup from a tampered source). The signing keys are NOT compromised.

Attack:
1. Read a legitimate WAL record (e.g., `Put(StoredObject{object_id: H_real, header, body})` where H_real = canonical_hash(header, body)).
2. Construct a forged WAL record: `Put(StoredObject{object_id: H_real, header: H', body: B'})` where (H', B') are attacker-chosen bytes — different content under the SAME claimed ID. (Or use a different victim ID and arbitrary content.)
3. Append the forged record to the WAL (compute checksum over the new envelope; the WAL checksum is over (version, seq, op) and is verifiable, but the content-ID inside the op is not.)
4. Restart the store. `apply_loaded_mutation` accepts the forged Put as a new object; subsequent `get(claimed_id)` returns attacker-chosen bytes.

Net effect: the content-addressing invariant is violated. Any caller that downstream verifies `object_id == hash(get(object_id))` will detect this — but the assumption baked into FCP3 is that an in-store object IS its hash. Subsystems that skip the redundant rehash trust the store's claim.

**Why this is exploitable even without disk access**:

The `MemoryObjectStore::put` API trusts the caller too. Any code path that constructs a `StoredObject` from partially-untrusted input (e.g., reconstructed from gossip + raptorq-decoded body) and forwards to `put` propagates the same trust violation. In the current codebase, this is the responsibility of the caller (MeshNode), but there is no defense-in-depth at the store boundary — a single bug in any caller silently breaks content addressing for the whole node.

**Spec violation**:
The FCP3 spec defines content addressing as a NORMATIVE property: object_id derives from header+body. `StoredObject::canonical_bytes` documents this. The store-level `put` and `insert_loaded` paths violate the invariant by treating object_id as a free-form lookup key.

**Fix plan**:

1. Add a `StoredObject::verify_object_id` method in fcp-core that recomputes `canonical_bytes(&self.header, &self.body)`, hashes it, and compares against `self.object_id`. Return a typed error.

2. **Defense in depth at every storage boundary**:
   - `MemoryObjectStore::put`: call `object.verify_object_id()?` BEFORE inserting. Reject with `ObjectStoreError::InvalidObjectId` (new variant) on mismatch.
   - `DurableObjectState::insert_loaded`: same check. Specifically critical because WAL/snapshot bytes are attacker-reachable (file-system access).
   - `DurableObjectState::apply_loaded_mutation` (Put branch): same check before `insert_loaded`.

3. **Performance**: BLAKE3 of a 64 MiB object body is ~80ms on commodity hardware. For typical small objects (manifests, headers, kilobyte payloads) the overhead is sub-millisecond. The runtime put is already on the hot path and pays for canonical CBOR encoding at `canonical_bytes`; the rehash is comparable.

4. **Migration**: existing stores may have old objects (from before the check) that don't satisfy the invariant — though if they were written by honest code, they should. Add a `scrub_invalid_object_ids` boot-time scan that logs+quarantines mismatched objects rather than failing recovery; reuses the existing quarantine_store mechanism.

5. Regression tests:
   - put with mismatched object_id → InvalidObjectId
   - WAL replay with crafted Put(forged_id, body) → recovery rejects (or quarantines) and continues
   - Round-trip: put(canonical_object) → ok, get returns the same bytes, hash still matches

**Severity**: MEDIUM. Requires write access to the persistent WAL file (local attacker, malicious backup restore, malicious snapshot import). However, this is the EXACT class of vulnerability that defense-in-depth at the storage boundary is supposed to mitigate, and FCP3 explicitly relies on content addressing as a security property — not just an indexing convenience.
close_reason: 8ba57671 enforces object_id == canonical_hash at put/replay (installed via with_verifier / open_with_verifier; fails closed on unknown zones with VerifierKeyMissing)

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text: Shipped in commit ee4b524a. Added `StoredObject::validate_structure()` (key-free structural check using `canonical_bytes` pipeline). Wired into MemoryObjectStore::put, DurableObjectState::validate_mutation, from_snapshot (now fallible), and the WAL replay loop in load_durable_object_state. Catches oversized bodies (>MAX_CANONICAL_OBJECT_BYTES = 64 MiB) and non-canonically-encodable headers. Full content-ID verification still requires zone keys and is the runtime caller's responsibility — documented in the new validate_structure doc comment. Regression test wal_replay_rejects_oversized_object_body builds a forged WAL envelope with a 64 MiB+1 body and confirms recovery rejects/truncates. 12/12 durable tests green.

title: [MOR/C1.2] Remove XOR filter from revocation-critical path; use exact membership

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text: WHAT: Remove the XOR filter (xorf::Xor8) from the revocation membership check path in gossip.rs. Replace with exact HashSet<ObjectId> membership testing for revocation checks. Keep XOR filter only for non-security-critical gossip set reconciliation (object availability, not revocation). WHY: H2 Adversarial found that XOR filters have ~0.4% false-positive rate. With 10K revocations, ~40 legitimate operations get false-positive revocation — a DoS against legitimate users. False positives in a security check are UNACCEPTABLE: if revoked={X}, we must reject X and ONLY X. A false positive is a security violation masquerading as availability issue. WHERE: crates/fcp-mesh/src/gossip.rs — the may_contain() method on XorFilterSet. The current code uses XOR filter for fast negative lookup of revocation status. Replace with: (1) Keep exact revocation set (HashSet<ObjectId> or BTreeSet) as authoritative. (2) XOR filter can remain as fast NEGATIVE check (if filter says not-present, definitely not revoked). (3) If filter says MAYBE-present, MUST fall through to exact set check. (4) For revocation specifically, skip the filter entirely and go straight to exact set. ACCEPTANCE: (1) Revocation checks use exact membership only (HashSet). (2) XOR filter remains for gossip reconciliation (non-security). (3) No false-positive revocation denials in test suite. (4) Performance regression within 10% for revocation checks up to 100K entries. (5) At least 4 tests: exact match, exact miss, no false positive on collision-prone IDs, performance benchmark. ESTIMATED EFFORT: 1-2 days. DESIGN NOTE: The XOR filter is a Bloom filter variant that is excellent for set reconciliation in gossip (where false positives cause unnecessary transfers, not security failures). It is NOT appropriate for security-critical revocation checks where a false positive means denying a legitimate operation.

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text: C1.2 done: Verified revocation uses HashMap exact membership (zero false positives). Added 4 tests (10K entries, collision-prone IDs, seal path, performance). Documented XOR filter security boundary in gossip.rs. Commit 68f14569.

title: fcp.llm-router: Intelligent Model Selection Connector
description:
## Goal
Provide an FCP2-compliant LLM routing connector that selects among providers/models based on capabilities/latency/budgets while preserving mechanical policy, auditability, and strict sandboxing.

## External surface (NetworkConstraints)
Default deny.
- Network egress MUST be restricted per-operation via manifest `NetworkConstraints` (defined in the connector’s manifest/cap map bead if present).
- Allow only the configured service host(s); HTTPS-only where applicable; deny redirects by default.
- Bound timeouts + response sizes; treat all remote responses as untrusted input; never leak secrets/PII in logs or errors.

## Zone model (mechanical)

<!-- fcp2-single-zone-note -->
**FCP2 single-zone binding note:** A connector instance binds to exactly one `ZoneId` for its entire lifetime.
The connector MUST NOT multiplex multiple zones internally.

Recommended deployment pattern: run separate connector instances in separate zones with different capability grants/policies.

## Manifest archetypes (closed set)

- `operational`

> Interaction patterns (non-archetype): Request/Response

## Overview
Meta-connector for intelligent routing between multiple AI/LLM providers, optimizing for cost, latency, and capability while enforcing budgets and providing usage analytics.

## Core Capabilities

### Cost-Based Routing
- Usage-based routing using deterministic estimates (tokens/bytes/duration) and/or `Simulate` `CostEstimate` (NO pricing tables).
- Token estimation before routing
- Prefer the lowest *estimated* cost option within policy/budget constraints (no embedded price tables).
- Cost threshold triggers for model downgrade
- Batch request optimization for cost savings

### Latency-Based Routing
- Provider health monitoring
- Historical latency tracking per model
- Geographic routing optimization
- Time-of-day latency patterns
- Streaming vs batch latency considerations

### Capability-Based Routing
- Task classification (coding, writing, analysis, etc.)
- Model capability matrix maintenance
- Context window requirement matching
- Vision/multimodal capability detection
- Tool use capability routing
- Specialized model selection (code, math, etc.)

### Fallback Chains
- Primary/secondary/tertiary provider chains
- Automatic failover on errors
- Partial failure handling (retry vs fallback)
- Circuit breaker implementation
- Graceful degradation strategies
- Provider outage detection

### Budget Enforcement
- Per-user budget limits
- Per-project budget allocation
- Daily/weekly/monthly caps
- Real-time spend tracking
- Budget alert thresholds
- Hard vs soft limit modes

### Usage Tracking and Analytics
- Request logging with metadata
- Cost attribution by user/project/task
- Model performance comparison
- Success rate tracking
- Token usage patterns
- ROI analysis per model

## Supported Providers (Initial)
- Anthropic (Claude models)
- OpenAI (GPT models)
- Google (Gemini models)
- AWS Bedrock (multi-model)
- Azure OpenAI
- Local models (Ollama, vLLM)

## Implementation Notes
- Unified request/response format across providers
- Provider-specific adapters
- Async request handling
- Request queuing for rate limits
- Credential management per provider
- Caching layer for repeated queries

## Configuration
- YAML-based routing rules
- Dynamic rule updates without restart
- A/B testing support for routing strategies
- Custom routing logic plugins

## Testing Requirements
- Mock providers for unit tests
- Routing decision validation
- Budget enforcement tests
- Failover scenario tests
- Load testing for routing performance

## Acceptance Criteria
- The functionality described in this bead is implemented with typed schemas + validation (no unstructured “stringly” interfaces).
- Errors map to the FCP error taxonomy with correct retry semantics and no secret/PII leakage.
- Mock-only unit/integration tests cover success paths and common failures and emit structured JSON logs per `flywheel_connectors-1n78.35`.

title: fcp.bigquery: Google BigQuery data warehouse connector
description:
## Goal
Provide an FCP2-compliant BigQuery connector for querying and dataset/table management with strict NetworkConstraints and audit for writes.

## Manifest archetypes (closed set)

- `storage`
- `operational`

> Interaction patterns (non-archetype): Request/Response (SQL) + polling for long queries

## Overview
Google BigQuery data warehouse connector for the Flywheel Connector Platform. Provides comprehensive access to BigQuery's analytics and data warehouse capabilities.

## Value Assessment
- **Value Score**: 49/100 (Tier 4)
- **Archetype**: Request-Response
- **Primary Use Cases**: Analytics, data warehousing, business intelligence, large-scale data processing

## Operations

### Query Zone (read-only analytics)
- **query.execute**: Execute SQL queries with parameterized inputs
- **query.dry_run**: Validate queries and estimate costs without execution
- **query.results**: Fetch paginated query results
- **query.cancel**: Cancel running queries

### Data Modification Zone
- **streaming.insert**: Real-time streaming inserts to tables
- **table.create**: Create new tables with schema definition
- **table.delete**: Delete tables
- **table.update**: Update table metadata and schema
- **table.patch**: Partial table updates
- **table.copy**: Copy tables within/across datasets

### Dataset Management
- **dataset.list**: List datasets in project
- **dataset.get**: Get dataset metadata
- **dataset.create**: Create new datasets
- **dataset.delete**: Delete datasets
- **dataset.update**: Update dataset properties

### Schema Management
- **schema.get**: Retrieve table schema
- **schema.update**: Modify table schema (add columns, change descriptions)
- **schema.validate**: Validate schema compatibility

### Job Management
- **job.list**: List jobs with filtering
- **job.get**: Get job status and metadata
- **job.cancel**: Cancel running jobs
- **job.query**: Submit query jobs

### Admin Zone (restricted)
- **iam.get**: Get IAM policies
- **iam.set**: Set IAM policies (requires elevated permissions)
- **routine.create**: Create stored procedures/functions
- **routine.delete**: Delete routines

## Zone Architecture

<!-- fcp2-single-zone-note -->
**FCP2 single-zone binding note:** A connector instance binds to exactly one `ZoneId` for its entire lifetime.
The *"zones"* described in this section are a **recommended deployment pattern** (run separate connector instances in separate zones with different capability grants/policies) and/or conceptual risk tiers.
The connector MUST NOT multiplex multiple zones internally.


```
Zone 1 (Query - Read Only):
  - query.execute, query.dry_run, query.results
  - dataset.list, dataset.get
  - table.list, table.get
  - schema.get
  - job.list, job.get

Zone 2 (Data Modification):
  - streaming.insert
  - table.create, table.update, table.delete, table.copy
  - dataset.create, dataset.update
  - schema.update

Zone 3 (Admin - Restricted):
  - dataset.delete
  - iam.get, iam.set
  - routine.create, routine.delete
  - job.cancel
```

## Dependencies
- **fcp-core**: Base connector traits and types
- **fcp-oauth**: Google OAuth 2.0 authentication (service account, user credentials)
- **fcp-ratelimit**: Rate limiting for API quota management
- **fcp-telemetry**: Metrics, logging, and tracing

## Implementation Approach

### Authentication
- Service account JSON key files
- Application Default Credentials (ADC)
- User OAuth flow for interactive use
- Workload Identity for GKE deployments

### API Integration
- BigQuery REST API v2 (primary)
- Consider gcp-bigquery-client crate for Rust native bindings
- Support for both sync and async operations

### Rate Limiting
- Per-project quota management
- Concurrent query limits
- Streaming insert rate limits (rows/second, bytes/second)

### Error Handling
- Query timeout handling
- Quota exceeded errors with retry logic
- Job failure recovery
- Partial insert failure handling for streaming

## Configuration Schema

```toml
[connector.bigquery]
project_id = "my-gcp-project"
location = "US"  # or specific region

[connector.bigquery.auth]
method = "service_account"  # or "adc", "oauth"
service_account_credential_id = "cred:<service_account_json>"  # do not store service account JSON on disk

[connector.bigquery.defaults]
query_timeout_ms = 30000
max_results_per_page = 10000
use_legacy_sql = false

[connector.bigquery.streaming]
insert_batch_size = 500
insert_timeout_ms = 5000

[connector.bigquery.rate_limits]
queries_per_minute = 100
streaming_rows_per_second = 100000
```

## Testing Strategy
- Unit tests with mocked BigQuery responses
- Integration tests against BigQuery sandbox/emulator
- Cost estimation validation tests
- Schema compatibility tests

## Documentation Requirements
- Authentication setup guide (service account, ADC, OAuth)
- Query best practices (parameterization, cost control)
- Streaming insert patterns
- Error handling guide
- Rate limiting and quota management

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All query zone operations implemented and tested
- [ ] Data modification operations with proper error handling
- [ ] Admin zone with appropriate permission checks
- [ ] OAuth and service account authentication working
- [ ] Rate limiting integrated with quota management
- [ ] Comprehensive test coverage (unit + integration)
- [ ] Documentation complete with examples

title: fcp-audit: ChainHead.signature_count is an unverifiable claim (has_quorum lies)
description:
## Finding
`ChainHead` (crates/fcp-audit/src/lib.rs:449) carries `signature_count: u32` with `has_quorum() -> bool { self.signature_count > 0 }` (lib.rs:473). However:

1. The struct does NOT carry a signatures list; no (issuer_kid, signature) pairs are represented.
2. `verify_chain` (lib.rs:927) performs zero signature verification — only hash linkage, seq monotonicity, zone consistency, head-tip match.
3. fcp-audit has NO dependency on fcp-crypto (Cargo.toml:14-21).

A consumer calling `head.has_quorum()` is making a trust decision on an unverifiable self-claim. A malicious/buggy producer can serialize `ChainHead{signature_count=7}` and every downstream check (`has_quorum`, `fcp_core::quorum::is_quorum_met`) treats it as signed.

## Why this is underspecified
The type surface promises "quorum" that the code cannot verify from the struct alone. Authenticity is presumably enforced at a wrapping layer but that contract is not documented in fcp-audit nor enforced at the API boundary.

## Recommendation (choose one)
- **Option A (strong):** Add `pub signatures: Vec<QuorumSignature>` with `QuorumSignature { issuer_kid, signature }`. Rewrite `has_quorum(threshold, key_lookup)` to require actual verification. Derive `signature_count` from `signatures.len()`.
- **Option B (docs-minimum):** Add crate-level rustdoc stating `ChainHead.signature_count` is producer-asserted, NOT a cryptographic proof. Rename `has_quorum` to `claims_quorum`.

## Evidence
- crates/fcp-audit/src/lib.rs:449-476 (ChainHead + has_quorum)
- crates/fcp-audit/src/lib.rs:927-1158 (verify_chain: no signature verification)
- crates/fcp-audit/Cargo.toml:14-21 (no fcp-crypto dep)
- crates/fcp-core/src/quorum.rs:185 (is_quorum_met consumes the unverifiable count)

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text: Fixed in bef626cf (ChainHead.signatures + signature_count_consistent + verify_chain head_signature_count_inconsistent issue) and 482760ae (golden_receipts snapshot). has_quorum() now requires signatures non-empty AND signature_count == signatures.len(). 364 lib tests pass.

title: [IDEA-21] Zone Policy Diff + Rollback Tooling
description:
## Background
Zone policies change over time. Operators need a safe way to review diffs and roll back with clear evidence and approvals.

## Goals

- Rollback outputs are deterministic and auditable.

title: [MOR/C3.2] Implement proof-carrying taint reduction via phantom types

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text: WHAT: Replace TaintFlags::remove() (which has a comment-only proof requirement) with a proof-carrying taint reduction system using phantom types. Taint flags can only be reduced by constructing a TaintReduction struct that references a SanitizerReceipt (a first-class mesh object proving the sanitization happened). WHY: A7 Type-Theoretic found that taint reduction currently has no enforcement — TaintFlags::remove() requires a SanitizerReceipt by COMMENT but not by API. A programmer could clear PUBLIC_INPUT taint without any proof and the compiler would allow it. This is a provenance violation: if tainted data appears clean without proof, the entire provenance lattice is untrustworthy. IMPLEMENTATION SKETCH: ```rust pub struct TaintReduction { pub sanitizer_receipt_id: ObjectId, pub cleared_flags: Vec<TaintFlag>, pub sanitizer_capability: CapabilityId, } impl TaintFlags { // Remove the bare remove() method entirely // Replace with: pub fn reduce_with_proof(mut self, reduction: &TaintReduction) -> Result<Self, TaintError> { // Verify reduction references valid flags for flag in &reduction.cleared_flags { if !self.0.contains(flag) { return Err(TaintError::FlagNotPresent(*flag)); } self.0.remove(flag); } // Record the reduction in provenance Ok(self) } // Keep add() — adding taint never needs proof pub fn add(&mut self, flag: TaintFlag) { self.0.insert(flag); } } ``` WHERE: crates/fcp-core/src/provenance.rs — TaintFlags, TaintFlag, TaintReduction. The SanitizerReceipt type may already exist or may need creation in crates/fcp-core/src/revocation.rs or a new file. ACCEPTANCE: (1) TaintFlags::remove() is deleted. (2) reduce_with_proof() requires TaintReduction with receipt reference. (3) TaintReduction is serializable and auditable. (4) Provenance carries taint_reductions: Vec<TaintReduction> (may already exist). (5) At least 5 tests: reduce with valid proof succeeds, reduce without proof compile error (no remove method), reduce non-present flag fails, reduction recorded in provenance, serialization round-trip. ESTIMATED EFFORT: 2-3 days.

# fcp.airtable: Linked Record Resolution and Management

## Goal
Provide first-class support for Airtable relational features:
- linked record fields
- lookup/rollup-style derived values

## External surface (NetworkConstraints)
Default deny.
- Network egress MUST be restricted per-operation via manifest `NetworkConstraints`.
- Allow only the configured service host(s); HTTPS-only where applicable; deny redirects by default.
- Bound timeouts + response sizes; treat all remote responses as untrusted input; never leak secrets/PII in logs or errors.

## Zone model (mechanical)

<!-- fcp2-single-zone-note -->
**FCP2 single-zone binding note:** A connector instance binds to exactly one `ZoneId` for its entire lifetime.
The connector MUST NOT multiplex multiple zones internally.

Recommended deployment pattern: run separate connector instances in separate zones with different capability grants/policies.

## Scope
- Read/write “link to another record” fields (arrays of record ids).
- Resolve linked record chains for agent-friendly outputs (bounded joins).
- Support computed field read semantics (lookup/rollup) without pretending they are writable.

## Key requirements
- Capability gated (reads vs writes).
- Bounded traversal:
  - prevent unbounded graph walks / cycles
  - explicit depth/record count limits
- Deterministic output:
  - stable ordering when expanding linked records
  - explicit “partial” indicators when traversal is truncated by bounds

## Tests
- Linked graph traversal (including cycles).
- Bounded expansion behavior.
- Error mapping for missing/deleted linked records.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Linked record expansion is safe and predictable.
- Computed fields are exposed read-only with clear typing.
close_reason: Implemented bounded linked-record expansion, field metadata, manifest updates, and coverage; verified with rch-backed fmt/check/test/clippy for fcp-airtable

title: TEST: RaptorQ Unit Tests (Encode/Decode, Chunking, DoS Bounds)
description:
# TEST: RaptorQ Unit Tests


## Goal
Prove RaptorQ encode/decode correctness and enforce decode DoS bounds (size/time) with reproducible test vectors.

## Scope
Comprehensive unit tests for RaptorQ symbol encoding/decoding and chunking.

## Test Categories

### Basic Encoding/Decoding
- [ ] Encode small object (< symbol size) → decode from K symbols
- [ ] Encode medium object (multiple symbols) → decode from K symbols
- [ ] Encode large object → ChunkedObjectManifest path
- [ ] Decode with exactly K source symbols
- [ ] Decode with K + repair symbols (erasure recovery)
- [ ] Decode with subset of repair symbols only

### Symbol Parameters
- [ ] Default symbol size (1024 bytes) produces expected symbol count
- [ ] Custom symbol sizes work correctly
- [ ] K (source symbols) calculation is correct for object sizes
- [ ] Repair ratio produces expected number of repair symbols

### ChunkedObjectManifest
- [ ] Objects > threshold produce manifest + raw chunks
- [ ] Manifest references correct chunk ObjectIds
- [ ] Chunks reconstruct to original object
- [ ] Chunk ordering is deterministic

### Decode DoS Mitigation
- [ ] Reject decode attempts exceeding CPU budget
- [ ] Reject decode attempts exceeding memory budget
- [ ] Timeout on pathological decode patterns
- [ ] Reject impossibly large symbol counts
- [ ] Reject impossibly large object sizes in manifest

### Symbol Identity
- [ ] Same object always produces same symbols (deterministic)
- [ ] ESI (encoding symbol identifier) is unique per symbol
- [ ] Symbols are self-describing (include ESI, K)

### Partial Availability
- [ ] DecodeStatus correctly reports received vs needed
- [ ] SymbolAck correctly acknowledges specific ESIs
- [ ] Missing symbol requests are targeted (not full retransmit)

## Golden Vectors
- 1KB object → expected symbols (with specific bytes)
- 100KB object → expected manifest structure
- Known erasure pattern → successful decode

## Fuzz Targets
- Malformed symbol streams
- Invalid ESI values
- Oversized object claims
- Corrupt manifest structures

## Performance Benchmarks
- Encode 1MB object: target < 10ms
- Decode 1MB from K symbols: target < 20ms
- Decode 1MB with 10% erasure: target < 50ms

## Logging Requirements
All tests emit:
```json
{
  "test_name": "...",
  "object_size": 12345,
  "symbol_size": 1024,
  "k": 13,
  "repair_symbols": 3,
  "decode_symbols_used": 13,
  "result": "pass|fail",
  "duration_us": 1234
}
```

## Acceptance Criteria
- All encoding/decoding paths tested
- DoS mitigations verified
- Performance benchmarks pass
- Golden vectors match
close_reason:
Implemented comprehensive RaptorQ unit tests with 79 passing tests covering:
- Golden vector tests for 1KB, 10KB, 100KB, and 300KB objects
- Symbol count verification (K source + repair ratio)
- Encode/decode roundtrip for all sizes
- Erasure recovery tests (10% loss, repair-only decode)
- Symbol determinism tests (same payload = same symbols)
- ESI uniqueness verification
- DoS mitigation tests (oversized payloads, concurrent limits, timeouts, memory/symbol buffer limits)
- Decode status tracking tests
- Chunked manifest tests (ID determinism, ordering, hash verification)
All acceptance criteria met.

title: TEST: Exactly-Once Semantics Unit Tests (Intent/Receipt, Idempotency, Fault Injection)
description:
# TEST: Exactly-Once Semantics Unit Tests

## Goal
Comprehensive unit tests verifying exactly-once semantics for OperationIntent + OperationReceipt.

## Test Categories

### 1. OperationIntent/Receipt Schema Tests
- Verify schema ID and hash correctness
- Test all required fields are present (idempotency_key, lease_seq, lease_object_id, refs)
- Validate upstream idempotency handle handling (optional field)
- Golden vector tests for deterministic CBOR serialization

### 2. Idempotency Key Tests
- Same key returns same receipt without re-execution (core idempotency property)
- Different keys produce independent executions
- Key collision resistance (hash-based keys)
- Key expiry/TTL semantics (if applicable)

### 3. Lease Fencing Tests
- OperationIntent MUST bind to lease fencing token (`lease_seq`)
- Stale lease holder attempts to execute (MUST be rejected)
- Lease renewal does not break in-flight intents
- Receipt references correct lease object

### 4. Fault Injection Tests
- Crash between intent creation and receipt creation
- Detect and reconcile incomplete intents on recovery
- Network partition during execution
- Storage failure during receipt write
- Timeout during external side effect

### 5. Audit Integration Tests
- AuditEvent emitted on intent creation
- AuditEvent emitted on receipt creation
- Audit chain integrity preserved across retries
- Decision receipts reference correct operation receipts

### 6. Concurrency Tests
- Concurrent requests with same idempotency key (only one executes)
- Concurrent requests with different keys (all execute)
- Race between intent creation and lease expiry

## Logging Requirements
- All test cases MUST log structured JSON with:
  - `test_name`, `test_phase` (setup/execute/verify)
  - `idempotency_key`, `lease_seq`, `operation_id`
  - `expected_outcome`, `actual_outcome`
  - `timing_ms` for each phase
- Failures MUST include full context for reproduction

## Golden Vectors
- Provide golden vectors for:
  - OperationIntent canonical CBOR
  - OperationReceipt canonical CBOR
  - Idempotency key derivation

## Acceptance Criteria
- All tests pass with `cargo test`
- Fault injection tests use deterministic chaos (seeded RNG)
- No flaky tests (deterministic outcomes)
- Coverage of all code paths in exactly-once module
close_reason: Implemented 60 comprehensive tests for exactly-once semantics: CBOR golden vectors, idempotency, lease fencing, fault injection, concurrency, and edge cases

title: fcp.jira: Sprint and board management
description:
# fcp.jira: Sprint and board management (FCP2)

## Goal
Implement Jira Agile operations for **boards** and **sprints** so agents can manage sprint workflows safely under FCP2 capability + approval enforcement.

This bead is specifically about Jira Software (Agile) surfaces (boards, sprints, backlog), not generic issue CRUD.

## Scope
### Read operations (low risk)
- List boards visible to the principal.
- Get board configuration (type, filters, location).
- List sprints for a board; get sprint metadata.
- List issues in a sprint/backlog (pagination; stable ordering).

### Write operations (medium/high risk)
- Create sprint (board-scoped).
- Start / complete sprint.
- Move issues into/out of sprint and backlog.

### Constraints
- Must work in both Jira Cloud and Server/DC (via `flywheel_connectors-3a9`).
- Must respect project permissions and Jira Software license availability.

## Capability model (illustrative)
Capability IDs MUST NOT encode hosts/ports.
- `jira.boards.read`
- `jira.sprints.read`
- `jira.sprints.write` (create/start/complete)
- `jira.sprints.assign_issues` (move issues)

Danger/approval guidance:
- Starting/completing sprints should be **approval-gated** by policy in many orgs.
  - Emit DecisionReceipt reason codes that are specific (e.g., `JIRA_SPRINT_START_REQUIRES_APPROVAL`).

## FCP2 requirements
- Single-zone binding.
- NetworkConstraints pinned to the Jira base hostname.
- For write ops: emit OperationReceipt + AuditEvent with:
  - board_id / sprint_id / issue_keys (IDs only; no secret data)
  - request correlation id

## Deliverables
- Operation schemas:
  - `jira.board.list`
  - `jira.board.get`
  - `jira.sprint.list`
  - `jira.sprint.get`
  - `jira.sprint.create`
  - `jira.sprint.start`
  - `jira.sprint.complete`
  - `jira.sprint.issues`
  - `jira.sprint.move_issues`
  - `jira.backlog.move_issues`
- Robust pagination helpers (bounded memory; streaming-friendly).
- Clear error mapping when Jira Software APIs are unavailable.

## Test strategy (MUST)
### Unit/integration (mock-only)
- Mock fixtures for Agile endpoints:
  - board listing and sprint listing
  - start/complete sprint happy paths
  - permission denied
  - missing Jira Software (feature not enabled)
  - rate-limit + retry/backoff

### Compliance
- Ensure capability-gating is enforced for each operation.
- Ensure write operations produce receipts/audit events.

## Acceptance criteria
- A mock-only test suite covers both Cloud and Server/DC variants.
- All write operations are capability + (policy-configurable) approval gated.
- No assumptions about “global boards”; all operations are explicitly scoped.

title: [MEDIUM] fcp-host verify_live_request: InstanceId::new() breaks instance-bound tokens + leaves non-bound tokens unchecked

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text: Closed in commit 93299d9c. CapabilityVerifier.instance_id is now Option<InstanceId>; existing new() constructor wraps Some(id) so all 50+ call sites are unchanged. New without_instance_binding(key, zone) constructor skips the match check while preserving parser-level non-Text rejection. fcp-host::verify_live_request switched to without_instance_binding — instance-bound tokens now reach the connector where the check is meaningful (the connector knows its own InstanceId; the gateway does not). Three regression tests cover the accepts-bound-token, rejects-malformed-in-unbound-mode, and no-claim-no-check paths. Staged only the 5qp7o hunks in fcp-host.rs via filtered patch; parallel agent's in-flight t623k work preserved unstaged in the worktree.

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text:
Verified: fix landed in commit 93299d9c (br-5qp7o).

Core (crates/fcp-core/src/capability.rs):
  - CapabilityVerifier::instance_id switched to Option<InstanceId> (line 1392).
  - New constructor CapabilityVerifier::without_instance_binding (line 1421).
  - verify_claims_inner skips match when instance_id is None, but still rejects non-Text INSTANCE_ID claim as a parser-level violation (lines 1555-1574).
  - Three regression tests at lines 2294/2332/2371:
      * without_instance_binding_accepts_token_that_declares_instance_id
      * without_instance_binding_still_rejects_non_text_instance_id
      * without_instance_binding_ignores_tokens_without_instance_claim

Host (crates/fcp-host/src/bin/fcp-host.rs):
  - verify_live_request now constructs verifier via without_instance_binding (line 1350) with an explanatory comment citing this bead.
  - InstanceId::new() no longer imported in this file.

Result addresses both arms of the original finding:
  (a) Instance-bound tokens are no longer spuriously rejected by the gateway — the gateway honestly declines to enforce, deferring to the connector process.
  (b) A non-bound token is no longer silently accepted-without-check; the verifier explicitly documents that instance enforcement does not happen at this layer.

Remaining (intentional, separate beads): capturing the connector's real instance_id from handshake so the host CAN enforce (Option 2 in the original finding) is larger work and not required for this close — the LOW-severity doc/defense-in-depth piece continues in t623k.

title: fcp.webhook-receiver: Inbound Event Gateway
description:
# Inbound Event Gateway Meta-Connector

**Force Multiplier:** Universal webhook receiver for external service integrations.

## Overview

Many services push events via webhooks (GitHub, Stripe, Discord, Slack, etc.). Instead of building separate webhook handlers for each service, this meta-connector provides a unified HTTP endpoint infrastructure with per-service configuration.

## Core Components

### 1. HTTP Endpoint Management
- Dynamic endpoint creation/deletion
- Unique URL per webhook source
- Support for path-based routing (`/webhooks/{service}/{id}`)
- Health check endpoints
- CORS and preflight handling
- Rate limiting per endpoint

### 2. Signature Verification (Per-Service)
- Pluggable verification strategies:
  - HMAC-SHA256 (GitHub, Stripe)
  - HMAC-SHA1 (legacy services)
  - Ed25519 (Discord)
  - API key header
  - Basic auth
  - Custom verification functions
- Timing-safe comparison
- Signature caching for replay prevention
- Failed verification alerting

### 3. Payload Transformation
- JSON schema validation
- Payload normalization to common event format
- Field mapping/extraction
- Nested payload unwrapping
- Binary payload handling (multipart)
- Compression support (gzip, deflate)

### 4. Event Routing to Zones
- Route events to appropriate FCP zones
- Support multiple destinations per event type
- Filter events based on payload content
- Priority-based routing
- Fan-out to multiple handlers

### 5. Retry/Dead-Letter Handling
- Configurable retry strategies:
  - Exponential backoff
  - Fixed interval
  - Fibonacci backoff
- Dead letter queue for failed events
- Manual retry interface
- Event replay capability
- TTL-based expiration

## Configuration Example

```toml
[[webhooks]]
name = "github-repo-events"
path = "/webhooks/github/main-repo"
signature_type = "hmac-sha256"
signature_header = "X-Hub-Signature-256"
secret = "${GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET}"
route_to = "zone.github-automation"
event_type_header = "X-GitHub-Event"

[[webhooks]]
name = "stripe-payments"
path = "/webhooks/stripe/payments"
signature_type = "stripe"
secret = "${STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET}"
route_to = "zone.billing"
retry_max = 5
retry_backoff = "exponential"

[[webhooks]]
name = "discord-interactions"
path = "/webhooks/discord/bot"
signature_type = "ed25519"
public_key = "${DISCORD_PUBLIC_KEY}"
route_to = "zone.discord-bot"
```

## Event Format (Normalized)

```json
{
  "id": "evt_abc123",
  "source": "github",
  "type": "push",
  "timestamp": "2024-01-15T10:30:00Z",
  "webhook_id": "github-repo-events",
  "payload": { ... },
  "metadata": {
    "delivery_id": "xyz789",
    "signature_valid": true,
    "received_at": "2024-01-15T10:30:00.123Z"
  }
}
```

## Success Criteria

- [ ] Support 10+ common webhook signature types
- [ ] Sub-50ms processing latency
- [ ] 99.9% uptime for webhook endpoints
- [ ] Complete audit trail for all received webhooks
- [ ] Zero data loss with dead-letter queue
- [ ] Hot-reload of webhook configurations

## Dependencies

- HTTP server framework (axum/actix-web)
- Persistent queue for dead-letter handling
- Zone routing system

## Security Considerations

- All secrets stored encrypted
- IP allowlisting per webhook (optional)
- Request size limits
- Timeout handling
- DDoS protection integration

# fcp.figma: Component extraction and inspection (FCP2)

## Goal
Expose Figma component metadata so agents can:

comments.text:
AFFECTED FILE: connectors/docusign/src/connector.rs:655-656

CURRENT STATE:
The stream_events operation is declared in the manifest and handled in invoke(), but the implementation returns an empty events array with a comment: 'Streaming is a placeholder — real implementation would poll Connect logs or use a webhook receiver. For now, return an empty events array.'

This means an agent calling docusign.stream_events gets an empty successful response, which is misleading — it looks like there are simply no events rather than that the feature is unimplemented.

FIX OPTIONS:
A) Implement real streaming via DocuSign Connect: Poll Connect change logs for envelope status changes. DocuSign Connect sends webhook notifications for envelope events; this connector could either register a webhook or poll the Connect logs API.
B) Remove stream_events from the manifest: If streaming isn't supported, don't declare the operation.
C) Return an explicit 'not implemented' error: Change the response to FcpError::NotImplemented with a clear message.

RECOMMENDATION: Option C as immediate fix (honest error), Option A as a future enhancement if there's user demand for DocuSign event streaming.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA:
- stream_events either works or returns a clear not-implemented error
- No empty-array 'success' response that hides the lack of implementation
- doctor() reports streaming support status honestly

title: [MOR/C3.4] Make capability constraints mandatory; reject null/empty constraints

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text: WHAT: Make capability constraints mandatory in CapabilityToken. Reject tokens with null/empty/missing constraints. Define a DENY-ALL default when constraints are absent (empty resource list = no operations allowed). WHY: H2 Adversarial found capability ceiling constraint bypass (#9, HIGH): if constraints are None, enforce_resource_constraints() is never called. An attacker-controlled issuer can issue unconstrained capabilities to arbitrary resources. J1 Deontic found this violates the default-deny principle — a null constraint should mean no access, not unlimited access. WHERE: crates/fcp-core/src/capability.rs — CapabilityToken verification path, specifically the constraint enforcement section. Change: if constraints is None, return Err(FcpError::CapabilityDenied) instead of skipping. Also update CapabilityToken construction to require constraints. ACCEPTANCE: (1) Tokens without constraints are rejected at verification time. (2) Token construction API requires constraints parameter (not Optional). (3) Empty constraint set = deny all (not allow all). (4) At least 4 tests: token with valid constraints passes, token with null constraints rejected, token with empty constraints rejected, token with overly-broad constraints still works (constraint narrowing is separate). ESTIMATED EFFORT: 1-2 days. DESIGN NOTE: This is one of the highest-impact-to-effort-ratio changes. Removing one Option<> wrapper eliminates an entire class of privilege escalation. DEPENDS ON: C3.1 (phantom tokens) — because the constraint check happens during verify(), and the phantom type ensures verify() is always called.

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text: CROSS-EPIC DEP: Depends on C1.3 (RevocationFreshnessClass in manifests) because both C1.3 and C3.4 add mandatory fields to the capability/manifest validation path. They should be coordinated to avoid two separate breaking changes to the validation pipeline. Implement them together in the same verification method.

title: fcp.figma: Plugin-like operations via REST API
description:
# fcp.figma: Plugin-like operations via REST API (FCP2)

## Goal
Provide higher-level **macro operations** that feel like “plugin actions” but are implemented purely via the Figma REST API + connector-side processing.

Rationale:
- Figma’s public API is mostly read + comments/webhooks.
- Many real workflows want “do the thing” operations (extract, package, compare, annotate) without writing a custom plugin.

## Scope
### Macro operations (examples)
- `figma.macro.export_component_bundle`:
  - input: file_key + node_ids
  - output: a canonical `ComponentBundle` object containing:
    - minimal node sub-tree
    - rendered assets (optional, bounded)
    - extracted tokens (optional)
    - metadata (component ids, names)
- `figma.macro.design_audit`:
  - detect missing tokens, inconsistent styles, naming issues
  - output: structured findings (no human text required)
- `figma.macro.annotate_with_comments` (write):
  - create a constrained set of comments referencing findings

### Boundaries
- These macros must be **compositions** of already-defined safe primitives (file access, export, comments).
- No attempt to emulate full plugin execution or arbitrary code.

## Capability model (illustrative)
- `figma.files.read`
- `figma.export.read` (if bundling includes exports)
- `figma.tokens.read` (if bundling includes tokens)
- `figma.comments.write` (only for annotate macros)

## FCP2 requirements
- Single-zone binding.
- NetworkConstraints pinned.
- Bounded outputs:
  - explicit max nodes per bundle
  - explicit max bytes for any embedded assets
- Structured logs include only IDs and counts (no raw design text).

## Deliverables
- Canonical types:
  - `ComponentBundle`
  - `DesignAuditFinding`
- Operation schemas:
  - `figma.macro.export_component_bundle`
  - `figma.macro.design_audit`
  - Optional: `figma.macro.annotate_with_comments`

## Test strategy (MUST)
- Mock-only tests for:
  - bundle construction determinism
  - bounds enforcement
  - comment annotation gating

## Acceptance criteria
- Macro ops are deterministic, bounded, and mechanically authorized.

# fcp.sentry: Issue listing and advanced search (FCP2)

## Goal
Provide efficient, correct access to Sentry **issue discovery** so agents can:
- list issues by project/environment
- search issues with filters (status, assignee, time range, error type)
- page reliably without missing/duplicating results

## Scope

  - status filters (unresolved/resolved/ignored)
  - environment filters (prod/staging)
  - time range filters
  - sort order (frequency, last seen, priority)

- Return **metadata** required for downstream workflows:
  - issue id
  - short title/message (PII risk: treat as tainted user content)

- `sentry.issues.read`

- Single-zone binding.
- NetworkConstraints pinned to the configured Sentry host.
- Treat issue titles/messages as **tainted** (they originate from external logs).
