title: Revocation System (RevocationObject/Registry/Chain)
description:
## Overview

Implement the revocation system as specified in V2 spec §14.3. This is CRITICAL security infrastructure - the spec explicitly states: "Without revocation, 'compromised device' recovery is mostly imaginary."

Revocations are mesh objects distributed like any other object and MUST be enforced before use.

## Background & Justification

When a device is compromised or a key is leaked, the mesh MUST be able to:
1. Revoke capabilities issued to that device
2. Revoke the device's issuer key (can no longer mint tokens)
3. Remove the device from the mesh entirely
4. Revoke compromised connector binaries
5. Force zone key rotation

Without revocation, security incidents cannot be recovered from.

## Normative Types (V2 Spec §14.3)

### RevocationObject
```rust
pub struct RevocationObject {
    pub header: ObjectHeader,
    /// ObjectIds being revoked
    pub revoked: Vec<ObjectId>,
    /// Scope of revocation
    pub scope: RevocationScope,
    /// Human-readable reason
    pub reason: String,
    /// When revocation becomes effective
    pub effective_at: u64,
    /// Optional expiry (None = permanent)
    pub expires_at: Option<u64>,
    /// Owner signature (revocations MUST be owner-signed)
    pub signature: Signature,
}
```

### RevocationScope
```rust
pub enum RevocationScope {
    /// Revoke capability objects/tokens
    Capability,
    /// Revoke issuer keys (node can no longer mint tokens)
    IssuerKey,
    /// Revoke node attestation (removes device from mesh)
    NodeAttestation,
    /// Revoke zone key (forces rotation)
    ZoneKey,
    /// Revoke connector binary (supply chain response)
    ConnectorBinary,
}
```

### RevocationEvent (Chain Node)
```rust
/// Hash-linked chain for revocation freshness
pub struct RevocationEvent {
    pub header: ObjectHeader,
    pub revocation_object_id: ObjectId,
    pub prev: Option<ObjectId>,
    /// Monotonic chain sequence number (NORMATIVE)
    /// Enables O(1) freshness comparison: seq_a > seq_b ⟹ a is fresher than b
    pub seq: u64,
    pub occurred_at: u64,
    pub signature: Signature,
}
```

### RevocationHead (Checkpoint)
```rust
/// Enables freshness semantics: tokens bound to a rev_head, verifiers MUST
/// have revocation state >= that head before accepting the token
pub struct RevocationHead {
    pub header: ObjectHeader,
    pub zone_id: ZoneId,
    pub head_event: ObjectId,
    /// Sequence number of head_event (NORMATIVE)
    /// Enables O(1) freshness comparison without chain traversal
    pub head_seq: u64,
    pub epoch_id: EpochId,
    pub quorum_signatures: Vec<(TailscaleNodeId, Signature)>,
}
```

### RevocationRegistry
```rust
pub struct RevocationRegistry {
    revocations: HashMap<ObjectId, RevocationObject>,
    bloom_filter: BloomFilter,  // Fast negative lookup
    /// Latest revocation head known for this zone
    pub head: Option<ObjectId>,
}

impl RevocationRegistry {
    /// Check if object is revoked (MUST be called before use)
    pub fn is_revoked(&self, object_id: &ObjectId) -> bool {
        // Fast path: bloom filter definitely-not check
        if !self.bloom_filter.might_contain(object_id.as_bytes()) {
            return false;
        }
        self.revocations.contains_key(object_id)
    }
}
```

## Implementation Requirements

### 1. RevocationObject Creation and Signing
- Owner-only signing (revocations are critical operations)
- Support all RevocationScope variants
- Validate effective_at is in future or now
- Propagate via mesh gossip immediately

### 2. RevocationEvent Chain
- Hash-linked for integrity
- Monotonic seq for O(1) freshness comparison
- Each new revocation creates new chain node
- Support chain traversal for full audit

### 3. RevocationHead Quorum
- Requires quorum signatures from mesh nodes
- Binds capability tokens to revocation state
- Verifiers MUST check token.rev_head <= local.head
- Enables freshness guarantees

### 4. Bloom Filter Optimization
- Fast negative lookup for non-revoked objects
- Size tuned for expected revocation volume
- Rebuild on restart from persistent store

### 5. Revocation Enforcement Points

EVERY capability verification MUST include:
```rust
fn verify_capability_token(&self, token: &CapabilityToken) -> Result<()> {
    // MANDATORY: Check revocation before any other validation
    if self.revocation_registry.is_revoked(&token.object_id) {
        return Err(Error::Revoked);
    }
    
    // Check revocation freshness
    if let Some(token_rev_head) = token.rev_head {
        if !self.revocation_registry.is_at_least(token_rev_head)? {
            return Err(Error::RevocationStateStale);
        }
    }
    
    // Continue with normal verification...
}
```

### 6. Revocation Propagation
- High-priority gossip (revocations supersede other traffic)
- Persist to local store immediately
- Trigger re-evaluation of cached capability decisions

## Use Cases by Scope

### Capability Revocation
- Revoke specific capability tokens (e.g., leaked token)
- Immediate effect on all nodes

### IssuerKey Revocation  
- Node can no longer mint new tokens
- Existing tokens remain valid until they expire
- Used for semi-trusted devices

### NodeAttestation Revocation
- Complete device removal from mesh
- All capabilities issued TO and BY this node revoked
- Used for compromised devices

### ZoneKey Revocation
- Forces zone key rotation
- All zone members must re-enroll
- Used for catastrophic key compromise

### ConnectorBinary Revocation
- Specific binary hash revoked
- Connectors using that binary MUST stop
- Used for supply chain incidents

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] RevocationObject with all scope variants
- [ ] Owner-only signature validation
- [ ] RevocationEvent hash-linked chain
- [ ] Monotonic seq numbers for O(1) freshness
- [ ] RevocationHead with quorum signatures
- [ ] RevocationRegistry with bloom filter
- [ ] is_revoked() check at all enforcement points
- [ ] Revocation freshness comparison
- [ ] High-priority gossip propagation
- [ ] Persistent storage with crash recovery
- [ ] Audit events for all revocation operations

## Dependencies

- Core Types (ObjectHeader, ObjectId, etc.)
- Zone Architecture (zone-scoped revocations)
- Capability System (enforcement points)
- MeshNode (gossip propagation)
- Observability (audit events)

title: fcp.browser - Headless Browser Automation Connector
description:
# fcp.browser - Headless Browser Automation Connector (FCP2)

## Strategic Context

### Value Assessment
**Strategic Value Score: 95/100** — Critical Tier 1 meta-connector.

**Why Critical**: This is the **"UNIVERSAL ADAPTER"** that lets agents interact with ANY web service, even those without APIs. Combined with vision models, this enables true general-purpose web automation. When there is no API, the browser connector is the fallback.

### Priority Matrix Position
- **Category**: Strategic Investment (High Value + Foundation)
- **Build Phase**: Phase 1 Foundation (immediate)

---

## V2 Specification Compliance (NORMATIVE)

### ConnectorArchetype
```rust
archetypes: vec\![ConnectorArchetype::Operational]
```
- **Operational**: Navigates, extracts, interacts with web pages

### ConnectorStateModel
```rust
state_model: ConnectorStateModel::SingletonWriter
```
- **SingletonWriter**: Browser session state, cookies, auth tokens
- State tracked: `{ session_id: String, cookies: CookieJar, auth_state: Option<AuthState> }`
- Lease required for session fencing

### ConnectorFormat
```rust
format: ConnectorFormat::Native
```
- **Native MANDATORY**: Requires OS-level process spawning for browser
- Sandboxed via seccomp/landlock
- Browser runs in separate process sandbox
- Note: WASI does not support browser automation

### NetworkConstraints (NORMATIVE)
```rust
NetworkConstraints {
    // DYNAMIC: host_allow populated from policy allowlist
    host_allow: vec\![/* policy-defined allowlist */],
    port_allow: vec\![80, 443],
    deny_localhost: true,
    deny_private_ranges: true,
    deny_tailnet_ranges: true,
    deny_ip_literals: true,
    require_sni: true,
    require_host_canonicalization: true,
}
```
**Note**: Browser navigation is ONLY permitted to explicitly allowlisted hosts.

### TaintFlags (NORMATIVE)
```rust
// ALL web content is adversarial
page_content.provenance.taint = TaintFlags::PUBLIC_INPUT
    | TaintFlags::EXTERNAL_INPUT
    | TaintFlags::PROMPT_SURFACE
    | TaintFlags::UNVERIFIED_LINK;

// Form inputs submitted by agent
form_data.provenance.taint = TaintFlags::USER_SUPPLIED;

// Extracted data inherits source taint
extracted_data.provenance.taint = page_content.provenance.taint;
```

### SafetyTier per Operation
| Operation | SafetyTier | Rationale |
|-----------|------------|-----------|
| `browser.navigate` | Risky | Visits external sites |
| `browser.screenshot` | Safe | Read-only capture |
| `browser.extract` | Safe | Read-only extraction |
| `browser.click` | Risky | Triggers actions |
| `browser.fill` | Risky | Submits data |
| `browser.submit` | Dangerous | Form submission |
| `browser.authenticate` | Dangerous | Credential handling |
| `browser.execute_js` | Dangerous | Arbitrary code execution |

---

## Agent Capabilities (Concrete Use Cases)

### Universal Web Access
- Navigate any allowlisted website
- Fill forms and submit data
- Extract structured data (scraping)
- Handle authentication flows
- Screenshot and visual verification
- PDF generation from web pages

### Automation Superpowers
- **Covers EVERY service without a dedicated connector**
- Handles legacy systems with only web UI
- Enables agents to do anything a human can do online
- Future-proof: works with any new website automatically

### Examples of Agent Workflows
```
"Log into this legacy system and export the report"
"Fill out this government form with the provided data"
"Screenshot the competitor pricing page daily"
"Extract product data from this e-commerce site"
"Complete this multi-step web workflow"
"Check if this website is accessible"
"Generate PDF invoice from this web portal"
```

---

## Flywheel Ecosystem Synergies

### ALL Other Connectors
**Universal fallback:**
- When no API exists, use browser
- Legacy system integration
- Complex web workflows

### Google AI/Vision Integration
- Screenshot → vision model analysis
- Visual understanding of pages
- Layout comprehension

### Vector DB Integration
- Scraped content → embeddings
- Web page indexing
- Content similarity search

### Agent Mail Integration
- Web form results → agent threads
- Screenshot reports
- Workflow status notifications

---

## Technical Implementation Notes

### Architecture
```
FCP Connector
      ↓
Browser Controller
      ↓
Chromium/Playwright
      ↓
Web (allowlisted hosts only)
```

### Recommended Crates
- `chromiumoxide` — Chrome DevTools Protocol
- `fantoccini` — WebDriver client
- `headless_chrome` — Chrome automation
- `image` — Screenshot handling

### Browser Options
| Engine | Recommendation |
|--------|----------------|
| Chromium | **Preferred** |
| Firefox | Supported |
| WebKit | Limited support |

### Security Hardening
- Browser runs with minimal permissions
- No extension installation
- Disk access disabled
- Network restricted to allowlist

---

## Zone Architecture

### Recommended Zones
| Zone | Description | Capabilities |
|------|-------------|--------------|
| `z:web:browser:allowlist` | Allowlisted sites | Navigate + extract |
| `z:web:browser:auth` | Auth-enabled | Can handle login |
| `z:web:browser:restricted` | Minimal | Screenshot only |

### Security Considerations
- EVERY navigated URL is adversarial
- Content extraction requires sanitization
- Form submission is high-risk
- JavaScript execution is DANGEROUS

---

## Manifest Archetypes (Closed Set)
- `operational` — Web interactions

---

## External Surface

### NetworkConstraints
Default-deny; DYNAMIC allowlist:
- Policy specifies permitted hosts
- No implicit wildcards
- Subdomain matching explicit

### Credential Injection
- Site credentials via egress proxy
- Session cookies managed securely
- Never persist login state

---

## Capability Model

### Navigation Operations
- `browser.navigate` — Load URL (allowlisted)
- `browser.back` / `browser.forward` — History navigation
- `browser.refresh` — Reload page

### Extraction Operations
- `browser.screenshot` — Capture page
- `browser.extract` — DOM extraction
- `browser.pdf` — Generate PDF

### Interaction Operations
- `browser.click` — Click element
- `browser.fill` — Fill form field
- `browser.submit` — Submit form (Dangerous)
- `browser.authenticate` — Login flow (Dangerous)

### Advanced Operations
- `browser.execute_js` — Run JavaScript (Dangerous)
- `browser.wait` — Wait for condition
- `browser.scroll` — Scroll page

---

## Operations (Representative)

### Navigate to URL
```json
{
  "operation": "browser.navigate",
  "url": "https://allowlisted-site.com/page",
  "wait_for": "networkidle"
}
```

### Take Screenshot
```json
{
  "operation": "browser.screenshot",
  "selector": "#main-content",
  "format": "png",
  "full_page": false
}
```

### Extract Data
```json
{
  "operation": "browser.extract",
  "selectors": {
    "title": "h1.title",
    "price": ".price-value",
    "description": ".product-desc"
  }
}
```

### Fill Form
```json
{
  "operation": "browser.fill",
  "fields": [
    {"selector": "#email", "value": "test@example.com"},
    {"selector": "#message", "value": "Hello"}
  ]
}
```

---

## Tests

### Unit Tests (Mock-Only)
- Command serialization
- Response parsing
- Selector validation
- Allowlist enforcement

### Integration Tests
- Mock browser responses
- Multi-step navigation
- Form interaction simulation
- Error handling

### E2E Compliance
- Validates NetworkConstraints (allowlist only)
- Dangerous operation approval flow
- Content taint propagation
- Audit logging

---

## Acceptance Criteria
- Passes connector compliance runner (static + dynamic)
- No real web navigation in unit tests
- URL allowlist enforced
- Screenshot capture functional
- DOM extraction works
- Form filling works
- JavaScript execution requires approval
- All V2 NORMATIVE requirements satisfied

title: CLI: fcp new <name> (Connector scaffold + compliance precheck)
description:
# CLI: `fcp new <name>` (Connector scaffold + compliance precheck)

## Goal
Make it fast and safe to create a new **FCP2-compliant** connector crate by generating a correct skeleton (manifest + SDK surface + tests) and running mechanical prechecks.

## Context
We will build many connectors (Telegram, Discord, etc.). The highest leverage DX improvement is a generator that enforces:
- single-zone binding,
- default-deny NetworkConstraints,
- secretless operation by default (no secrets on disk; no logging secrets),
- structured JSON logging,
- unit test + E2E scaffolding,
- and a clear “what you must fill in” checklist.

This command is **developer tooling**. It must not weaken production security assumptions.

## Scope
In scope:
- Create a new connector crate with a minimal-but-correct FCP2 skeleton.
- Emit a default manifest with placeholder capabilities, sandbox profile, and NetworkConstraints.
- Emit placeholder operations and the correct receipts / error taxonomy wiring.
- Create deterministic unit test scaffolding and an E2E script skeleton.
- Run mechanical validation checks and print actionable diagnostics.

Out of scope:
- Any compatibility shim for legacy FCP1 protocols.
- Generating real credentials or storing secrets.

## Command UX (proposal)

### Basic usage
```bash
fcp new fcp.myservice
```

### Optional flags
- `--archetype request-response|streaming|bidirectional|polling|webhook|queue|file|database|cli|browser`
- `--zone z:project:<name>` (default: `z:project:default` or prompt)
- `--no-e2e` (if generating only unit test scaffolding)
- `--dry-run` (print planned files without writing)
- `--check` (validate an existing connector directory)

### Outputs
- Prints:
  - created file list
  - next steps
  - compliance precheck results (pass/fail with reasons)
- Supports `--json` output like the rest of `fcp-cli`.

## Skeleton contents (must generate)

### 1) Cargo crate
- Path: `connectors/<name>/`
- Library crate (or bin, depending on repo conventions) with:
  - minimal `Cargo.toml`
  - dependency on `fcp-sdk`
  - `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`

### 2) Manifest
Generate an initial FCP2 manifest that is:
- syntactically valid TOML
- references:
  - connector id
  - version
  - zone binding (single-zone)
  - capabilities list
  - sandbox profile
  - NetworkConstraints (default deny)

### 3) Operations + schemas
- Provide placeholder operations that demonstrate:
  - typed input/output schemas
  - error taxonomy usage (FCP-XXXX)
  - receipt emission
  - tracing fields (`correlation_id`, `zone_id`, `connector_id`, `operation_id`)

### 4) Tests
- Unit test scaffold:
  - a “happy path” operation test using a mock transport
  - negative tests for missing capability / denied NetworkConstraints
  - redaction test: assert secrets are never logged

- E2E scaffold:
  - a script or harness integration that:
    - installs the connector
    - invokes an operation
    - verifies DecisionReceipt / AuditEvent shape
    - exercises default-deny failure path

## Mechanical prechecks (must run)
At creation time (and for `--check`), run:
- Manifest validation
- Connector compliance checklist (structure + fields)
- NetworkConstraints default-deny invariant
- “no secrets on disk” lint (no examples with plaintext tokens)

These checks should reuse the platform’s mechanical compliance runner where possible.

## Acceptance Criteria
- `fcp new <name>` creates a connector skeleton that builds in the workspace.
- Generated connector starts V2-only and includes no FCP1 language or compatibility shims.
- Generated manifest includes single-zone binding + default-deny NetworkConstraints.
- Generated tests include at least:
  - happy path
  - default deny
  - redaction
- `fcp new --check` produces actionable diagnostics and supports `--json`.

title: fcp.semanticscholar connector - Academic paper search and citation analysis
description:
# fcp.semanticscholar - Academic Paper Search and Citation Analysis Connector (FCP2)

## Goal
Provide an FCP2-compliant Semantic Scholar connector for paper search, citations, and metadata retrieval under safe NetworkConstraints and input validation.

## Zone model (mechanical)

<!-- fcp2-single-zone-note -->
**FCP2 single-zone binding note:** A connector instance binds to exactly one `ZoneId` for its entire lifetime.
The connector MUST NOT multiplex multiple zones internally.

Recommended deployment pattern: run separate connector instances in separate zones with different capability grants/policies.

## Strategic Context

### Value Assessment
**Strategic Value Score: 77/100** — Specialized Tier 3 connector (Research family).

**Why Critical**: Semantic Scholar is an **AI-powered academic search engine** with 200M+ papers and rich citation analysis. Complements ArXiv with citation graphs, paper recommendations, and AI-extracted insights. Essential for comprehensive research automation.

### Priority Matrix Position
- **Category**: Specialized Investment (Research + AI-Enhanced)
- **Build Phase**: Phase 3 Enterprise (weeks 9-12)

### ArXiv Comparison
- **ArXiv**: Raw preprints, full PDFs, direct source
- **Semantic Scholar**: Citation graphs, abstracts, AI-enhanced metadata, cross-platform coverage
- Use together for complete research access

---

## Agent Capabilities (Concrete Use Cases)

### Paper Discovery
- Semantic search for papers
- Author search
- Citation-based exploration
- Venue/conference filtering

### Citation Analysis
- Citation counts and trends
- Influential citations identification
- Citation graph traversal
- Paper influence metrics

### Research Intelligence
- Paper recommendations
- Author influence metrics
- Field of study analysis
- Temporal trend analysis

### Examples of Agent Workflows
```
"Find influential papers on attention mechanisms"
"Who are the top authors in NLP?"
"What papers cite this foundational work?"
"Get citation counts for these papers"
"Find related work for my research topic"
"Analyze citation trends for transformers"
"Identify seminal papers in this field"
```

---

## Flywheel Ecosystem Synergies

### ArXiv Integration
**Complete research stack:**
- Semantic Scholar for discovery and metadata
- ArXiv for full PDF access
- Combined for comprehensive literature review

### CASS (Context-Aware Semantic Search)
- Leverage S2 embeddings
- Build research knowledge base
- Semantic paper discovery

### Vector DB Integration
- Store paper embeddings
- Similarity search across corpus
- Research recommendation engine

### AI Provider Integration
- Summarize paper abstracts
- Generate literature reviews
- Extract key findings

### Agent Mail Integration
- Research updates → agent threads
- Collaboration on literature reviews
- Paper recommendations sharing

---

## Technical Implementation Notes

### API Surface
- **Paper Search** — Full-text and semantic search
- **Paper Details** — Metadata and citations
- **Author Search** — Author information
- **Recommendations** — Related papers
- **Citations API** — Citation graph data

### Recommended Crates
- `reqwest` — HTTP client
- `serde_json` — JSON handling

### Authentication
- API key required for higher rate limits
- Unauthenticated access available (limited)

### Paper IDs
Multiple ID formats supported:
- S2 ID: `649def34f8be52c8b66281af98ae884c09aef38b`
- DOI: `10.18653/v1/N18-1202`
- ArXiv: `arXiv:1706.03762`
- PMID, MAG, ACL, etc.

---

## Zone Architecture

### Recommended Zones
| Zone | Description | Capabilities |
|------|-------------|--------------|
| `z:research:s2:full` | Full access | All operations |
| `z:research:s2:search` | Search only | Discovery |
| `z:research:s2:citations` | Citation data | Graph analysis |

### Data Considerations
- Academic papers are generally public
- Some metadata may be incomplete
- Citation data is valuable IP

---

## Manifest Archetypes (Closed Set)
- `operational` — REST API operations

---

## External Surface

### NetworkConstraints
Default-deny; allow only:
- `api.semanticscholar.org:443`

### Credential Injection
- API key via `CredentialId` (optional but recommended)
- Never write credentials to disk

---

## Capability Model

### Read Operations
- `s2.papers.search` — Search papers
- `s2.papers.get` — Get paper details
- `s2.papers.citations` — Get citing papers
- `s2.papers.references` — Get referenced papers
- `s2.authors.search` — Search authors
- `s2.authors.get` — Get author details
- `s2.recommendations` — Get paper recommendations

---

## Operations (Representative)

### Search Papers
```json
GET /graph/v1/paper/search
Query params:
  query: attention is all you need
  fields: title,abstract,year,citationCount,authors
  limit: 10
```

### Get Paper Details
```json
GET /graph/v1/paper/{paper_id}
Query params:
  fields: title,abstract,year,citationCount,influentialCitationCount,references,citations
```

Response:
```json
{
  "paperId": "649def34f8be52c8b66281af98ae884c09aef38b",
  "title": "Attention Is All You Need",
  "abstract": "...",
  "year": 2017,
  "citationCount": 100000,
  "influentialCitationCount": 5000,
  "authors": [{
    "authorId": "1234",
    "name": "Ashish Vaswani"
  }]
}
```

### Get Citations
```json
GET /graph/v1/paper/{paper_id}/citations
Query params:
  fields: title,year,citationCount,authors
  limit: 100
```

### Get Author
```json
GET /graph/v1/author/{author_id}
Query params:
  fields: name,paperCount,citationCount,hIndex,papers
```

### Get Recommendations
```json
GET /recommendations/v1/papers/forpaper/{paper_id}
```

---

## Research Workflow Patterns

### Literature Review
1. Start with seed topic/paper
2. Get recommendations
3. Traverse citation graph
4. Extract influential papers
5. Build annotated bibliography

### Author Analysis
1. Identify key researchers
2. Get publication history
3. Analyze citation impact
4. Track collaboration networks

### Field Mapping
1. Start with foundational papers
2. Follow citation chains forward
3. Identify research branches
4. Map evolution of ideas

---

## Rate Limiting

### API Limits
- Unauthenticated: 100 requests/5 minutes
- With API key: 1 request/second sustained
- Respect 429 responses

### Best Practices
- Batch requests where possible
- Cache results for repeated queries
- Use pagination efficiently

---

## Tests

### Unit Tests (Mock-Only)
- Search query construction
- Paper ID normalization
- Citation parsing
- Author data handling

### Integration Tests
- wiremock-based API simulation
- Citation graph traversal
- Multi-paper scenarios

### E2E Compliance
- Validates NetworkConstraints
- Rate limit enforcement
- Audit logging

---

## Acceptance Criteria
- Passes connector compliance runner (static + dynamic)
- No real S2 calls in unit tests
- Paper search works
- Citation data accessible
- Author search functional
- Recommendations work
- Multiple paper ID formats supported

title: [CONNECTORS-V3] New Connector Expansion: 36 connectors across messaging, cloud, database, developer, productivity, commerce, communication, and emerging ecosystems
description:
# New Connector Expansion Program (V3-native)

## Goal
Expand the FCP connector library from 89 existing connectors to 125 total connectors by adding 36 strategically selected new connectors across messaging, cloud infrastructure, databases, developer platforms, productivity, commerce, communication, and high-value emerging ecosystems.

This campaign is the execution-ready version of the connector-gap analysis. Future contributors should be able to implement directly from these beads without reopening the original planning discussion.

## Why this campaign exists
FCP's core value proposition is that AI agents can operate through one secure protocol across many external systems. Every missing connector is a real workflow the agent cannot automate.

The campaign is driven by three inputs:
1. The current Flywheel connector inventory and its remaining coverage gaps.
2. The latest OpenClaw channel ecosystem, especially the messaging and collaboration surfaces that are broadly useful rather than niche.
3. The most universal 2026 integration categories for agent workflows: communication, cloud, data, deployment, knowledge, commerce, and scheduling.

## Prioritization logic
- **Tier 1** focuses on the most accretive universal gaps: broad messaging, major clouds, and key databases.
- **Tier 2** covers high-utility professional tools that extend real agent workflows once core coverage exists.
- **Tier 3** captures important but narrower ecosystems and regional platforms.

Within Tier 1, the campaign deliberately balances:
- hosted SaaS APIs,
- self-hosted collaboration systems,
- bridge-backed connectors,
- federated/open ecosystems,
- cloud-control surfaces, and
- database/file-local execution patterns.

That mix is intentional: a strong connector platform cannot only optimize for polished hosted REST APIs.

## V3 protocol contract for every implementation bead
All new connectors in this campaign must be designed and verified as Flywheel Connector Protocol V3 connectors from the start.

That means every implementation path must converge on the following truths:
- `ConnectorRuntime` owns lifecycle, shutdown, and background contexts.
- `RetryLoop` owns retry semantics instead of hand-rolled connector-local loops.
- `ConnectorErrorMapping` translates transport, auth, timeout, and service failures truthfully.
- typed `OperationInfo` declares safety tier, risk level, and idempotency accurately enough for policy engines and operators to trust it.
- manifests express capabilities, prerequisites, network constraints, sandbox expectations, and operator setup requirements honestly.
- readiness, doctor, introspection, and conformance evidence must be operator-actionable rather than decorative.

## Campaign structure
The campaign is split into:
- tier epics per connector family,
- one feature bead per connector,
- internal child tasks that break each connector into contract/scoping, implementation, and verification phases,
- cross-cutting V3 acceptance and testing infrastructure beads,
- a final campaign verification gate.

The dependency model is intentional:
- early scoping tasks depend on the shared V3 acceptance contract and `OperationInfo` taxonomy,
- implementation tasks depend on the archetype checklists and scaffold templates,
- terminal verification tasks depend on shared readiness/test/compliance infrastructure,
- the final verification sweep depends on every connector's terminal verification bead.

## Expanded connector scope
The merged roadmap now includes 36 new connectors and explicitly folds in the most valuable OpenClaw-adjacent additions that were missing from the earlier draft:
- Mattermost
- Nextcloud Talk

Those were added because they are highly general, complementary to existing chat coverage, and important for self-hosted/regulatory environments.

## Success criteria
Success for this campaign means:
- 36 new connectors are fully planned and implementation-ready.
- The end state is 125 total connectors (89 existing + 36 new).
- Every connector bead is self-contained enough that future agents can work from Beads alone.
- Every connector path is explicitly V3-native rather than retrofitted later.
- Final verification can prove campaign completeness without caveats about missing manifests, unclear safety semantics, or under-specified bridge/operator requirements.

title: [T1-MSG] Tier 1 Messaging: WhatsApp, Teams, Signal, Matrix, iMessage, Mattermost, Nextcloud Talk
description:
# Tier 1 Messaging Connectors

## Why messaging is still the biggest connector gap
FCP already covers Telegram, Discord, Slack, and Google Chat, but the highest-leverage missing channels are still broad messaging and collaboration surfaces. This epic now includes both the mainstream global platforms and the highest-value self-hosted complements so the campaign does not overfit to hosted SaaS alone.

## Connectors in scope
- **WhatsApp**: highest-impact global messaging channel, Meta Cloud API, webhook-driven business messaging
- **Microsoft Teams**: dominant enterprise collaboration surface, Bot Framework + Microsoft Graph
- **Signal**: privacy-focused messaging via `signal-cli` bridge, important for security-sensitive deployments
- **Matrix**: open federated messaging standard, self-hostable and protocol-driven
- **iMessage / BlueBubbles**: Apple ecosystem reach via a macOS bridge that exposes a stable HTTP/webhook surface
- **Mattermost**: self-hosted enterprise/team chat, technically adjacent to Slack and broadly useful in regulated/self-managed environments
- **Nextcloud Talk**: self-hosted SMB collaboration and messaging surface that complements the broader Nextcloud ecosystem

## Architectural through-line
Most connectors in this epic are V3 bidirectional or webhook-oriented connectors, but they split into three subfamilies:
1. **Hosted webhook APIs**: WhatsApp, Teams
2. **Bridge/daemon-backed connectors**: Signal, iMessage/BlueBubbles
3. **Self-hosted real-time collaboration APIs**: Matrix, Mattermost, Nextcloud Talk

Every connector in this epic must still satisfy the same V3 protocol obligations:
- `ConnectorRuntime` owns lifecycle and background contexts
- `RetryLoop` owns retries and timeout policy
- `ConnectorErrorMapping` translates API and bridge failures consistently
- typed `OperationInfo` declares safety, risk, and idempotency truthfully
- manifests declare capabilities, network constraints, and prerequisites honestly
- readiness/doctor outputs provide operator-actionable remediation

## Build-order rationale
Start with WhatsApp and Teams to anchor the hosted webhook pattern, then cover Signal and Matrix to exercise bridge and federated inbound flows, then land Mattermost and Nextcloud Talk as the high-value self-hosted complements, and keep BlueBubbles/iMessage after those because of the macOS bridge constraint.

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text:
Dependency note: WhatsApp (j05nu.1.1) should be built first as its webhook handler pattern (HMAC-SHA256 signature verification, Meta webhook challenge-response) establishes the template that Teams (Activity handler), Signal (bridge polling), and Matrix (long-poll /sync) will follow. Each connector is independently buildable but lessons from WhatsApp inform the others.

Architecture note for messaging connectors: all should support the fcp-webhook crate's WebhookHandler<V> trait for inbound messages where applicable. Signal and Matrix use polling instead of webhooks, so they need a different inbound pattern (polling loop with ConnectorRuntime background context).

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text: Scope expansion note: Mattermost and Nextcloud Talk were added here intentionally because they are the most accretive incremental additions beyond the earlier broad connector list. Both close important self-hosted collaboration gaps and exercise a different but still highly general V3 messaging archetype from purely hosted webhook APIs.

title: [T1-MSG.1] fcp.whatsapp — WhatsApp Cloud API Connector
description:
# WhatsApp Cloud API Connector

## Why
WhatsApp has 2B+ users globally and is the #1 messaging platform. Meta's Cloud API
is now the ONLY supported integration path (On-Premises API deprecated Oct 2025).
This is the single highest-impact connector we can add.

## API surface
Meta WhatsApp Cloud API (graph.facebook.com/v21.0):
- Send text, image, video, audio, document, location, contact messages
- Send interactive messages (buttons, lists, product catalogs)
- Send template messages (pre-approved for business-initiated conversations)
- Receive messages via webhook (message, status, error callbacks)
- Manage phone number profiles, business profiles
- Read/update message status (delivered, read)

## Auth model
- Business Account → System User → Access Token (long-lived)
- Phone Number ID identifies the sending number
- Webhook verification via hub.verify_token challenge-response

## Key operations
- whatsapp.send_text: Send text message to a phone number
- whatsapp.send_media: Send image/video/audio/document
- whatsapp.send_template: Send pre-approved template message
- whatsapp.send_interactive: Send button/list interactive message
- whatsapp.send_location: Send location pin
- whatsapp.mark_read: Mark a message as read
- whatsapp.get_profile: Get business profile
- whatsapp.update_profile: Update business profile

## Network constraints
- host_allow: [graph.facebook.com]
- Webhook inbound from Meta's IP ranges

## Rate limits
- 80 messages/second default per phone number (upgradable)
- 1000 unique users/24h for unverified businesses
- Template messages: varies by quality rating

## Connector archetype
Bidirectional (send + receive via webhook)

## Testing strategy
- Unit: wiremock for all send operations, template rendering, webhook parsing
- Integration: webhook signature verification, replay detection
- E2E: full send → webhook receive cycle with mock server

comments.text:
V3 contract for WhatsApp (Cloud API):

**Archetype**: Bidirectional + Webhook (follows Telegram exemplar pattern)
**Auth model**: WhatsApp Cloud API via Meta Business Platform. Requires: Business Account ID, Phone Number ID, Permanent System User Access Token (or short-lived user token with refresh). OAuth not supported by Cloud API — token-based only.
**Network**: graph.facebook.com:443 only. TLS required.

**Operations (first slice)**:
| Operation | SafetyTier | RiskLevel | IdempotencyClass | Capability |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| whatsapp.send_text | Risky | Medium | BestEffort | whatsapp.send |

| whatsapp.register_webhook | Risky | Medium | Strict | whatsapp.admin |

title: [T1-MSG.6] fcp.mattermost — Mattermost Self-Hosted Collaboration Connector
description:
# Mattermost Connector

## Why this belongs in Tier 1
Mattermost is one of the most valuable self-hosted enterprise chat additions because it complements Slack rather than duplicating it: same broad collaboration shape, but with on-prem and regulated-environment deployment models.

## API surface
- REST API for channels, posts, users, teams, files, reactions, and preferences
- WebSocket/event stream for inbound message events, thread updates, reactions, and presence
- Bot token or personal access token authentication depending on deployment model

## Expected operations
- `mattermost.posts.create|get|search|reply`
- `mattermost.channels.list|get|create_direct`
- `mattermost.teams.list|get`
- `mattermost.files.upload|get`
- `mattermost.reactions.add|remove`
- `mattermost.users.list|get`

## V3 considerations
- Bidirectional real-time connector with outbound REST mutations and inbound event handling
- Must model self-hosted base URL, websocket reconnect policy, channel/thread identity, and token redaction carefully
- Manifest must expose configurable host constraints rather than hard-coded SaaS hosts

Pin down the self-hosted deployment assumptions, base URL and auth model, operation inventory across posts or channels or teams or files or reactions or users, and how administrative or membership-changing actions should be risk-classified under V3.

comments.text:
V3 contract for Mattermost:

**Archetype**: Bidirectional + Webhook (self-hosted Slack alternative)
**Auth model**: Personal access token or OAuth 2.0 app. Server URL configurable (no default — self-hosted). Bot account or user account.
**Network**: Mattermost server URL (configurable). TLS recommended but not required (self-hosted). deny_localhost=false (server may be local), deny_private=false.

**Operations (first slice)**:
| Operation | SafetyTier | RiskLevel | IdempotencyClass | Capability |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| mattermost.send_message | Risky | Medium | BestEffort | mattermost.send |
| mattermost.update_message | Risky | Medium | BestEffort | mattermost.send |
| mattermost.delete_message | Dangerous | High | Strict | mattermost.send |
| mattermost.send_reaction | Risky | Low | BestEffort | mattermost.send |
| mattermost.get_channels | Safe | Low | None | mattermost.read |
| mattermost.get_channel_posts | Safe | Low | None | mattermost.read |
| mattermost.get_user | Safe | Low | None | mattermost.read |
| mattermost.search_posts | Safe | Low | None | mattermost.read |
| mattermost.upload_file | Risky | Medium | BestEffort | mattermost.send |
| mattermost.set_status | Risky | Low | BestEffort | mattermost.admin |
| mattermost.health | Safe | Low | Strict | mattermost.read |

**Webhook inbound**: Mattermost outgoing webhooks or slash commands. Signature verification via webhook secret. Event types: post_created, post_edited, post_deleted.

**Safety policy**: Message deletion is Dangerous (permanent on server). Server version >= 7.0 required for full API surface. WebSocket for real-time events. Rate limits: server-configurable, default 10 req/s.

**Provisioning**: Create bot account or personal access token in Mattermost System Console. Doctor checks: server reachable, token valid, bot has required permissions.

**Non-goals (first slice)**: No server administration, no team/channel creation, no user management, no plugin management, no compliance export.

# Nextcloud Talk Connector

## Why this belongs in Tier 1
Nextcloud Talk is the most broadly useful self-hosted SMB collaboration connector missing from the campaign. It complements hosted messaging tools while pulling FCP closer to privacy-conscious and self-managed deployments.

## API surface
- Nextcloud OCS / Talk APIs for rooms, messages, participants, mentions, attachments, and room metadata
- Webhook or event-driven inbound notifications where available, with polling fallback expectations documented explicitly
- App password or token-based authentication against a self-hosted Nextcloud instance

## Expected operations
- `nextcloud_talk.messages.send|get|list`
- `nextcloud_talk.rooms.list|get|create`
- `nextcloud_talk.participants.list|add|remove`
- `nextcloud_talk.files.upload|get`
- `nextcloud_talk.calls.get_state` where supported by the exposed API surface

## V3 considerations
- Self-hosted base URL and admin-configured app capabilities must be reflected truthfully in readiness and doctor outputs
- Must separate room-management writes from message-content writes in `OperationInfo` risk modeling
- Needs clear operator guidance around Talk app enablement, auth setup, and event-delivery expectations

description: Define the V3 contract for Nextcloud Talk before implementation expands. Pin down the supported Nextcloud and Talk app versions, auth model, room or message or participant or file operation inventory, event-delivery assumptions, and the boundary between Talk messaging, room administration, and broader Nextcloud functionality.

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text:
V3 contract for Nextcloud Talk:

**Archetype**: Bidirectional + Polling (self-hosted collaboration)
**Auth model**: Nextcloud user credentials (username + app password) or OAuth 2.0. Server URL configurable. App passwords recommended over user passwords.
**Network**: Nextcloud server URL (configurable). TLS recommended. deny_localhost=false (self-hosted), deny_private=false.

**Operations (first slice)**:
| Operation | SafetyTier | RiskLevel | IdempotencyClass | Capability |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| nextcloud_talk.send_message | Risky | Medium | BestEffort | nextcloud_talk.send |
| nextcloud_talk.delete_message | Dangerous | High | Strict | nextcloud_talk.send |
| nextcloud_talk.get_conversations | Safe | Low | None | nextcloud_talk.read |
| nextcloud_talk.get_messages | Safe | Low | None | nextcloud_talk.read |
| nextcloud_talk.get_participants | Safe | Low | None | nextcloud_talk.read |
| nextcloud_talk.send_reaction | Risky | Low | BestEffort | nextcloud_talk.send |
| nextcloud_talk.set_read_marker | Risky | Low | BestEffort | nextcloud_talk.send |
| nextcloud_talk.share_file | Risky | Medium | BestEffort | nextcloud_talk.send |
| nextcloud_talk.health | Safe | Low | Strict | nextcloud_talk.read |

**Polling**: Talk API uses polling (GET /ocs/v2.php/apps/spreed/api/v1/chat/{token}?lookIntoFuture=1). Long-poll with timeout. Cursor: lastKnownMessageId. No native WebSocket (Nextcloud-specific HPB may exist but not standard).

**Safety policy**: Message deletion is Dangerous (server removes content). File sharing uses Nextcloud Files API internally. Rate limits: server-configurable. Server version >= Talk 17.0 (Nextcloud 27+) for full API.

**Provisioning**: Create app password in Nextcloud Settings > Security. Doctor checks: server reachable, credentials valid, Talk app enabled, API version compatible.

**Non-goals (first slice)**: No conversation creation/administration, no call/video signaling, no file management (beyond sharing to chat), no Nextcloud Deck/Calendar integration.

title: Teams: tenant topology, app registration, and platform scope
description: Front-load the Teams-specific platform scoping that sits between the generic V3 contract and the concrete implementation tasks: tenant topology, bot registration model, channel/install prerequisites, conversation identity boundaries, and which Graph surfaces are truly in the first slice. This task exists because Teams is more platform-shaped than a simple chat API and future contributors should not have to reconstruct those deployment assumptions from scratch.

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text:
Teams platform scoping:

**Tenant topology**: Teams operates within Microsoft 365 tenants. Each tenant is an isolated Azure AD directory. A Teams app (bot) registers in a single tenant or as a multi-tenant app. For FCP, single-tenant registration is the default scope (admin-controlled, no marketplace listing).

**App registration model**: Teams bots use Azure Bot Service, registered in Azure AD. The bot has: Application (client) ID, Client Secret (or certificate), Tenant ID, and a Bot Framework messaging endpoint. Registration via Azure Portal > App Registrations > New Registration > Add Bot Channel.

**Channel topology**:
- Team -> Channels (standard, private, shared)
- Group chats (up to 250 members)  
- 1:1 chats
- Meeting chats (ephemeral, tied to meeting lifecycle)
Bot receives activities via the Bot Framework SDK's messaging endpoint.

**Conversation identity boundaries**:
- conversationId uniquely identifies a chat/channel context
- turnContext.activity contains sender, channel, team, tenant info
- Bot can only respond in conversations where it's installed
- Channel vs. personal scope determined by installation context

**Graph API surfaces (first slice)**:
- Chat messages: GET /teams/{id}/channels/{id}/messages (delegated or application)
- Channel messages: POST to send, PATCH to update
- Teams/channels: list, get (read-only in first slice)
- Users/members: list members of teams/channels
- Proactive messaging: requires serviceUrl + conversationId from prior activity

**Prerequisites**:
- Azure AD tenant with Teams license
- Azure Bot Service registration
- App manifest (teams-app-manifest.json) with bot section
- Admin consent for application permissions (optional; user consent for delegated)

**Non-goals (first slice)**: No Adaptive Cards authoring, no meeting integration, no Tabs/Task modules, no SharePoint integration, no Power Platform connectors, no Marketplace listing.

title: [T1-MSG.3] fcp.signal — Signal Messenger Connector (via signal-cli bridge)
description:
# Signal Connector (via `signal-cli` bridge)

## Why this belongs in Tier 1
Signal is one of the most important privacy-first messaging gaps in the current connector inventory. It does not have the raw global reach of WhatsApp, but it is disproportionately important for security-sensitive teams and users who explicitly avoid cloud-hosted chat platforms.

## API surface and operating model
This connector targets a self-hosted `signal-cli` bridge rather than a first-party bot API. That choice has architectural consequences that must stay visible in the implementation plan:
- outbound send operations are bridge-mediated request/response calls,
- inbound messages and group events are bridge-backed polling or event delivery flows,
- account registration and trust state are external prerequisites,
- readiness and doctor outputs must explain bridge health instead of pretending Signal is a plain hosted API.

## Expected operations
- `signal.messages.send_text|send_attachment`
- `signal.messages.receive|list`
- `signal.contacts.list|get`
- `signal.groups.list|get`
- `signal.identities.trust`
- `signal.profile.get`

## V3 implementation shape
This feature is intentionally broken into a five-step V3 ladder:
1. define the connector contract, auth boundary, bridge topology, safety matrix, and first-slice non-goals;
2. build typed config, client, state, and error mapping for the bridge boundary;
3. wire the V3 runtime, manifest, handlers, and introspection surfaces;
4. implement receive loops, group/message state handling, and attachment flows;
5. close with readiness, remediation guidance, privacy-safe observability, and explicit conformance evidence.

## Critical considerations
- The manifest must declare the bridge prerequisite truthfully.
- Logging and doctor output must never leak sensitive identifiers or message content.
- The first safe slice should stay conservative about identity/trust mutation semantics.
- The verification bead must prove the bridge-backed architecture is operable, not just compilable.

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text:
V3 contract for Signal (signal-cli bridge):

**Archetype**: Bridge/Daemon + Bidirectional (unique: requires external bridge process)
**Auth model**: signal-cli daemon must be running with registered phone number. Connector communicates via signal-cli JSON-RPC HTTP API (localhost). No direct Signal Protocol implementation — all crypto delegated to signal-cli.
**Network**: localhost only (bridge HTTP API). deny_private=true, deny_localhost=false.

**Bridge prerequisites**:
- signal-cli >= 0.13.0 installed and in PATH
- Phone number registered: signal-cli -u +NUMBER register / verify
- Daemon mode: signal-cli -u +NUMBER daemon --http --receive-mode=on-connection
- Bridge health endpoint: GET http://localhost:8080/v1/about

**Operations (first slice)**:
| Operation | SafetyTier | RiskLevel | IdempotencyClass | Capability |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| signal.send_message | Risky | Medium | BestEffort | signal.send |
| signal.send_reaction | Risky | Low | BestEffort | signal.send |
| signal.receive | Safe | Low | None | signal.read |
| signal.list_contacts | Safe | Low | None | signal.read |
| signal.list_groups | Safe | Low | None | signal.read |
| signal.get_group | Safe | Low | None | signal.read |
| signal.update_profile | Risky | Low | BestEffort | signal.admin |
| signal.delete_message | Dangerous | High | Strict | signal.send |
| signal.health | Safe | Low | Strict | signal.read |

**Safety policy**: End-to-end encryption handled by signal-cli. Connector never sees plaintext keys. Delete message is Dangerous (irreversible from sender perspective). Group creation/management deferred to future slice.

**Provisioning**: Manual phone registration via signal-cli CLI. Connector's doctor checks bridge availability, version, and registration status.

**Non-goals (first slice)**: No group creation/administration, no file attachments > 100MB, no Signal Desktop linking, no direct libsignal integration.

# Matrix Federated Messaging Connector

## Why this belongs in Tier 1
Matrix is the highest-value open and federated messaging addition in the campaign. It complements proprietary chat platforms by giving FCP a protocol-native path into self-hosted and federation-aware deployments.

## API surface and workflow role
The connector targets the Matrix Client-Server API and therefore needs to handle both read-heavy synchronization and write-capable room workflows:
- room and membership discovery,
- message and media send flows,
- sync-loop event ingestion,
- room state and membership transitions,
- configurable homeserver deployment assumptions.

## Expected operations
- `matrix.messages.send|get|list`
- `matrix.media.send|get`
- `matrix.rooms.list|get|join|leave`
- `matrix.members.list|invite`

1. define homeserver assumptions, auth boundary, `OperationInfo` safety semantics, and first-slice E2EE non-goals;
2. build typed client/config/error/state foundations;
3. wire runtime, manifest, operation handlers, and truthful introspection;
4. implement sync-loop state, membership, media, and event translation flows;
5. finish with readiness, federation-aware remediation guidance, observability, and conformance evidence.

## Critical considerations
- The first slice must be explicit about what is not yet supported around E2EE.
- Self-hosted homeserver configuration and federation caveats must appear in readiness and manifest surfaces.

title: [T1-MSG.5] fcp.imessage — iMessage Connector (macOS BlueBubbles bridge)
description:
# iMessage Connector (BlueBubbles bridge)

## Why this belongs in Tier 1
This connector gives the campaign an Apple ecosystem path without pretending Apple provides a normal bot platform. The realistic route is the BlueBubbles bridge, which exposes a stable HTTP/event surface over a macOS host that is already running Messages.app.

## API surface and operating model
This is a bridge-backed connector with strong local-privacy implications:
- outbound message and media sends are proxied through BlueBubbles,
- inbound message/chat updates come from bridge event delivery or polling,
- a macOS host is an explicit prerequisite,
- doctor/readiness output must surface host and bridge health truthfully.

## Expected operations
- `imessage.messages.send_text|send_attachment|get|search`
- `imessage.chats.list|get`
- `imessage.messages.mark_read`
- `imessage.sync.events`

## V3 implementation shape
The feature is deliberately structured as a five-step ladder:
1. define macOS/bridge prerequisites, auth boundary, safe first-slice operation inventory, and non-goals;
2. build typed config, bridge client, error mapping, and chat/message state foundations;
3. wire runtime, manifest, handlers, and introspection around a bridge-backed connector;
4. implement event delivery, chat/thread mapping, and media synchronization behavior;
5. close with operator guidance, bridge-health doctor checks, privacy-safe observability, and conformance evidence.

## Critical considerations
- The manifest must tell the truth about macOS and BlueBubbles prerequisites.
- Local/private deployment must not become an excuse for weak safety modeling.
- Logging and diagnostics must stay careful around message content and identifiers.
- Verification must prove bridge operability and remediation clarity, not just API happy paths.

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text:
Testing requirements (per project standard):

UNIT TESTS (50+ minimum, wiremock-based):
- All operations: success path, error paths (auth fail, rate limit, not found, server error)
- Client retry: 429 with retry-after, 500 backoff, cancellation during sleep
- Error mapping: every error variant → FcpError, is_retryable classification
- Config parsing: all auth modes, validation (both/neither auth), URL trim
- Webhook/event parsing: all message/event types, malformed payloads
- Serialization: request/response roundtrips

INTEGRATION TESTS (10+ minimum):
- ConnectorSuite: introspection returns correct operation count
- ComplianceSuite: default-deny for unconfigured operations  
- Full operation cycle: configure → invoke → response validation
- Rate limit exhaustion and recovery
- Shutdown: runtime.shutdown() propagates to client
- E2E compliance script passes

STRUCTURED LOGGING:
- Every operation emits tracing spans with connector_id, operation_id, duration_ms
- Retry events emit attempt, delay_ms, error fields
- All logs machine-parseable JSON

V3 contract for iMessage / BlueBubbles:

**Archetype**: Bridge/Daemon + Bidirectional (macOS-only via BlueBubbles server)
**Auth model**: BlueBubbles server password (HTTP basic auth to local bridge). Bridge handles Apple ID auth. macOS host required with Messages.app logged in.
**Network**: localhost only (BlueBubbles HTTP API, default port 1234). deny_private=true, deny_localhost=false.

**Bridge prerequisites**:
- macOS host with Apple ID signed into Messages.app
- BlueBubbles Server >= 1.9.0 running
- Bridge URL: http://localhost:1234
- Bridge password configured

**Operations (first slice)**:
| Operation | SafetyTier | RiskLevel | IdempotencyClass | Capability |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| imessage.send_text | Risky | Medium | BestEffort | imessage.send |
| imessage.send_attachment | Risky | Medium | BestEffort | imessage.send |
| imessage.send_reaction | Risky | Low | BestEffort | imessage.send |
| imessage.get_chats | Safe | Low | None | imessage.read |
| imessage.get_messages | Safe | Low | None | imessage.read |
| imessage.get_contacts | Safe | Low | None | imessage.read |
| imessage.mark_read | Risky | Low | BestEffort | imessage.send |

**Safety policy**: No message deletion (iMessage does not support programmatic delete via BlueBubbles). Reactions are tapbacks only. Media attachments capped at bridge limit. Platform-locked to macOS.

**Provisioning**: Install BlueBubbles Server on macOS, configure password, start server. Doctor checks bridge reachability, version, Apple ID login status.

**Non-goals (first slice)**: No group creation, no FaceTime, no message effects/animations, no Memoji, no iCloud sync management.

# Final Verification Sweep

This bead is the campaign-wide closeout gate after the connector expansion and the no-grandfathering V3 audit work land.

## Goal
Prove that the connector workspace is V3-conformant, test-complete, and operationally coherent: both the 36 new connectors in this campaign and the existing implemented connector inventory must satisfy the V3 contract or have completed their tracked remediation path.

## Required evidence
1. `cargo check --workspace --all-targets` succeeds via `rch`
2. `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` succeeds via `rch`
3. `cargo test --workspace` succeeds via `rch`
4. Every new connector and every existing implemented connector in scope demonstrates or has completed its tracked path to V3-native `ConnectorRuntime`, `RetryLoop`, `ConnectorErrorMapping`, and typed `OperationInfo`
5. Every manifest passes `fwc manifest fix --check` and expresses prerequisites/network constraints truthfully
6. Every connector has archetype-appropriate unit, integration, and E2E coverage attached to its implementation or remediation bead history
7. `fcp-conformance` / `fcp-e2e` evidence is updated where a new archetype or protocol surface required it
8. README and workspace inventory reflect the new connector count and the workspace-wide V3 compliance claim accurately
9. Bridge-backed and local-host connectors document dedicated environment assumptions and operator remediation paths
10. No implemented connector remains implicitly grandfathered outside the V3 acceptance contract

## Count correction
The expanded merged roadmap is 36 new connector features. Success means 89 existing connectors + 36 new connectors = 125 total connectors, all governed by the same V3 acceptance contract.

## Success criteria
- The campaign can claim V3 connector expansion completeness without caveats
- No connector remains on legacy retry/lifecycle patterns without an explicit tracked remediation bead
- No connector remains undocumented about bridge prerequisites, auth models, network constraints, or operator remediation
- Self-hosted and bridge-backed connectors are verified to the same truthfulness standard as hosted SaaS connectors
acceptance_criteria:
- workspace-wide `cargo check`, `cargo clippy`, and `cargo test` evidence is captured via `rch` and linked from the bead history
- every connector in scope has explicit unit, integration, and replayable E2E or host-backed verification evidence plus detailed structured logs and artifact locations

title: [CROSS-V3] Workspace-Wide V3 Connector Alignment: acceptance contract, archetype mapping, manifest policy, conformance checklist
description:
# Workspace-Wide V3 Connector Specification Alignment

## Goal
Create the cross-cutting acceptance contract that governs the entire connector inventory, not just newly planned connectors. This bead exists so no future implementation or retrofit task has to re-derive what “V3-compliant” means from scattered docs.

## No-grandfathering rule
The Flywheel Connector Protocol V3 contract applies to:
- every open bead in the new-connector expansion campaign,
- every existing implemented connector already shipped in the workspace,
- every shared harness or manifest/readiness pattern that those connectors rely on.

There are no implicit exemptions for older connectors. Existing implementations may require audit and remediation rather than greenfield implementation, but they are still bound by the same V3 truths.

## Why this exists
The workspace spans radically different connector archetypes: request-response APIs, webhook-driven messaging connectors, daemon/bridge connectors, database connectors, cloud-control connectors, and local-host/process/browser connectors. The V3 invariants must stay stable across all of them:
- `ConnectorRuntime` manages lifecycle and contexts
- `RetryLoop` owns retry behavior
- `ConnectorErrorMapping` defines error translation and retryability
- typed `OperationInfo` carries safety, risk, and idempotency semantics
- manifests declare capabilities, network constraints, and prerequisites truthfully
- readiness, doctor, introspection, and conformance evidence remain operator-actionable

## Outcome
This epic turns protocol truth into concrete reusable checklists, templates, policy anchors, and retrofit expectations for both new connectors and existing connector remediation work.

# Existing Connector Inventory Audit & Remediation

## Goal
Make the workspace-wide V3 claim true for the connectors that already exist today, not only the connectors being added in this expansion campaign.

## Why this is required
A connector platform cannot claim V3 conformance if older connectors are implicitly grandfathered onto legacy lifecycle, retry, manifest, readiness, or operation-metadata patterns. Existing connectors may differ by archetype and maturity, but they are still part of the product surface agents rely on.

## Scope
This epic covers the currently implemented connector inventory that predates the 36 new connectors in this campaign. The work is to inventory, classify, audit, retrofit, and close compliance gaps across the existing connector workspace in a disciplined, dependency-aware way.

## Expected outcome
By the time this epic closes, every existing implemented connector is either:
- demonstrably aligned with the workspace-wide V3 contract, or
- covered by explicit remediation beads that were created, executed, and closed as part of this audit wave.

No existing connector should remain outside tracked V3 accountability.

description:
AWS multi-service connector covering the most commonly used AWS services beyond S3
(which we already have). Uses aws-sdk-rust for native Rust AWS SDK integration.

## Services and operations
- **Lambda**: aws.lambda.invoke, aws.lambda.list_functions, aws.lambda.get_function,
  aws.lambda.create_function, aws.lambda.update_code
- **SQS**: aws.sqs.send_message, aws.sqs.receive_messages, aws.sqs.delete_message,
  aws.sqs.list_queues, aws.sqs.get_queue_attributes
- **SNS**: aws.sns.publish, aws.sns.subscribe, aws.sns.list_topics,
  aws.sns.list_subscriptions, aws.sns.create_topic
- **CloudWatch**: aws.cloudwatch.get_metrics, aws.cloudwatch.put_metric,
  aws.cloudwatch.describe_alarms, aws.cloudwatch.get_log_events
- **IAM**: aws.iam.list_users, aws.iam.get_user, aws.iam.list_roles,
  aws.iam.list_policies (read-only for safety)

## Auth model
- AWS credentials via environment (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID/AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY)
- Or secretless credential_id for egress proxy injection
- Region configuration required

## Architecture decision
Single connector crate with per-service modules rather than 5 separate crates.
This mirrors how aws-sdk-rust is structured and reduces manifest proliferation.
Each service is a module (lambda.rs, sqs.rs, sns.rs, cloudwatch.rs, iam.rs)
with its own operation set, but they share the AWS credential + region config.

## Network constraints
- host_allow: [*.amazonaws.com, *.aws.amazon.com]
- Region-specific endpoints

## Safety tiers
- Lambda invoke, SQS send/receive, SNS publish: Risky (side effects)
- IAM operations: Safe (read-only)
- Lambda create/update, SNS create_topic: Dangerous (infrastructure mutation)

## 4 subtasks: types/client/error, connector/manifest, per-service modules, tests

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text:
V3 contract for AWS:

**Archetype**: Cloud Control Plane (multi-service)
**Auth model**: AWS IAM credentials (access_key_id + secret_access_key), IAM role (instance profile), or STS assume-role. Region required. credential_id for secretless.
**Network**: *.amazonaws.com:443, *.aws.amazon.com:443. TLS required.

**Operations (first slice — S3/EC2/Lambda/STS focus)**:
| Operation | SafetyTier | RiskLevel | IdempotencyClass | Capability |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| aws.s3.list_buckets | Safe | Low | None | aws.s3.read |
| aws.s3.list_objects | Safe | Low | None | aws.s3.read |
| aws.s3.get_object | Safe | Low | None | aws.s3.read |
| aws.s3.put_object | Risky | Medium | Strict | aws.s3.write |
| aws.s3.delete_object | Dangerous | High | Strict | aws.s3.write |
| aws.ec2.describe_instances | Safe | Low | None | aws.ec2.read |
| aws.ec2.start_instance | Risky | Medium | Strict | aws.ec2.write |
| aws.ec2.stop_instance | Risky | Medium | Strict | aws.ec2.write |
| aws.ec2.terminate_instance | Dangerous | Critical | Strict | aws.ec2.write |
| aws.lambda.list_functions | Safe | Low | None | aws.lambda.read |
| aws.lambda.invoke | Risky | Medium | BestEffort | aws.lambda.write |
| aws.sts.get_caller_identity | Safe | Low | None | aws.iam.read |
| aws.health | Safe | Low | Strict | aws.iam.read |

**Safety policy**: Terminate instance = Dangerous/Critical. Delete operations across all services = Dangerous. IAM/permission operations deferred to Critical tier in future slice. Region scoping explicit in every operation input.

**Provisioning**: AWS credentials via environment, config file, or IAM role. Doctor: STS GetCallerIdentity validates credentials.

**Non-goals (first slice)**: No IAM management, no CloudFormation/CDK, no RDS/DynamoDB (separate connectors if needed), no billing/cost explorer, no VPC management.

title: [T1-DB.1] fcp.mysql — MySQL/MariaDB Database Connector
description: MySQL/MariaDB connector. Most widely deployed RDBMS globally. Operations: mysql.query (parameterized SELECT), mysql.execute (parameterized INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE), mysql.list_databases, mysql.list_tables, mysql.describe_table, mysql.explain (query plan), mysql.begin_transaction, mysql.commit, mysql.rollback. Auth: connection string (host/port/user/password/database) or credential_id. Uses mysql_async Rust crate for async MySQL protocol. Network: configurable host:port. Safety: query=Safe, execute=Risky, DDL=Dangerous. Parameterized queries mandatory to prevent SQL injection. Pattern closely mirrors our PostgreSQL connector. 3 subtasks.

comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text: Testing requirements: 50+ unit tests (wiremock), 10+ integration tests (ConnectorSuite/ComplianceSuite), E2E compliance script, structured JSON logging with connector_id/operation_id/duration_ms, retry telemetry with attempt/delay_ms/error. comments.author: jemanuel
comments.text:
SECURITY-CRITICAL TESTING for MySQL:
- Parameterized query injection test: verify $1, $2 placeholders prevent SQL injection
- Test with special characters in string parameters: quotes, semicolons, dashes, Unicode
- Connection string validation: reject connection strings with embedded commands
- Credential redaction: verify connection passwords never appear in Debug/Display/logs
- TLS enforcement: test that connections require TLS by default
- Query timeout: verify long-running queries respect context deadline
- Transaction isolation: test that concurrent transactions don't interfere

**Auth model**: File path only. No network credentials. File permissions enforced by OS.
**Network**: NONE. allowed_hosts=[], allowed_ports=[]. This is the only zero-network connector in the database family.

**Safety policy**: Parameterized queries only. WAL mode recommended. PRAGMA writes deferred to admin capability. ATTACH DATABASE deferred (security surface). File path must be within declared sandbox fs_writable paths.

**Implementation notes**: Uses rusqlite or sqlite3-sys. No reqwest needed (no HTTP). ConnectorRuntime for lifecycle. ConnectorErrorMapping maps rusqlite errors to FcpError. Health check: open database and run 'SELECT 1'.

comments.author: RoseAspen
comments.text:
V3 contract for Zoom:

**Archetype**: Request-response SaaS admin connector. First slice is outbound REST only; no inbound event receiver in this slice.
**Auth model**: Server-to-Server OAuth using the account-credentials grant with `account_id`, `client_id`, and `client_secret`. Authority is account-level admin context, not per-user delegated OAuth. `user_id` selects which user inside the installed account is targeted.
**Network**: `api.zoom.us` for REST API calls and `zoom.us/oauth/token` for token acquisition. TLS required. `deny_localhost=true` and `deny_private_ranges=true` remain appropriate.

**Operations (first slice)**:
| Operation | SafetyTier | RiskLevel | IdempotencyClass | Capability |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| zoom.meetings.list | Safe | Low | None | zoom.meetings.read |
| zoom.meetings.get | Safe | Low | None | zoom.meetings.read |
| zoom.meetings.create | Risky | Medium | Strict | zoom.meetings.write |
| zoom.meetings.update | Risky | Medium | Strict | zoom.meetings.write |
| zoom.meetings.delete | Dangerous | High | Strict | zoom.meetings.write |
| zoom.users.list | Safe | Low | None | zoom.users.read |
| zoom.users.get | Safe | Low | None | zoom.users.read |
| zoom.recordings.list | Safe | Low | None | zoom.recordings.read |
| zoom.webinars.list | Safe | Low | None | zoom.webinars.read |
| zoom.health | Safe | Low | Strict | zoom.users.read |

**Event/webhook stance**: Zoom supports webhook subscriptions, and Server-to-Server OAuth apps can manage them with the account-credentials grant, but this connector's first slice defers webhook subscription management and inbound event delivery. Future event work must request the marketplace event-subscription scopes plus event-specific read scopes.

**Non-goals (first slice)**: No Zoom Chat, Phone, Team Chat, admin/account settings, reports, meeting summaries, registrants/polls/live-stream controls, webinar create/update/delete, recording download/delete/recover, or webhook receiver.

**Truthfulness note**: The official Zoom Meeting API currently supports webinar creation, but the implemented connector slice is list-only for webinars today; the manifest now reflects the actual implemented inventory and the actual outbound hosts (`api.zoom.us` and `zoom.us/oauth/token`).

title: [CROSS-V3] Connector Test Infrastructure: unit/integration/E2E harnesses, detailed logging, compliance suite
description:
# Cross-Cutting Test Infrastructure

## Goal
Establish shared V3-native test patterns and a reusable compliance harness so both new connectors and existing connectors are verified against the current Flywheel Connector Protocol V3 contract instead of legacy ad hoc expectations.

## Why this bead exists early
The workspace spans messaging, cloud, database, developer platform, productivity, commerce, communication, and local-host/process archetypes. Without shared scaffolding, each connector team or retrofit pass would re-invent retry tests, webhook fixtures, manifest validation, readiness checks, and conformance evidence.

## Deliverables

### 1. Connector scaffold template update
Update `fwc` scaffold generation so new connector crates start V3-native by default:
- `ConnectorRuntime`, `RetryLoop`, and `ConnectorErrorMapping` already wired into the generated client and error paths
- wiremock-based unit test scaffolding for success, retry, timeout, cancellation, auth failure, and config validation

File: fuzz/fuzz_targets/fcpc_frame.rs:15-36

Finding: the fuzz body only exercises `FcpcFrameHeader::decode`, `FcpcFrame::decode[_with_limit]`, and `FcpcFrameFlags::from_bits_truncate`, then drops every success case.

title: [LOW] fcp-graphql GraphqlClient constructors build a fresh HttpClient per call (foot-gun, not a leak)
description:
crates/fcp-graphql/src/client.rs:302-320: both GraphqlClient::new and GraphqlClient::with_config call HttpClientBuilder::new().build() and wrap the result in Arc<HttpClient>. Each constructed GraphqlClient owns its own connection pool.

GraphqlClient implements Clone by sharing the Arc<HttpClient>, so the intended pattern is "construct once, clone everywhere." A caller that instead calls GraphqlClientBuilder::new(url).build() per request will spawn a fresh pool each time; those pools release when the client drops, but HTTP connections held in the pool do not close eagerly.

Not a leak, but the API surface invites the foot-gun. Improvements:

  (a) Accept an Arc<HttpClient> in the builder so callers can share a single pool across many GraphqlClients.
  (b) Add a #[doc] warning on GraphqlClient::new explicitly calling out that each new instance spawns its own pool and recommending Clone.
  (c) Cache-by-endpoint: GraphqlClientBuilder could intern HttpClient instances by (endpoint, tls config, timeout) to share pools across callers. More complex; only if the foot-gun bites in production.

Files: crates/fcp-graphql/src/client.rs:302-320 (constructors), client.rs:193-264 (builder).

title: fcp-core VerifiedToken does not encode whether instance binding was enforced
description:
Evidence:
- crates/fcp-core/src/capability.rs:1407-1425 exposes CapabilityVerifier::without_instance_binding() as a public constructor that intentionally skips the instance match check.
- crates/fcp-core/src/capability.rs:1440-1467 still returns the same CapabilityToken<CryptographicallyVerified> marker from verify(), regardless of whether the verifier was constructed with new(...) or without_instance_binding(...).
- crates/fcp-host/src/bin/fcp-host.rs:1491-1497 uses without_instance_binding() in the live request path.

Impact:
- The Rust type system proves signature/timing/zone/op checks ran, but it does NOT prove instance binding ran. Downstream code can receive a VerifiedToken and assume full capability-token enforcement even when the host explicitly skipped the instance check.
- This makes an auth-critical invariant convention-only: callers must know out-of-band which verifier mode produced the token.

Fix shape:
- Split the verification state so instance-bound and instance-unbound verification produce different marker types, or carry an explicit verified binding mode in the returned token/claims surface.
- Reserve the stronger VerifiedToken surface for fully bound checks; make gateway-level partial verification explicit in the type/API.

title: fcp-graphql: GraphQL Client Infrastructure Library
description:
# fcp-graphql: GraphQL Client Infrastructure Library


## Goal
Provide a shared, typed GraphQL client library for connectors with retries/pagination/subscriptions, mapping errors to the FCP taxonomy and fully mock-tested.

## Overview
Shared GraphQL client library for connectors that interface with GraphQL APIs (Linear, GitHub, Notion, Shopify, etc.).

## Features

### Core Client
- Async GraphQL client with connection pooling
- Query/mutation/subscription support
- Automatic retry with exponential backoff
- Request batching and deduplication
- Query complexity estimation

### Query Building
- Type-safe query builder
- Fragment composition
- Variable handling
- Directive support

### Pagination
- Cursor-based pagination (Relay-style)
- Offset-based pagination
- Automatic page traversal
- Total count estimation

### Subscriptions
- WebSocket transport
- Reconnection handling
- Subscription multiplexing
- Heartbeat management

### Introspection
- Schema introspection caching
- Type validation
- Deprecation warnings

### Error Handling
- GraphQL error parsing
- Partial data handling
- Network error recovery
- Rate limit detection

## Dependencies
- reqwest (HTTP)
- tokio-tungstenite (WebSocket)
- serde_json
- fcp-core

## Consumers
- fcp.linear (GraphQL-only API)
- fcp.github (GraphQL API v4)
- fcp.notion (REST+GraphQL hybrid)
- fcp.shopify (Admin API)

## Testing
- Mock GraphQL server
- Response recording/playback
- Schema validation tests

## Acceptance Criteria
- The functionality described in this bead is implemented with typed schemas + validation (no unstructured “stringly” interfaces).
- Errors map to the FCP error taxonomy with correct retry semantics and no secret/PII leakage.
- Mock-only unit/integration tests cover success paths and common failures and emit structured JSON logs per `flywheel_connectors-1n78.35`.

title: fcp.jira: Bidirectional Beads sync integration
description:
# fcp.jira: Bidirectional Beads sync integration (FCP2)

## Goal
Implement **bidirectional synchronization** between Flywheel Beads issues and Jira issues for the connector’s bound zone.

This enables:
- Jira → Beads: convert incoming Jira work into native Beads (agent-ready tasks)
- Beads → Jira: propagate Beads updates back into Jira to keep humans in their existing workflows

## Non-goals
- “Backwards compatibility” with any older sync format or FCP1 behavior.
- Cross-zone sync from a single connector instance (still single-zone bound).

## Core requirements (hard)
- **Deterministic mapping** (same inputs produce same object updates).
- **Loop prevention** (Jira update triggers Beads update triggers Jira update… must stop).
- **Conflict detection** (concurrent edits) with explicit policy:
  - default: fail-closed + raise a conflict event
  - optional: last-write-wins only if explicitly enabled
- **Idempotency**: repeated webhook deliveries or retries must not duplicate issues/comments.

## Scope
### Mapping surface (minimum viable)
- Bead fields ↔ Jira fields:
  - title ↔ summary
  - description ↔ description (ADF/markdown conversion)
  - status ↔ workflow status
  - priority ↔ priority mapping
  - labels ↔ labels
  - assignee ↔ assignee
  - due date ↔ duedate
  - estimates ↔ timeoriginalestimate (if policy allows)
  - bead_id ↔ a dedicated custom field (or label) for stable correlation

### Sync directions
- `jira_to_beads`
- `beads_to_jira`
- `bidirectional`

### Event sources
- Jira webhooks (issue created/updated/commented/transitioned).
- Beads change events (local event stream from the platform).

## Connector state model (FCP2)
This bead MUST use the platform connector-state mechanism:
- Store a persistent mapping table:
  - `bead_id ↔ jira_issue_id/key`
  - last_seen_revision / fingerprint
  - last_sync_origin (jira|beads)
  - tombstones for deletions/archives
- Use singleton-writer lease semantics if the connector runs in multiple locations.

## Capability + approval model
Illustrative capabilities:
- `jira.issues.read` / `jira.issues.write`
- `jira.comments.write`
- `jira.webhooks.manage` (dangerous; provisioning only)

Policy guidance:
- Creating/transitioning issues in Jira is a write and must produce receipts/audit.
- Bulk sync operations may require an ApprovalToken depending on org policy.

## Deliverables
- A sync engine with:
  - field mapping layer
  - ADF ↔ markdown conversion
  - conflict detection + resolution policy
  - loop prevention via origin stamps + revision fingerprints
- Operation schemas:
  - `jira.sync.push_bead`
  - `jira.sync.pull_issue`
  - `jira.sync.reconcile`
- Structured logging:
  - correlation_id per sync run
  - per-item reason codes for skips/conflicts

## Test strategy (MUST)
### Unit/integration (mock-only)
- Webhook replay tests:
  - duplicate webhook deliveries do not duplicate Beads/Jira updates
- Conflict tests:
  - concurrent edits produce conflict events and do not silently overwrite
- Loop tests:
  - Beads update → Jira update → webhook does not re-trigger Beads update
- State tests:
  - mapping table persists across restarts
  - lease enforcement prevents double writers

### E2E compliance
- Use the shared compliance runner to confirm:
  - default deny on all sync operations
  - receipts/audit for all writes
  - NetworkConstraints enforcement

## Acceptance criteria
- A round-trip sync of a single issue converges in ≤2 sync cycles without loops.
- Conflict cases are explicit, logged, and surfaced as events.
- Sync behavior is deterministic and idempotent.
