title: [CUAL] CLI Universal Agent Access Layer — Phase 2 Agent Ergonomics
description:
# CLI Universal Agent Access Layer (CUAL) — Phase 2 Agent Ergonomics

## Vision
Make the fwc CLI the single, intuitive, universal interface through which any AI agent can discover, invoke, compose, and manage absolutely ANY operation across ALL 85+ connectors. An agent should never need to drop to raw HTTP, guess schemas, or build ad-hoc tooling.

## Relationship to FWC Phase 1 (1g7z0)
The FWC epic (1g7z0) established the foundation: scaffold, discovery, config, lifecycle, invoke, intent compilation, workflow capsules, and cohort parity. CUAL Phase 2 builds on that foundation to close every remaining gap between 'the CLI exists' and 'an agent can do literally anything through it.'

## What Phase 1 covers (already planned/built):
- CLI scaffold with global flags and format plumbing (1g7z0.6) ✅
- Discovery/search/show/schema/example commands (1g7z0.7) ✅
- UX contract, output rendering, progressive disclosure (1g7z0.1, .2) ✅
- Host admin API, config store, lifecycle, config commands (1g7z0.4, .5, .8, .9)
- Invoke/simulate/batch/stream commands (1g7z0.10)
- Intent compiler, workflow capsules, self-resolving capsules (39v14, 2wecj, 3kbu1) ✅
- Aliases, completions, confusion corpus (1g7z0.11, .23, .24, .26)

## What Phase 2 adds (THIS epic):
1. **MCP/Tool Schema Export & Dynamic Server** — Expose connectors as MCP tools, Claude tools, OpenAI functions
2. **Semantic Discovery & Smart Routing** — Cross-connector NL search, capability filtering, auto-routing
3. **Credential & Auth Lifecycle** — Keychain store, test/verify, rotation tracking, secretless injection
4. **Operation History, Replay & Undo** — Audit trail, replay, undo, result diffing
5. **Output Transformation & Extraction** — jq-style extraction, templates, table/CSV modes
6. **Pipeline & Composition Engine** — Chain operations across connectors, conditional branching, recipes
7. **Bulk & Parallel Execution** — Map-over-inputs, batch-from-file, progress tracking, concurrency control
8. **Streaming & Reactive Event Engine** — Unified event tailing, filtering, replay, triggers
9. **Rate Limit Intelligence** — Dashboard, auto-throttle, forecasting
10. **Health & Diagnostics** — Cross-connector health dashboard, trends, auto-diagnosis
11. **Schema Exploration & Validation** — Deep navigator, template generator, pre-invoke validation
12. **Multi-Zone Orchestration** — Zone overview, cross-zone coordination, migration
13. **Agent Session & Collaboration** — Session tracking, locking, Agent Mail integration
14. **Error Recovery & Resilience** — Structured taxonomy, auto-retry, fallback routing, circuit breakers

## Guiding Principles
- **Schema-driven, not hand-coded**: New capabilities should work across ALL connectors automatically
- **Token-efficient by default**: Agents pay per token; every output byte must earn its keep
- **Honest about capabilities**: Never claim to have done something the backend can't yet support
- **Composable primitives**: Complex workflows build from simple, testable, inspectable commands
- **Fail loud, recover gracefully**: Structured errors with actionable recovery guidance

## Success Criteria
An AI agent can, through fwc alone:
- Find any operation across 85+ connectors by intent, capability, risk level, or keyword
- Invoke any operation with auto-auth, schema validation, and approval gating
- Chain operations across connectors in a single pipeline
- Process bulk inputs in parallel with rate-limit awareness
- Stream and filter events from any streaming connector
- Export connector operations as MCP/Claude/OpenAI tool schemas
- Replay, undo, and diff past operations
- Monitor health, rate limits, and auth status across all connectors
- Coordinate with other agents via session management and locks

comments.author: Jeff Emanuel
comments.text: PRIORITIZATION GUIDE: Tracks are ordered by agent-impact. Track A (MCP Server) and Track K (Schema Validation) provide the highest immediate ROI because they make ALL 85+ connectors instantly usable by any MCP-compatible agent. Track B (Semantic Discovery) and Track E (Output Transformation) are the next tier: they save agents massive token budgets on every interaction. Track C (Auth) and Track N (Errors) are infrastructure: less visible but prevent entire classes of agent failures. Tracks F/G/H (Pipeline/Bulk/Streaming) enable advanced workflows that multiply agent productivity. Tracks I/J/L/M are observability and coordination: important for production multi-agent environments but not blocking for single-agent use.

comments.author: Jeff Emanuel
comments.text: IMPLEMENTATION STRATEGY: Phase 2 should be implemented in 3 waves. Wave 1 (highest leverage, no new infrastructure): K.1 (schema navigator), K.2 (template generator), K.3 (validation), E.1 (jq extraction), N.1 (error taxonomy). These require only processing existing introspection data differently. Wave 2 (new CLI features): A.1-A.2 (tool schema export), B.1 (search), C.1 (auth store), D.1 (history). Wave 3 (new runtime infrastructure): A.3 (MCP server), F.1-F.2 (pipelines), G.1-G.2 (batch/map), H.1-H.2 (streaming).

comments.author: Jeff Emanuel
comments.text: RELATIONSHIP TO FWC PHASE 1: CUAL Phase 2 is NOT a replacement for FWC Phase 1 (1g7z0). Phase 1 provides the foundational CLI scaffold, discovery, config, lifecycle, and invoke commands. Phase 2 extends those foundations with: (1) new output modes that make existing commands more useful (jq, templates, tables), (2) new execution modes (batch, parallel, pipeline), (3) new integration surfaces (MCP server, Agent Mail), (4) new intelligence layers (semantic search, auto-diagnosis, circuit breakers). Every Phase 2 bead depends on Phase 1 beads being complete.

comments.author: Jeff Emanuel
comments.text: DESIGN PHILOSOPHY: 'Schema-driven, not hand-coded'. The #1 lesson from Phase 1 connector development is that 85+ connectors with 500+ operations CANNOT be individually hand-tuned in CLI code. Every new feature in Phase 2 MUST work across all connectors automatically by consuming introspection data (OperationInfo, ai_hints, input_schema, etc.). If a feature requires per-connector logic, it is architecturally wrong. The exceptions are: (1) pre-built pipeline recipes (F.5) which are intentionally connector-specific, and (2) reactive rules (H.4) which are user-defined.

title: [CUAL-A.1] OperationInfo-to-tool-schema codec (MCP, Claude, OpenAI formats)
description:
## Goal
Build a codec module that translates FCP OperationInfo structs into tool schemas for MCP, Claude tool-use, and OpenAI function-calling formats.

## Background
Every FCP connector exposes operations via handle_introspect() returning Vec<OperationInfo>. Each OperationInfo contains:
- id (e.g. github.create_issue), summary, description
- input_schema / output_schema (JSON Schema)
- capability, risk_level, safety_tier, idempotency
- ai_hints (when_to_use, common_mistakes, examples, related)

MCP tools need: { name, description, inputSchema }
Claude tools need: { name, description, input_schema }
OpenAI functions need: { name, description, parameters }

The mapping is nearly 1:1 but needs careful handling of:
- Namespace prefixing (fcp.github.create_issue vs github_create_issue)
- Risk/safety metadata as tool annotations or description suffixes
- ai_hints.when_to_use folded into description for AI consumption
- Rate limit info as tool metadata/annotations
- Approval requirements surfaced in description

## Deliverables
- New module: crates/fwc/src/tool_schema/mod.rs (or crates/fcp-cli/src/tool_schema/)
- Codec trait with format-specific implementations
- Format enum: MCP, ClaudeToolUse, OpenAIFunction, Generic
- Full round-trip tests: OperationInfo -> schema -> validate structure
- Property tests: any valid OperationInfo produces valid tool schema

## Acceptance Criteria
- Given any connector's Introspection, produce valid tool schemas in all 3 formats
- ai_hints.when_to_use and common_mistakes are preserved in descriptions
- Risk/safety metadata is machine-extractable from annotations
- Output is deterministic (same input -> byte-identical output)

Key crate dependencies: serde_json (already in workspace). The MCP format is the primary target since Claude Code is our main consumer. OpenAI format differs mainly in field naming (parameters vs input_schema). The Claude tool-use format is identical to MCP except for the container structure.

title: [CUAL-A.2] fwc export-tools command for batch schema export
description:
## Goal
Add 'fwc export-tools' command that exports tool schemas for one or all connectors in the specified format.

## Commands
- fwc export-tools --format mcp                    # All connectors, MCP format
- fwc export-tools --format claude github           # One connector, Claude format
- fwc export-tools --format openai --zone z:work    # Zone-scoped, OpenAI format
- fwc export-tools --format mcp --risk-max medium   # Filter by max risk level
- fwc export-tools --format mcp --output tools.json # Write to file

## Behavior
- Uses the A.1 codec to transform connector introspections
- Respects --zone flag to only include zone-authorized operations
- Supports --risk-max flag to filter out dangerous/critical operations
- Supports --capability filter to include only specific capability families
- TOON output by default (summary table), --json for machine consumption
- --output flag writes to file instead of stdout

## Why Agents Need This
When an agent starts a session, it needs to know what tools are available. 'fwc export-tools --format mcp --json' gives it a complete tool manifest it can register with its runtime.

## Dependencies
- Requires A.1 codec module
- Requires connector introspection (1g7z0.7 already provides this)

title: [CUAL-A.3] fwc serve-mcp: dynamic MCP server exposing connectors as tools
description:
## Goal
Add 'fwc serve-mcp' that runs fwc as a live MCP server, dynamically exposing all configured connectors as MCP tools.

## Background
MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers expose tools, resources, and prompts to AI agents via a JSON-RPC transport (stdio or SSE). By running fwc as an MCP server, any MCP-compatible agent (Claude Code, Cursor, etc.) can use FCP connectors as native tools without any manual configuration.

## Commands
- fwc serve-mcp                          # stdio transport (for Claude Code)
- fwc serve-mcp --transport sse --port 8080  # SSE transport
- fwc serve-mcp --zone z:work            # Only expose zone-authorized tools
- fwc serve-mcp --connectors github,slack # Only expose specific connectors

## Architecture
1. On startup: introspect all configured connectors, generate MCP tool definitions via A.1 codec
2. Register tools/list handler that returns tool schemas
3. Register tools/call handler that routes to connector invoke
4. Handle auth: verify MCP client has appropriate zone/capability tokens
5. Optionally expose resources: connector health, rate limits, operation history
6. Optionally expose prompts: how to use each connector

## Dynamic Behavior
- When connectors are added/removed/reconfigured, update tool list
- When connectors go unhealthy, mark tools as unavailable
- Rate limit enforcement: reject tool calls that would exceed limits

## Deliverables
- MCP server implementation using mcp-server-rs or equivalent
- stdio and SSE transports
- Tool registration from connector introspection
- Tool call routing to connector invoke
- Tests with mock MCP client

## Why This Is Transformative
This single feature means: install Claude Code + fwc serve-mcp, and your AI agent has native access to 85+ external service integrations. No per-tool MCP server installation, no manual configuration per service.

title: [CUAL-A.4] Per-zone MCP tool scoping and capability enforcement
description:
## Goal
Ensure MCP server mode respects FCP zone boundaries: agents only see/invoke tools they are authorized to use in their current zone.

## Background
FCP zones enforce security boundaries. A connector bound to z:work should not expose its tools to an agent operating in z:public. MCP has no native zone concept, so we must enforce this at the fwc MCP server layer.

## Behavior
- fwc serve-mcp --zone z:work only registers tools for connectors authorized in z:work
- If no --zone flag, derive zone from agent identity or MCP client metadata
- tool/call requests are validated against zone capability tokens before dispatch
- Unauthorized tool calls return structured MCP errors with explanation
- Zone transitions (agent moving from z:work to z:private) update available tools

## Deliverables
- Zone-aware tool registration logic in MCP server
- Capability token validation middleware for tool calls
- Structured error responses for zone violations
- Tests: same connector, different zones, different tool visibility

If the client doesn't support notifications, the server should log a warning and continue with the original tool set. Test: zone transition while MCP session is active should update available tools and notify the client.

title: [CUAL-J.2] Auto-diagnosis with fix-it recipes for common issues
description:
## Goal
When a connector is unhealthy, automatically diagnose the issue and suggest specific fix-it commands.

## Commands
- fwc doctor github                        # Diagnose GitHub connector
- fwc doctor --all                         # Diagnose all connectors
- fwc doctor --fix github                  # Apply automatic fixes where safe

## Diagnosis Rules
1. Auth failure (401/403) -> 'fwc auth test github' then 'fwc auth add github --token ...'
2. Rate limited (429) -> 'Wait 12 minutes for reset' or 'Reduce batch concurrency'
3. High latency -> 'Check network' or 'Try different API endpoint'
4. Connection refused -> 'Service may be down, check status page: https://...'
5. Config invalid -> 'fwc config doctor github' to validate and repair
6. Certificate error -> 'Check system time' or 'Update CA certificates'

## Auto-Fix
Safe auto-fixes (--fix mode):
- Refresh expired OAuth tokens
- Clear stale caches
- Reset circuit breakers
- Retry failed health checks

Unsafe fixes (require confirmation):
- Re-authenticate
- Change configuration
- Restart connector

## Deliverables
- Diagnosis rule engine (pattern -> suggestion mapping)
- fwc doctor command
- Auto-fix executor for safe fixes
- Confirmation flow for unsafe fixes
- Tests: each diagnosis rule, auto-fix scenarios

description:
## Goal
Add 'fwc schema' that provides a rich, interactive-style schema exploration experience showing required vs optional fields, types, constraints, and examples at each level.

## Commands
- fwc schema github.create_issue                     # Full schema with annotations
- fwc schema github.create_issue --required-only     # Only required fields
- fwc schema github.create_issue --field labels       # Drill into one field
- fwc schema github.create_issue --examples          # Show example values
- fwc schema github.create_issue --output            # Show output schema

## Output (TOON default)
github.create_issue input schema:
  owner*     string   Repository owner (e.g. 'octocat')
  repo*      string   Repository name (e.g. 'hello-world')
  title*     string   Issue title (e.g. 'Bug report: login fails')
  body       string   Issue body in markdown
  assignees  [string] List of GitHub usernames to assign
  labels     [string] List of label names (e.g. ['bug', 'priority:high'])
  milestone  integer  Milestone number

* = required

## Why Agents Need This
Agents looking at raw JSON Schema see a wall of type definitions. This command presents schemas in a flat, scannable format with real examples pulled from ai_hints.examples. The --required-only flag is particularly valuable: agents can construct minimal valid inputs quickly.

## Deliverables
- JSON Schema walker/flattener
- Required vs optional annotation
- Example value extraction from ai_hints
- Nested field drill-down
- TOON and JSON output modes

title: [CUAL-K.3] Pre-invoke input validation with human-readable error messages
description:
## Goal
Validate operation inputs BEFORE sending to the connector, providing clear error messages that tell the agent exactly what is wrong and how to fix it.

## Behavior
- Automatically validate input against operation's input_schema before every invoke
- If validation fails: report structured errors, do NOT invoke
- Errors include: field path, expected type/constraint, actual value, fix suggestion

## Error Output
Validation failed for github.create_issue:
  - owner: required field missing (add 'owner' with a string value like 'octocat')
  - labels: expected array of strings, got string 'bug' (wrap in array: ['bug'])
  - milestone: expected integer, got string '3' (use number: 3)

## Commands
- fwc validate github.create_issue --input '{...}'    # Explicit validation
- fwc invoke github.create_issue --input '{...}'      # Auto-validates before invoke
- fwc validate github.create_issue --input-file in.json

## Why Agents Need This
Without pre-validation, agents send malformed requests, get cryptic API errors, then waste tokens debugging. Pre-validation catches 100% of schema errors locally with clear fix instructions, saving round-trips and tokens.

## Deliverables
- JSON Schema validator (jsonschema crate) integration
- Human-readable error formatter with fix suggestions
- Auto-validation middleware in invoke path
- fwc validate standalone command
- Tests: missing required, wrong type, wrong format, nested errors, valid input

title: [CUAL-L.3] Zone migration and data portability helpers
description:
# Zone Migration and Data Portability Helpers

## Goal
Enable agents to safely migrate connector configurations between zones with full visibility into what changes and what breaks.

## Deliverables

### fwc zones migrate
- `fwc zones migrate <connector> <source-zone> to <target-zone>` — migrates connector config between zones
- Pre-flight check shows: config fields that change, credentials that need re-provisioning, policies that differ
- `--dry-run` flag shows migration plan without executing
- `--force` flag to proceed despite warnings
- Atomic: either fully migrates or rolls back

### fwc zones export/import
- `fwc zones export <zone> > config.json` — exports all connector configs in a zone to portable JSON
- `fwc zones import config.json --zone <target>` — imports configs into target zone
- Export includes: connector IDs, config values (secrets redacted), enabled state, policy bindings
- Import validates compatibility before applying

### Output Format
- Default: TOON with migration diff showing added/removed/changed fields
- `--json` flag for machine-readable output with structured migration plan
- `--format table` for summary view of affected connectors

## Test Criteria
Unit tests (8 minimum):
- migrate happy path: config transferred, old zone cleaned up
- migrate dry-run: no state changes, plan output correct
- migrate with policy conflict: shows warning, blocks without --force
- migrate rollback on failure: partial migration reverted
- export round-trip: export then import produces identical config
- export redacts secrets in output
- import validates zone compatibility
- import detects conflicting existing configs

## Acceptance Criteria
- Migration is atomic (all-or-nothing)
- Dry-run output matches actual migration outcome
- Export/import round-trip preserves all non-secret config
- TOON output clearly shows before/after diff
- --json output is schema-consistent with other CUAL commands

title: [CUAL-N] Error Recovery & Resilience Patterns
description: Track N: Error Recovery and Resilience. Phase 1 has intent recovery (1g7z0.23) for typos/aliases. 1. Error taxonomy, retry, fallback routing, and circuit-breaker behavior are explicit, deterministic, and safe-by-default rather than a bag of hidden heuristics.
2. Recovery controllers remain honest about confidence, cost, approval needs, and the boundary between recommended fallback and automatic behavior.
3. Unit, integration, interference, and transcript-style E2E verification with detailed logging are required for retries, breaker trips, fallback selection, and terminal failure reporting.

title: [CUAL-N.2] Auto-retry with exponential backoff and jitter
description: Add configurable auto-retry for transient failures (rate_limited, timeout, 5xx). Exponential backoff: 1s, 2s, 4s with +/-25% jitter. Use retry_after_ms from error details when available. Flags: --retry N, --no-retry, --retry-backoff 2s, --retry-on rate_limited,timeout. Applied to invoke, map, batch, pipeline. Final error includes retry history.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Retry behavior is bounded, jittered, and explicit about eligibility, stop conditions, and interaction with rate limits, approvals, and idempotency.
2. Automatic recovery never silently converts an unsafe action into a repeated side effect, and it exposes when manual intervention is required.
3. Unit, interference, and transcript-style E2E verification with detailed logging are required for retryable, non-retryable, and exhaustion cases.

comments.author: Jeff Emanuel
comments.text: DESIGN IMPROVEMENT: Auto-retry MUST respect idempotency class. For IdempotencyClass::Strict: safe to retry with same idempotency_key. For IdempotencyClass::BestEffort: retry with warning. For IdempotencyClass::None: NEVER auto-retry write operations (only reads). This prevents the catastrophic scenario of retrying a non-idempotent 'send_message' or 'create_issue' and getting duplicates. Display retry safety in error output: 'Retryable: yes (operation is idempotent)' or 'Retryable: NO (operation is not idempotent, manual retry required)'.

comments.author: Jeff Emanuel

title: [CUAL-N.3] Fallback connector routing and circuit-breaker patterns
description:
# Fallback Connector Routing and Circuit-Breaker Patterns

## Goal
When a connector fails persistently, automatically protect against cascading failures via circuit breakers and suggest alternative connectors for the same operation.

## Deliverables

### Circuit Breaker State Machine
- States: CLOSED (normal) -> OPEN (failing, reject immediately) -> HALF-OPEN (probe)
- Transition: CLOSED->OPEN at 50% error rate over 10-request window
- OPEN->HALF-OPEN after 30s cooldown
- HALF-OPEN->CLOSED on 1 success, HALF-OPEN->OPEN on 1 failure
- State persisted in ~/.fwc/circuit_breakers.json per connector
- When OPEN: immediate FCP_ERR_CIRCUIT_OPEN with time until next probe

### Fallback Suggestions
- When circuit is OPEN, suggest alternative connectors for the same operation
- Uses B.3 (routing) capability families and connector categories
- Ranked by: health status, zone availability, capability match

### CLI Integration
- `fwc invoke` checks circuit state before executing; rejects if OPEN
- `fwc health` shows circuit breaker states alongside health status
- `fwc circuit reset <connector>` force-resets circuit to CLOSED
- `fwc circuit status` shows all circuit states

### Output Format
- Default: TOON showing circuit state, error counts, cooldown timer, fallback suggestions
- `--json` flag for machine-readable circuit state and fallback list

## Test Criteria
Unit tests (10 minimum):
- CLOSED -> OPEN transition at error threshold
- OPEN -> HALF_OPEN after cooldown timer
- HALF_OPEN -> CLOSED on success
- HALF_OPEN -> OPEN on failure
- Persistent state across fwc invocations (file-backed)
- Concurrent request handling in HALF_OPEN (single probe, queue others)
- Cooldown timer accuracy (not early/late)
- Force-reset command returns to CLOSED
- Fallback suggestions from B.3 routing match operation capability
- Circuit status output in TOON and JSON formats

## Acceptance Criteria
- Circuit state is correct after any sequence of success/failure events
- State survives process restart (file-backed)
- FCP_ERR_CIRCUIT_OPEN includes time-until-probe and fallback list
- Force-reset is immediate and atomic
- TOON output is human-scannable, --json output is machine-parseable
acceptance_criteria:
1. Fallback routing and circuit-breaker behavior are explicit about confidence, eligibility, and the difference between recommended alternatives and automatic failover.
2. Breakers fail safe, preserve operator trust, and avoid fighting with retry or throttling controllers.
3. Unit, integration, and transcript-style E2E verification with detailed logging are required for failover, breaker-open, breaker-reset, and no-safe-fallback cases.

comments.author: Jeff Emanuel
comments.text:
DESIGN CONSIDERATION: Circuit breaker state machine must be per-connector and persistent across fwc invocations (not just in-memory). Store state in ~/.fwc/circuit_breakers.json: {connector_id, state, error_count, last_error_time, last_probe_time}. State transitions: CLOSED->OPEN when error_rate > 50% over window of 10 requests. OPEN->HALF_OPEN after 30s cooldown. HALF_OPEN->CLOSED on 1 success, HALF_OPEN->OPEN on 1 failure. When OPEN, 'fwc invoke' should immediately return FCP_ERR_CIRCUIT_OPEN with time until next probe and fallback suggestions.
TESTING: ≥10 unit tests: full state machine transitions, persistent state across invocations, concurrent request handling in HALF_OPEN, cooldown timer accuracy, force-reset command, fallback suggestions from B.3 routing.

title: [CUAL-T] Comprehensive Testing & Quality Assurance
description:
# Track T: Comprehensive Testing and Quality Assurance

## Why This Track Exists
The CUAL implementation has ~890 unit tests across individual modules, but there are critical testing gaps:
1. NO E2E test scripts exercising full workflows (discover -> search -> validate -> invoke -> verify)
2. NO integration tests validating cross-module interactions (search + validate + pipe + history)
3. NO performance benchmarks for search indexing, batch throughput, or MCP server latency
4. Dead-code modules have unit tests but no integration with CLI dispatch

## What This Track Delivers
- E2E bash test scripts with detailed logging for every CUAL track
- Rust integration test suite (tests/cual_integration.rs) for cross-module flows
- Performance benchmark suite
- Test observability: structured logging in tests so failures are debuggable
- Regression test gates that run before any CUAL release

## Testing Philosophy
- Every CUAL feature must have at least one happy-path E2E script
- Every error path must have a unit test with the exact error code verified
- Integration tests must exercise the full CLI dispatch path, not just module internals
- E2E scripts must emit structured logging (JSON lines) for automated verification
acceptance_criteria:
1. The CUAL test track covers comprehensive unit, integration, transcript-style E2E, and benchmark verification across all implemented command families with detailed redaction-safe logging.
2. Dispatch tests exercise the real CLI entrypoints and structured error envelopes, not only module internals, and every major track produces replayable artifacts for regression triage.
3. Test execution guidance includes remote-offloaded cargo commands via rch exec when compilation or benchmark work is CPU-intensive.

title: [CUAL-T.2] Rust integration test suite for cross-module CUAL workflows
description:
## Goal
Create a Rust integration test file that exercises cross-module CUAL workflows: search -> validate -> invoke -> history -> replay.

## Test File
crates/fwc/tests/cual_integration.rs (or inline in relevant modules)

## Integration Test Scenarios

### Workflow 1: Discovery-to-Invoke
1. Build search index from mock connector introspections
2. Search for 'create issue', verify correct operation found
3. Generate template for found operation
4. Validate a well-formed input against schema
5. Validate a malformed input, verify structured error
6. (When invoke is wired) Execute operation, verify history entry created

### Workflow 2: Batch-with-Throttle
1. Configure throttle with mock rate limit pools
2. Create batch input (10 operations)
3. Execute with concurrency=2
4. Verify throttle delays are applied when quota is low
5. Verify progress tracking reports correct counts
6. Verify all results collected even with partial failures

### Workflow 3: Pipe-with-Validation
1. Set up two mock operations with known schemas
2. Create pipe mapping from A output to B input
3. Validate pipe mapping against both schemas
4. Execute pipe in dry-run mode
5. Verify estimated API calls match expected

### Workflow 4: MCP Server Protocol
1. Initialize McpServerState with mock connectors
2. Send tools/list request, verify tool schemas match introspection
3. Send tools/call, verify routing to correct connector
4. Send resources/list, verify connector state resources
5. Send invalid request, verify JSON-RPC error response

### Workflow 5: Auth-History-Replay Lifecycle
1. Add credential to store
2. Execute operation (verify credential used)
3. Query history for the operation
4. Replay operation from history
5. Verify replay used same credential

### Workflow 6: Event-Filter-React
1. Create mock event stream
2. Subscribe with type filter
3. Verify only matching events pass through
4. Add reactive rule
5. Verify rule triggers on matching events
6. Verify throttle prevents excess triggers

## Test Infrastructure
- Use wiremock::MockServer for HTTP mocking
- Use tokio::test for async tests
- Use tempdir for credential store and history files
- Each test is fully isolated (no shared state)

## Acceptance Criteria
- All 6 workflows have passing tests
- Tests run in < 10 seconds total
- Each test has clear setup/act/assert sections with comments
- Tests are deterministic (no flaky behavior)
acceptance_criteria:
1. Integration tests exercise cross-module CUAL workflows through realistic dispatch and shared state boundaries rather than isolated unit seams.
2. Coverage includes success, ambiguity, denial, recovery, and partial-failure interactions across search, auth, history, output, pipeline, and event surfaces as implemented.
3. Detailed logs and reproducible fixtures make cross-module regressions attributable quickly.

7. access-gap -> approval bundle -> attach -> resume -> history inspection

Each workflow must assert both TOON and JSON output, structured blocker/recovery codes, and artifact/log emission suitable for replay.

title: [CUAL-T.3] Performance benchmarks for search, batch, MCP, and pipeline operations
description:
## Goal
Create criterion benchmarks for latency-sensitive CUAL operations to establish baselines and detect regressions.

## Benchmarks

### Search Performance
- Index building time for 100 / 500 / 1000 operations
- Search latency for keyword, faceted, and NL queries
- Target: < 1ms search latency for 500 operations

### Batch Throughput
- Map-over-inputs throughput (operations/second) with mock connector
- Batch scheduling overhead vs raw sequential execution
- Target: < 5% overhead vs sequential for non-throttled batches

### MCP Server
- tools/list response time for 10 / 50 / 100 connectors
- tools/call routing latency (time from request to connector dispatch)
- Target: < 5ms tools/list for 100 connectors

### Pipeline
- Two-operation pipe overhead (mapping + validation time)
- Multi-step pipeline scheduling time for 5 / 10 / 20 steps
- Target: < 10ms pipeline setup for 10 steps

### Schema Validation
- Validation time for simple vs deeply nested schemas
- Template generation time
- Target: < 1ms validation for typical operation schemas

## Location
crates/fwc/benches/cual_bench.rs

## Acceptance Criteria
- All benchmarks have clear descriptions and units
- Baselines documented in comments
- cargo bench --bench cual_bench runs in < 30 seconds
- No benchmark exceeds 10x its target (soft alert)
acceptance_criteria:
1. Benchmarks cover search, batch, MCP, and pipeline workloads that are representative of real agent usage rather than synthetic micro-optimizations only.
2. Thresholds and measurement rules are explicit enough to distinguish regressions from expected variance.
3. Benchmark execution is designed for rch exec usage and emits detailed structured logs and artifacts.

title: [CUAL-W] CLI Dispatch Wiring and Command-Family Activation
description:
# Track W: CLI Dispatch Wiring and Command-Family Activation

## Why This Track Exists
Two different kinds of CLI work belong here, and both are easy to under-specify if they stay scattered across feature beads:
1. substantial CUAL modules already exist with real logic and tests but still need explicit CLI dispatch glue
2. newer ergonomic tracks introduce major command families such as `fwc access`, `fwc setup`, and `fwc mesh`, and those families need an explicit home for clap wiring, routing, output shaping, preview-vs-execute behavior, and exit-code consistency

## Current State
Existing modules with implemented logic that still need dedicated or remaining dispatch glue:
- serve_mcp.rs (2,159 lines, 116 tests) — MCP server, needs `fwc serve-mcp` command wiring
- credential_store.rs (1,265 lines, 93 tests) — needs `fwc auth` command wiring
- audit.rs (2,112 lines, 93 tests) — needs audit query integration
- event_stream.rs (1,000 lines, 76 tests) — needs `fwc events` command wiring
- throttle.rs (1,398 lines, 68 tests) — needs execution-path middleware injection

Track G already owns map/batch execution and progress surfaces, so this track should not duplicate batch wiring unless a concrete new dispatch gap is discovered.

CLI commands using `planned()` stubs or otherwise incomplete routing still include:
- invoke, simulate, status, enable, disable, start, stop, restart, install, update, pin, unpin, config, logs, events

In addition, new command families introduced by later CUAL tracks must not be treated as implicitly wired just because their behavior is designed. They need explicit activation beads here.

## What This Track Delivers
- explicit clap/dispatch/output wiring beads for remaining dead-code or partially routed modules
- command-family activation beads for `fwc access`, `fwc setup`, and `fwc mesh`
- clear ownership for read-only versus side-effecting subcommands, preview-versus-execute semantics, session-context interaction, TOON/JSON output parity, and stable `FCP_ERR_*` envelopes at the CLI boundary
- a rule that no feature track is considered user-ready while its command surface is still partially stubbed, ambiguously routed, or missing dispatch tests

## Blocked By
Some glue work depends on host admin APIs or upstream feature tracks. That does not change ownership: Track W remains the place where user-facing command activation is made explicit and testable.
acceptance_criteria:
1. No CUAL feature or command family is considered user-ready until it is reachable through real clap and dispatch wiring with stable preview-versus-execute semantics and TOON or JSON parity.
2. Command activation remains explicit about context defaults, side effects, unsupported states, exit codes, and FCP_ERR envelopes so hidden logic cannot masquerade as usable CLI behavior.
3. Unit, integration, help-contract, and transcript-style E2E verification with detailed logging are required for every newly activated command family.
notes: Treat Track W as the canonical home for CLI glue rather than feature semantics. Tracks A-O/P/Q define what the system should do; Track W defines how that behavior becomes reachable, inspectable, and mechanically consistent from the `fwc` binary. For new command families, include clap parsing, help text, routing, context/default handling, preview-execute boundaries, TOON/JSON formatting, exit status, and structured diagnostics/log hooks.

title: [CUAL-O] Access Planning, Authorization Gap Analysis, and Approval Request Workflows
description:
# [CUAL-O] Access Planning, Authorization Gap Analysis, and Approval Request Workflows

## Goal
Give agents a connector-centric way to move from "blocked or denied" to "here is the smallest safe authorization change or approval request that would make this possible."

## Why this track exists
The current `FWC` + `CUAL` graph already covers discovery, schema inspection, simulation, pending-approval queues, zone summaries, and history. What it still does not make first-class is the remediation path between those surfaces. In FCP, explicit authority is a foundational invariant: if an operation is blocked because the current zone, capability chain, approval context, revocation freshness, or policy ceiling is insufficient, the CLI should help the caller understand that gap mechanically and prepare the correct next action without spelunking raw policy objects.

This track is intentionally distinct from:
- preflight/explain/simulate, which say whether a request is blocked
- pending-approval queue/history, which show what is already waiting
- zone status/policy summaries, which describe the current world

This track answers the next question: what exact authorization delta or approval artifact would bridge the gap safely?

## Scope
- connector- and operation-level capability gap analysis for a concrete zone/profile/request
- least-privilege grant or role-diff planning rather than blanket "ask for admin" suggestions
- approval-request bundle generation with exact risky step, evidence, requested scope, expiry, and resume command
- inspection of revocation freshness, policy ceilings, grant-object drift, and other non-obvious blockers
- explicit TOON/JSON surfaces that remain compact enough for agent loops but exact enough for audit and handoff

## Deliverables
- access-planning command surfaces and output contract
- minimal-grant / approval-bundle schema shared by primitive, workflow, and MCP-adjacent flows
- deterministic reason vocabulary for authorization gaps and remediation guidance
- snapshot, integration, and E2E coverage proving blocked work can be diagnosed and resumed cleanly

## Acceptance criteria
- an agent can answer "why exactly is this blocked?" and "what is the smallest safe change or approval request?" from `fwc` alone
- access guidance stays least-privilege, explicit, and auditable
- the CLI never hand-waves authorization state with vague generic advice
acceptance_criteria:
1. `fwc` can explain why connector work is blocked and what the smallest safe authorization change or approval request would be, without requiring raw policy archaeology.
2. Access-planning outputs stay least-privilege, explicit, and auditable across primitive commands, workflow handles, and later MCP-adjacent flows.
3. Approval-bundle, resume, revocation, and blocker-inspection semantics are integrated as one coherent user story rather than isolated helpers.
4. Track O is not complete without unit, integration, dispatch, and logged E2E coverage with replayable remediation artifacts.
notes: Treat this as connector-centric access planning layered on top of existing  discovery, preflight, history, and zone work. It should translate raw policy/capability state into operational next steps that future agents can actually use, while staying aligned with FCP's explicit-authority model and least-privilege design.

## Goal

title: [CUAL-O.3] Revocation, freshness, and policy-conflict inspector for blocked connector work
description:
## Goal
Add an inspector for the subtle blockers that make authorization failures confusing in practice: stale revocation data, expired or superseded grants, capability-chain mismatches, and policy conflicts that are not obvious from a simple allow/deny verdict.

## Illustrative commands
- `fwc access inspect github issues.create --zone z:work`
- `fwc access inspect --request <request-or-history-handle>`
- `fwc access explain-blocker <request-id>`

## Scope
- identify whether the blocker comes from revocation freshness, expired approval, stale capability chain, zone ceiling, role mismatch, or policy conflict
- show the exact object or freshness boundary that failed and the next command to repair or re-request it
- integrate with zone and history surfaces so blockers are navigable from prior denied work
- keep output compact by default, with drill-down for receipts, grant objects, and revocation metadata

## Deliverables
- blocker taxonomy and structured explanation surface
- history/queue integration points for denied or stale work
- tests for stale-revocation, expired-approval, ceiling-violation, and mismatched-grant scenarios

## Acceptance criteria
- confusing authorization failures become mechanically diagnosable instead of forcing policy archaeology
- the CLI tells the caller whether they need refresh, re-approval, a smaller request, or a true policy change
acceptance_criteria:
1. Blocker inspection distinguishes revocation freshness, expired approval, stale capability chain, zone ceiling, role mismatch, and policy conflict instead of collapsing them into generic denial.
2. Output tells the caller whether to refresh, re-approve, shrink the request, or change policy, with exact next-command guidance.
3. Denied or stale work can be navigated from history/queue surfaces without reconstructing context manually.
4. Unit, integration, and logged E2E coverage are required for each blocker family plus redaction-safe replay hints.
notes: This issue should bridge connector-centric CLI ergonomics with FCP's revocation and freshness model. Do not reduce everything to generic 'permission denied'; preserve exact blocker categories and exact remedy paths so approvals, revocation, and policy changes are auditable and debuggable.

title: [CUAL-P] Connector Onboarding, Prerequisite Automation, and Ready-State Repair
description:
# [CUAL-P] Connector Onboarding, Prerequisite Automation, and Ready-State Repair

## Goal
Make first-run connector bring-up and long-lived prerequisite repair a first-class `fwc` experience, not a pile of connector-specific tribal knowledge.

## Why this track exists
The current graph now covers auth, config, lifecycle, diagnostics, and host-backed execution planning. That still leaves a real usability hole: many connectors require service-side setup that is not reducible to a token or config key. Examples include webhook registration, callback URL or redirect setup, API enablement, bot/app registration, subscription creation, tenant binding, service-account wiring, or endpoint exposure. `AGENTS.md` is explicit that we should automate everything we can. The CLI needs a generic framework for onboarding and repair so connector-specific provisioning work lands behind one consistent mental model.

## Scope
- machine-readable prerequisite descriptors exposed through host/introspection surfaces
- guided onboarding plans that ask the minimum necessary human questions and automate everything else
- verification and repair flows for drifted prerequisites such as stale callback URLs, missing subscriptions, rotated webhook secrets, or disabled APIs
- redaction-safe artifact capture so onboarding and repair can be replayed, audited, and handed off

## Deliverables
- universal prerequisite / readiness descriptor contract for connectors
- onboarding and repair command surfaces plus deterministic output vocabulary
- snapshot, integration, and E2E coverage across multiple prerequisite archetypes

## Acceptance criteria
- a new connector can be brought to a truthful ready state from `fwc` with minimal human intervention
- service-side prerequisite drift is diagnosable and repairable from the same CLI surface
- connector-specific provisioning automation can plug into this framework without inventing a new UX each time
acceptance_criteria:
1. `fwc setup` can move a connector from missing prerequisites to truthful ready state with minimal human intervention and explicit automation boundaries.
2. Service-side prerequisite drift is diagnosable and repairable from the same command family instead of being scattered across connector-specific folklore.
3. Prerequisite evidence, manual blockers, resume handles, and repair receipts are durable and handoff-friendly.
4. Track P is not complete without unit, integration, dispatch, and logged E2E coverage across prerequisite archetypes and drift scenarios.
notes: This is the universal CLI/operator framework that per-connector provisioning beads should eventually plug into. Keep the boundary crisp: auth handles credentials/identity, config handles durable settings, lifecycle handles runtime state, and this track covers service-side prerequisites and external setup steps that sit before or around those layers.

comments.author: Jeff Emanuel
comments.text: Track P now includes a dedicated verification child so onboarding and repair work cannot close on happy-path demos alone. Completion requires evidence across prerequisite descriptors, partial-automation blockers, resumable setup, drift diagnosis, and repair flows with artifact-rich logging.

title: [CUAL-P.1] Prerequisite descriptor schema and ready-state doctor surface
description:
## Goal
Define a standard prerequisite descriptor and doctor surface so `fwc` can tell an agent exactly what non-auth, non-runtime setup a connector still needs before it is truly ready.

## Illustrative commands
- `fwc setup inspect github`
- `fwc setup inspect slack --json`
- `fwc setup doctor slack`

## Scope
- descriptor fields for webhook endpoints, redirect URLs, API enablement, subscriptions, external resources, bot/app registration, tenant binding, and similar prerequisites
- readiness status for each prerequisite: satisfied, missing, drifted, unverifiable, or policy-blocked
- connector-authored hints plus host-authored verification evidence
- compact summaries with drill-down into the blocking prerequisite and the smallest follow-up action

## Deliverables
- prerequisite descriptor schema shared by host and CLI
- `inspect`/`doctor` style read surfaces for prerequisite readiness
- tests covering multiple prerequisite archetypes and missing-evidence cases

## Acceptance criteria
- an agent can ask "what is still missing before this connector is actually usable?" and get a precise answer
- prerequisite readiness becomes explicit state rather than hidden setup folklore
acceptance_criteria:
1. `fwc setup inspect` and `fwc setup doctor` expose a stable prerequisite descriptor with explicit statuses such as satisfied, missing, drifted, unverifiable, and policy-blocked.
2. The descriptor covers webhook, redirect, API-enablement, subscription, app/bot registration, tenant binding, endpoint exposure, and similar archetypes without hard-coding service-specific UX.
3. Output includes verification evidence and the smallest next-step hint needed to make the connector truly usable.
4. Unit, integration, and logged E2E coverage are required for multiple prerequisite archetypes and missing-evidence cases.
notes: Model prerequisites as first-class connector metadata with stable reason codes and structured verification evidence. The descriptor should be rich enough to cover bot/webhook/callback/cloud-enablement cases without hard-coding those services into CLI logic.

title: [CUAL-P.2] Guided onboarding workflows for service-side setup and resource binding
description:
## Goal
Turn prerequisite bring-up into a guided onboarding plan that automates service-side setup where possible and asks only the smallest human questions when automation cannot finish the job alone.

## Illustrative commands
- `fwc setup plan slack`
- `fwc setup run slack --profile work-bot`
- `fwc setup resume <setup-handle>`

## Scope
- guided plans for webhook/redirect registration, API enablement, subscription creation, app or bot registration, endpoint exposure, tenant binding, and service-account wiring where supported
- exact automation boundaries so the caller can see which step is automatic and which still needs human confirmation or external credentials
- success verification immediately after each onboarding step rather than a vague final "probably ready"
- resumable setup handles so long-running onboarding can survive handoff or rate limits

## Deliverables
- setup-plan and setup-run workflow contract
- automation step taxonomy with explicit manual-blocker semantics
- tests for fully automated, partially automated, and blocked onboarding cases

## Acceptance criteria
- onboarding becomes a guided, inspectable workflow instead of a scattered README ritual
- future connector-specific provisioning logic can plug into one common CLI contract
acceptance_criteria:
1. `fwc setup plan`, `run`, and `resume` make automated versus human-required steps explicit and verify readiness after each step instead of hand-waving a final ready state.
2. Setup runs emit resumable handles, manual-step receipts, and machine-readable reports suitable for handoff and later repair.
3. Fully automated, partially automated, and blocked onboarding cases all stay truthful about what changed and what still requires human action.
4. Unit, integration, and logged E2E coverage are required for plan/run/resume flows, and any documented cargo-backed commands use `rch exec -- ...`.
notes: This should be the CLI home for the "automate everything" principle from AGENTS.md. It is intentionally broader than auth bootstrap: cover the non-secret, service-side prerequisites that make a connector truly usable, but keep every automated step explicit and replayable.

title: [CUAL-P.3] Ready-state repair and prerequisite drift reconciliation flows
description:
## Goal
Provide a repair and reconciliation surface for connectors whose service-side prerequisites have drifted after the initial setup succeeded.

## Illustrative commands
- `fwc setup repair slack`
- `fwc setup repair github --check-only`
- `fwc setup explain-drift <setup-or-doctor-handle>`

## Scope
- detect and explain drift such as rotated webhook secrets, deleted subscriptions, stale callback URLs, disabled APIs, broken endpoint exposure, or mismatched tenant/resource binding
- propose or execute safe repair steps with clear preview and confirmation boundaries
- distinguish auth breakage, config breakage, lifecycle breakage, and prerequisite drift so remediation starts in the right place
- emit repair artifacts and receipts that can be replayed or attached to docs and incident threads

## Deliverables
- prerequisite-drift taxonomy and repair contract
- check-only, preview, and execute modes for repairs
- tests covering common drift and partial-repair scenarios

## Acceptance criteria
- the CLI can tell whether a connector needs auth repair, config repair, lifecycle repair, or service-side prerequisite repair
- repair guidance is concrete enough that future agents do not rediscover the same setup failures from scratch
acceptance_criteria:
1. `fwc setup repair` and related drift surfaces distinguish prerequisite drift from auth, config, and lifecycle failures and provide exact repair previews or execution receipts.
2. Rotated webhook secrets, deleted subscriptions, stale callbacks, disabled APIs, broken endpoint exposure, and binding mismatches are all surfaced as explicit drift classes.
3. Check-only versus execute modes stay explicit, replayable, and safe for handoff.
4. Unit, integration, and logged E2E coverage are required for common drift and partial-repair scenarios.
notes: Keep this tightly integrated with diagnostics and auth repair so the CLI can route the caller to the right remedy instead of collapsing every failure into 'connector unhealthy'. Drift explanation and repair receipts should be stable enough for handoff, docs, and later regression tests.

title: [CUAL-Q] Mesh Context, Node Targeting, and Execution Placement Ergonomics
description:
# [CUAL-Q] Mesh Context, Node Targeting, and Execution Placement Ergonomics

## Goal
Make the mesh-native nature of FCP operationally legible from `fwc` so agents can choose where connector work should run, understand why the host picked a given node or instance, and reason about offline or mirrored availability without dropping into lower-level tools.

## Why this track exists
The README and spec promise a personal device mesh, computation migration, mirrored connector distribution, and device-aware execution. The current `fwc` graph covers connector/session context, zone context, lifecycle state, and host-backed execution contracts, but it does not yet give agents a connector-centric UX for node targeting, placement explanations, rollout cohorts, or offline mirror awareness. That is a major gap between the project architecture and what the dedicated connector CLI currently plans to expose.

## Scope
- mesh-context and node inventory for connectors, runtimes, health, and placement
- explicit target selection for reads, risky writes, lifecycle actions, and workflow capsules
- placement explanation and override semantics including locality, health, auth scope, and secret/material availability
- node-scoped or cohort-scoped lifecycle and rollout flows
- mirrored-install / offline-availability visibility for install and invoke paths

## Deliverables
- mesh-aware command surfaces and output contract for `fwc`
- placement explanation vocabulary shared by primitive and workflow surfaces
- snapshot, integration, and E2E coverage for node-targeted and offline-aware workflows

## Acceptance criteria
- an agent can answer "where will this run, why there, and how do I change it?" from `fwc` alone
- mesh placement and offline availability become inspectable operational state instead of hidden host behavior
- node-targeted lifecycle work stays safe, explicit, and auditable
acceptance_criteria:
1. `fwc mesh` and mesh-aware lifecycle/install surfaces make run location, placement reasons, overrides, rollout scope, and offline availability explicit from the CLI alone.
2. Mesh context, target selection, and offline/mirror state stay inspectable and auditable instead of being hidden inside host scheduling internals.
3. Node- and cohort-scoped actions preserve explicit scope, convergence visibility, and safe override semantics for agents.
4. Track Q is not complete without unit, integration, dispatch, and logged E2E coverage across inventory, placement, rollout, and availability paths.
notes: This is intentionally about connector-centric mesh ergonomics, not generic platform administration. Keep the emphasis on what an agent needs at decision time: which mesh context is active, which node or cohort is eligible, why placement was chosen, whether offline mirrors exist, and how node-scoped changes converge.

comments.author: Jeff Emanuel
comments.text: Track Q now includes a dedicated verification child so mesh ergonomics are proven, not assumed. Completion requires synthetic multi-node coverage for target selection, placement explanation, node-scoped rollouts, and offline or mirror availability with clear logs and replayable artifacts.

title: [CUAL-Q.1] Mesh inventory, context selection, and explicit execution-target UX
description:
## Goal
Expose mesh contexts, nodes, connector placements, and eligible execution targets so the caller can deliberately choose the execution surface instead of inheriting opaque defaults.

## Illustrative commands
- `fwc mesh status`
- `fwc mesh nodes github`
- `fwc mesh use laptop-work`
- `fwc mesh target github --node desktop`

## Scope
- list mesh contexts, nodes, connector instances, and current placement/eligibility metadata
- surface which nodes are healthy, authorized, reachable, and currently hosting a connector instance
- explicit default-target and override semantics for primitive commands and workflow capsules
- stable serialization so session context and automation can persist target choices intentionally

## Deliverables
- mesh inventory and target-selection contract
- context/target persistence rules that avoid hidden ambient authority
- tests for target selection, missing-node handling, and stale-context recovery

## Acceptance criteria
- the caller can intentionally select or inspect the execution target before a risky operation
- mesh context and target state are visible enough that handoffs do not rely on unstated defaults
acceptance_criteria:
1. `fwc mesh status`, `nodes`, `use`, and `target` make active target, eligible nodes, placement metadata, and persisted context explicit without creating hidden ambient authority.
2. Target persistence and override semantics are stable, inspectable, and reversible for future handoff and automation.
3. Missing-node, stale-target, and changed-context cases are surfaced with concrete recovery guidance.
4. Unit, integration, and logged E2E coverage are required for inventory listing, context selection, target override, and stale-context recovery.
notes: Make mesh targeting as explicit as zone targeting. Persisted target choice should integrate with existing workflow/session context work, but remain inspectable and reversible so node selection never becomes invisible ambient state.

title: [CUAL-Q.2] Execution placement explanation and override semantics
description:
## Goal
Explain host placement decisions in plain operational terms so agents can understand why a connector operation was routed to a given node and what tradeoffs would change that choice.

## Illustrative commands
- `fwc mesh explain github issues.create`
- `fwc mesh explain --task w:deadbeef`
- `fwc mesh explain github issues.create --override-node desktop --check-only`

## Scope
- show placement signals such as node health, zone authorization, secret/material availability, data locality, rate-limit headroom, and device suitability
- make overrides explicit, previewable, and honest about safety or performance costs
- expose when placement is impossible because no eligible node satisfies the request
- integrate with workflow and preflight surfaces so placement is visible before execution

## Deliverables
- placement explanation schema and TOON/JSON render contract
- previewable override semantics and error language for impossible placements
- tests covering healthy, degraded, offline, and no-eligible-node scenarios

## Acceptance criteria
- an agent can answer "why this node?" and "what would happen if I forced another node?" without guessing
- placement overrides remain explicit and safe rather than becoming another opaque flag
acceptance_criteria:
1. `fwc mesh explain` makes placement signals such as health, authorization, secret/material locality, data locality, and headroom legible in operational language.
2. Override previews truthfully show safety, performance, and eligibility tradeoffs, including no-eligible-node and degraded/offline cases.
3. Placement explanation works for primitive requests and task/workflow handles before execution occurs.
4. Unit, integration, and logged E2E coverage are required for healthy, degraded, offline, override-preview, and impossible-placement scenarios.
notes: This should translate host scheduling and placement logic into a human/agent-usable explanation, not merely dump scheduler internals. Make the tradeoffs legible: security boundary, locality, health, availability, and expected operational cost.

title: [CUAL-Q.3] Node-scoped lifecycle, rollout cohorts, and convergence reporting
description:
## Goal
Extend lifecycle and rollout work so agents can act on one node, a named cohort, or the full eligible mesh while still seeing convergence and partial-failure state clearly.

## Illustrative commands
- `fwc status github --by-node`
- `fwc restart github --node desktop`
- `fwc update github --cohort laptops --canary 10%`
- `fwc wait github --cohort laptops --until converged`

## Scope
- node-scoped and cohort-scoped status, enable/disable, start/stop/restart, update, and pin/unpin flows
- clear desired-vs-observed reporting for partially converged rollouts or node-specific failures
- safe bulk semantics that make scope obvious before mutation happens
- wait/watch surfaces that can explain which nodes are still converging and why

## Deliverables
- node/cohort lifecycle command contract
- rollout and convergence vocabulary shared by TOON and JSON modes
- tests for node-specific failure, partial convergence, and canary-style rollout cases

## Acceptance criteria
- agents can safely change runtime state across a mesh without losing track of scope or convergence
- node- and cohort-level lifecycle work is no longer forced through one-machine assumptions
acceptance_criteria:
1. Node- and cohort-scoped lifecycle/update/pin/wait/watch flows make mutation scope explicit before execution and report desired-versus-observed convergence clearly.
2. Partial convergence, canary rollout, and node-specific failure states stay visible enough for safe follow-up actions and handoff.
3. Mesh-scoped lifecycle work layers on the existing lifecycle model instead of inventing parallel state semantics.
4. Unit, integration, and logged E2E coverage are required for node-specific failure, partial convergence, canary rollout, and convergence-wait cases.
notes: This should layer cleanly on existing lifecycle and rollout work rather than inventing a parallel system. The missing value is mesh scope: which nodes or cohorts are targeted, which are converged, which are failing, and how that state stays legible for agents.

title: [CUAL-Q.4] Mirror-aware install and offline availability surfaces for connector work
description:
## Goal
Expose mirrored-install sources, offline readiness, and availability implications so install and invoke decisions stay aligned with the mesh-native/offline-capable architecture promised by the project docs.

## Illustrative commands
- `fwc mesh availability github`
- `fwc install github --prefer mirror`
- `fwc mesh explain-availability github --zone z:work`
- `fwc mesh repair-hints github`

## Scope

title: [CUAL-B.1] Cross-connector semantic operation search engine
description:
## Goal
Add 'fwc search' that finds operations across ALL connectors by natural language intent, keywords, or capability patterns.

## Commands
- fwc search 'send a message to my team'         # NL intent
- fwc search 'create issue' --connector github    # Scoped search
- fwc search --capability write --risk low        # Faceted search
- fwc search 'file upload' --format json          # Machine output

## How It Works
1. Build a search index from all connector introspections at startup (or lazily on first search)
2. Index fields: operation ID, summary, description, ai_hints.when_to_use, capability, risk_level, safety_tier, connector categories
3. Score matches using: exact ID match (highest), keyword match in summary/description, semantic similarity via ai_hints.when_to_use, capability family match, category match
4. Return ranked results with: connector ID, operation ID, match reason, risk level, one-line summary

## Faceted Filters
- --capability <pattern>: filter by capability family (e.g. 'write', 'read', 'admin')
- --risk <level>: filter by max risk (low, medium, high)
- --safety <tier>: filter by max safety tier
- --archetype <type>: filter by connector archetype (operational, streaming, etc.)
- --category <cat>: filter by connector category (messaging, productivity, etc.)
- --idempotent: only show idempotent (safe to retry) operations

## Why Agents Need This
An agent with a goal ('notify the team about a deployment') needs to find the right operation across 85+ connectors, 500+ operations. Linear scan is prohibitively expensive in tokens. Faceted search lets agents narrow to exactly the right tool in one command.

## Deliverables
- Search index builder from connector introspections
- Scoring/ranking algorithm with configurable weights
- fwc search command with all filter flags
- TOON output (compact table) and JSON output
- Tests: keyword, NL intent, faceted, scoped, and no-match scenarios

comments.author: Jeff Emanuel
comments.text: IMPLEMENTATION NOTE: The search index should be built lazily on first search (not at startup, to avoid penalizing non-search commands). Use a simple TF-IDF or BM25 scoring algorithm — no need for embedding-based semantic search at this stage. The ai_hints.when_to_use field is the highest-value search target because it's written specifically for AI consumption. Consider weighting: when_to_use (3x), summary (2x), description (1x), operation ID (1x for exact match). The index can be a simple in-memory HashMap since we're searching ~500 operations, not millions.

title: [CUAL-B.2] Context-aware operation suggestions and what-can-I-do queries
description:
## Goal
Add 'fwc what-can-i-do' (or 'fwc suggest') that shows relevant operations based on current context: configured connectors, recent operations, zone, and stated goal.

## Commands
- fwc suggest                              # What can I do with my configured connectors?
- fwc suggest --goal 'manage my tasks'     # Goal-directed suggestions
- fwc suggest --after github.list_issues   # What commonly follows this operation?
- fwc suggest --connector slack            # What can I do with Slack specifically?
- fwc suggest --unused                     # Operations I haven't used yet

## How It Works
1. Survey all configured and healthy connectors
2. For goal-directed: use search engine (B.1) to find matching operations
3. For --after: use ai_hints.related fields to suggest next steps
4. For general: show categorized overview grouped by action family (read, write, manage, monitor)
5. Rank by: relevance to goal, safety (safe first), frequency of use, connector health

## Why Agents Need This
Agents often know WHAT they want to accomplish but not WHICH connector or operation to use. This is the 'exploration' mode that turns fwc from a tool-you-must-already-know into a tool-that-teaches-you.

## Deliverables
- Suggestion engine using search index + operation graph (related operations)
- fwc suggest command with all flags
- Grouped output by action family
- Tests for goal-directed, follow-up, and general suggestions

title: [CUAL-B.3] Smart connector auto-routing for ambiguous intents
description:
## Goal
When multiple connectors can fulfill an intent, automatically rank and suggest the best option based on context: connector health, zone authorization, rate limit headroom, recent success rate, and user preference history.

## Background
Many operations exist across multiple connectors: 'send a message' works via Slack, Discord, Telegram, etc. 'Create an issue' works via GitHub, Jira, Linear, etc. When an agent searches or invokes by intent, it needs intelligent routing.

## Routing Signals (Priority Order)
1. Zone authorization (must be allowed)
2. Connector health (must be healthy or degraded, not error)
3. Rate limit headroom (prefer connectors with more quota remaining)
4. Historical success rate (prefer connectors that succeed more often)
5. User/agent preference history (learned from past choices)
6. Safety tier (prefer lower risk for equivalent operations)
7. Latency (prefer faster connectors)

## Integration Points
- Used by fwc search to annotate results with 'recommended' flag
- Used by intent compiler (39v14) to select default connector
- Used by pipeline engine (Track F) to choose connectors in recipes

## Deliverables
- Routing score calculator with configurable signal weights
- Preference history store (simple file-based)
- Integration with search and intent compiler
- Tests: multi-connector scenarios, degraded routing, preference learning

title: [CUAL-C.1] Keychain-backed credential store with CRUD commands
description:
## Goal
Add 'fwc auth' command family for managing connector credentials: add, list, remove, and update credentials stored securely in the OS keychain.

## Commands
- fwc auth add github --token ghp_xxxx              # Store a token
- fwc auth add twilio --account-sid AC... --auth-token xx  # Multi-field auth
- fwc auth add slack --credential-id cred_xxx        # Secretless reference
- fwc auth list                                       # Show all stored credentials (redacted)
- fwc auth list --json                                # Machine-readable
- fwc auth remove github                              # Remove stored credential
- fwc auth show github                                # Show credential details (redacted)

## Storage Backend
1. Primary: OS keychain (macOS Keychain, Linux secret-service, Windows Credential Manager) via keyring crate
2. Fallback: encrypted file in ~/.fwc/credentials.enc (ChaCha20-Poly1305, key derived from machine identity)
3. Never: plaintext files, environment variables as primary store

## Security Invariants
- Credentials never appear in process arguments (use stdin or file for sensitive values)
- 'fwc auth list' always redacts actual secret values
- Credentials never appear in logs, traces, or error messages
- 'fwc auth show' displays metadata (connector, auth type, created_at, last_used) but NOT the secret

## Integration
- fwc invoke automatically looks up credentials from store (no --token flag needed)
- fwc auth add auto-detects auth type from connector manifest
- Supports both direct credentials and CredentialId references for secretless mode

## Deliverables
- crates/fwc/src/auth/store.rs with keychain and file backends
- fwc auth subcommand (add, list, show, remove, update)
- Redaction middleware for all credential display
- Tests: add/list/remove lifecycle, redaction verification, fallback to file backend

title: [CUAL-C.2] Auth test, verify, and health commands per connector
description:
## Goal
Add 'fwc auth test' that verifies stored credentials work by performing a lightweight probe against each connector's API.

## Commands
- fwc auth test github                # Test GitHub credentials
- fwc auth test --all                 # Test all stored credentials
- fwc auth test --all --json          # Machine-readable results

## How It Works
1. Look up stored credential for the connector
2. Call connector's handle_health() which performs a lightweight API call (e.g., GET /user for GitHub)
3. Report: auth_valid (bool), connector_healthy (bool), latency_ms, expiry_info (if token has expiry)
4. For OAuth connectors: check token refresh eligibility

## Output
TOON default:
  github     ok   12ms  token valid, no expiry
  slack      ok   45ms  token valid, expires in 3d
  twilio     FAIL 0ms   401 Unauthorized - check auth_token

## Why Agents Need This
Before starting a multi-step workflow, agents should verify all required connectors are authenticated. One failed auth mid-pipeline wastes all prior work. 'fwc auth test --all' is the preflight check.

## Deliverables
- fwc auth test command
- Per-connector health probe via handle_health()
- Token expiry detection where available
- Structured error output with fix suggestions

title: [CUAL-C.4] Secretless credential injection end-to-end plumbing
description:
## Goal
Complete the end-to-end secretless credential injection flow: agents configure connectors with a CredentialId instead of raw secrets, and the egress proxy injects actual credentials at the network boundary.

## Background
FCP spec describes secretless connectors where credentials never enter the connector process. Instead:
1. Agent stores a CredentialId reference: fwc auth add github --credential-id cred_github_work
2. Connector sends requests with X-FCP-Credential-ID header instead of Authorization
3. Egress proxy (fcp-host) intercepts, looks up the real credential, injects it into the outgoing request
4. Connector never sees the raw secret

## Current State
- Connector code already supports CredentialId auth mode (GitHubAuth::CredentialId, TwilioAuth::CredentialId, etc.)
- Missing: egress proxy implementation, credential store on the proxy side, fwc integration

## Deliverables
- Credential store for the egress proxy (host-side)
- X-FCP-Credential-ID injection middleware in fcp-host
- fwc auth add --credential-id flow
- fwc auth map: link a CredentialId to an actual secret (admin-only, proxy-side)
- E2E test: agent configures with CredentialId, invoke succeeds via proxy injection

This track adds: append-only operation audit log, replay-from-history, idempotent undo for reversible operations, and result diffing.

1. Operation history, replay, undo, and diff flows are built on real operation receipts, idempotency semantics, and explicit reversibility boundaries rather than reconstructed guesses.
2. Replay and undo surfaces preserve approval, auth, and zone constraints, and they clearly distinguish safe re-run, safe compare, and truly irreversible actions.
3. Unit, integration, and transcript-style E2E coverage with detailed logging are required for history inspection, replay overrides, undo denial, and result comparison.

title: [CUAL-D.1] Append-only operation audit log with structured history
description:
## Goal
Record every fwc operation invocation in a structured, append-only local audit log that agents can query for history, debugging, and replay.

## Log Entry Structure
{
  entry_id: uuid,
  timestamp: ISO8601,
  connector_id: 'fcp.github',
  operation_id: 'github.create_issue',
  zone: 'z:work',
  input_hash: blake3(input),    // NOT the full input (may contain secrets)
  input_summary: 'owner=octocat repo=hello-world title=Bug report',
  output_hash: blake3(output),
  output_summary: 'issue #43 created',
  status: 'success' | 'error' | 'timeout' | 'rate_limited' | 'denied',
  latency_ms: 234,
  error_code: null | 'FCP_ERR_RATE_LIMITED',
  idempotency_key: null | 'idem-xxx',
  agent_session: null | 'SunnyMoose-session-42',
  capability_token_hash: blake3(token),
}

## Commands
- fwc history                             # Show recent operations (last 20)
- fwc history --connector github          # Filter by connector
- fwc history --status error              # Filter by status
- fwc history --since 1h                  # Time range
- fwc history --json                      # Machine-readable
- fwc history <entry_id>                  # Show full details of one entry

## Storage
- Append-only JSONL file at ~/.fwc/history.jsonl
- Automatic rotation at 10MB (history.jsonl.1, .2, etc.)
- Never store raw input/output (only hashes and summaries) for security

## Why Agents Need This
- Debug failed operations: what exactly was sent and when?
- Avoid duplicate work: did I already create this issue?
- Replay: re-execute a successful operation with same/modified inputs
- Accountability: which agent did what and when?

## Deliverables
- History logger middleware that wraps every invoke/simulate call
- History query engine with filters
- fwc history command
- Rotation and cleanup logic
- Tests: log, query, rotate, filter
close_reason: HistoryEntry with entry_id, timestamps, input/output hashes, OpStatus, content_hash, 10MB rotation. history.rs 800+ lines.

REVISED POLICY: Store encrypted inputs in a separate sidecar file (history_data.enc), keyed by entry_id, with configurable TTL (default 7 days). The main history.jsonl keeps only hashes and summaries (for quick scanning). Decryption requires the same machine identity key used by credential_store. This enables replay (D.2) and diff (D.4) while maintaining security.

title: [CUAL-D.2] Operation replay from history with input override
description:
## Goal
Add 'fwc replay' that re-executes a previous operation from the audit log, optionally with modified inputs.

## Commands
- fwc replay <entry_id>                          # Exact replay
- fwc replay <entry_id> --override title='New title'  # Replay with modifications
- fwc replay --last                               # Replay last operation
- fwc replay --last-of github.create_issue        # Replay last of specific operation
- fwc replay <entry_id> --dry-run                 # Show what would be replayed

## How It Works
1. Look up entry in audit log
2. Reconstruct full input (requires storing encrypted input alongside hash, or prompting for re-entry)
3. Apply any --override modifications
4. Show preview and require confirmation for risky/dangerous operations
5. Execute via normal invoke path (includes auth, validation, capability check)
6. Log new operation in history with reference to original entry_id

## Security Considerations
- Full inputs are stored encrypted in a separate replay store (not in the JSONL log)
- Replay store entries expire after configurable TTL (default 7 days)
- Replaying dangerous operations still requires approval
- Capability tokens are re-generated (not reused from original)

## Deliverables
- Encrypted replay store for operation inputs
- fwc replay command
- Input override/merge logic
- Tests: replay, override, dry-run, approval gating

title: [CUAL-D.3] Idempotent undo for reversible operations
description:
## Goal
Add 'fwc undo' that reverses a previous operation where the operation type supports it (e.g., create -> delete, enable -> disable).

## Background
Some operations have natural inverses:
- github.create_issue -> github.close_issue (or delete)
- slack.send_message -> slack.delete_message
- todoist.create_task -> todoist.delete_task
- kubernetes.create_pod -> kubernetes.delete_pod
- connector.enable -> connector.disable

## How It Works
1. Look up operation in history
2. Check if operation has a declared inverse in manifest (new manifest field: inverse_operation)
3. If inverse exists: construct inverse input from original output (e.g., use created issue ID)
4. If no declared inverse: suggest manual reversal steps
5. Show preview and require confirmation
6. Execute inverse operation
7. Log undo in history with reference to original

## Manifest Extension
[provides.operations.'github.create_issue']
inverse_operation = 'github.delete_issue'
inverse_input_mapping = { 'owner' = '$.input.owner', 'repo' = '$.input.repo', 'issue_number' = '$.output.issue.number' }

## Deliverables
- Inverse operation lookup from manifest
- Input mapping from original output to inverse input
- fwc undo command
- Manual reversal guidance for non-reversible operations
- Tests: create-undo cycle, non-reversible handling

comments.text:
DESIGN CONSIDERATION: Inverse operation mapping should come from connector manifest metadata, NOT hardcoded tables. Add an 'inverse_of' field to OperationInfo.ai_hints that declares the reverse operation. For create->delete pairs, the undo implementation must extract the created resource ID from the original response and pass it to the delete operation. Some operations have no inverse (read operations, irreversible mutations like email.send). The 'fwc undo' command MUST clearly refuse non-reversible operations with an explanation rather than silently failing.

title: [CUAL-D.4] Operation result diffing and comparison
description:
## Goal
Add 'fwc diff' that compares two operation results to show what changed, useful for monitoring state changes and debugging.

## Commands
- fwc diff <entry_id_1> <entry_id_2>     # Compare two invocations

## Output
Shows structured diff of JSON outputs:
  github.list_issues (2026-03-09 14:00 vs 2026-03-09 15:00):
  + issues[3]: {number: 44, title: 'New bug', state: 'open'}
  ~ issues[0].labels: ['bug'] -> ['bug', 'priority']
  - issues[1]: {number: 41, title: 'Fixed issue'} (removed/closed)

## Why Agents Need This
- Monitor state changes: 'what changed in my GitHub issues since last check?'
- Verify side effects: 'did my create_issue actually add the expected issue?'
- Debug regressions: 'why is this connector returning different data now?'

## Deliverables

- fwc diff command
- Baseline save/load for periodic comparison
- TOON and JSON output modes
- Tests: identical, added, removed, modified, nested diff
